We split it explicitly into an encoder and a head, exactly as in Section 2. The average training loss falls each epoch, so the network is learning as expected. The interesting part comes next. After training, we throw away the head, keep the encoder, and use its 128 outputs as a new representation of every image. Then we give that representation to exactly the same linear probe as before. The ranking is now clear: | Representation | Numbers per image | Validation accuracy | |---|---|---| | Handcrafted features | 7 | 0.694 | | Raw pixels | 784 | 0.803 | | Learned by the MLP encoder | 128 | 0.868 | The learned representation uses about a sixth as many numbers as the raw pixels, yet the same simple classifier does better with it. The network has found features that make the classes easier to separate with a straight line, which is exactly what a good representation should do. Be precise about why the learned features won, because this is easy to overstate. The encoder had something the other two did not: it was trained on 40,000 additional labelled images. Representation learning does not create information from nothing. It moves the work of finding good features from a person to the training process, and that process needs data. 3.5 Why "a shift, not an elimination" It is tempting to say that deep learning makes feature engineering obsolete. It does not. Look back at what we still decided in this section: - We converted pixel values from 0–255 to 0–1 by dividing by 255. - We chose a network with one hidden layer of 128 units and a ReLU activation. - We decided how to split the data so the comparison was fair. In later notes, these human decisions become even more important: CNNs build in the assumption that nearby pixels belong together, and tokenisers decide how text is chopped into pieces before any learning happens. The accurate statement is that deep learning shifts much of the representation-building into the model, while people still design the conditions under which it is learned. Common mistake: concluding that learned features are "better" in general. They were better here, on this task, given 40,000 extra labelled examples. With very little data, or when an expert knows exactly what matters (for example, a physics formula), carefully designed features can still win. You saw a similar lesson in the gradient-boosting vs. neural-network comparison in Module 4. Check yourself. 1. The MLP encoder was trained on 40,000 labelled images, but the linear probe on top of it used only the 10,000 probe images. Why would it be wrong to train the encoder on the 10,000 validation images as well? Worked answer The validation images are supposed to be unseen, so that the accuracy we measure on them tells us how the method performs on new data. If the encoder had trained on them, it could have learned features tuned to those specific images, and the validation accuracy would be optimistic. This is data leakage: information from the evaluation set leaking into training.

title: How Networks Build Hierarchical Representations
text: We now know that a learned representation can beat raw pixels. The natural next question is: what did the network actually learn? Opening the box also leads us to one of the most important ideas in deep learning, the idea of a hierarchy of features. 4.1 Looking inside one layer Each of the 128 hidden units in our encoder computes a weighted sum of all 784 pixels and then applies ReLU (which outputs the sum if it is positive and 0 otherwise). So a unit "switches on", meaning it outputs a value above zero, when an image matches the pattern in its weights. We can investigate each unit in two ways: look at its weights directly, and find the images that switch it on most strongly. The cell below records every unit's output for every validation image and summarises what each unit responds to. A few things stand out. First, 14 of the 128 units never switch on for any validation image. These units are inactive on this validation sample: their pre-activation is non-positive for every example we checked, so ReLU outputs 0. This alone does not prove they are dead for every possible input. This is a known side effect of ReLU, and it means our encoder is really using 114 units, not 128. Second, many units have become detectors for particular kinds of clothing, even though nobody told them to. Unit 125 is the clearest: 98% of the 50 images that switch it on most are bags. Across all 114 live units, the typical (median) unit has 78% of its top-50 images from a single class, and 36 units reach at least 90%. Third, the eight units we printed are the eight with the highest average output, and they are less specialised than typical (46% to 82%). That makes sense: units that switch on strongly for many images tend to respond to anything large and bright, such as tops, pullovers and coats, rather than to one class. The figure below shows these eight units. The top row shows each unit's 784 weights arranged back into a 28×28 grid: red pixels push the unit on, blue pixels push it off. The bottom row is the average of the 50 images that switch that unit on most. The weight maps are noisy, but the averaged images make the pattern clear: each unit has become tuned to a whole-garment outline, such as a long-sleeved shape, a T-shirt shape or a bag with a handle. 4.2 How deeper networks build a hierarchy Our encoder has only one layer, so each unit has to go straight from individual pixels to something like "bag-shaped". That is a big leap, and it is why the weight maps look like blurry whole-object templates. A template like that is fragile: shift the bag a few pixels to the left and the template no longer lines up. Deeper networks avoid this by building understanding in stages, each stage reusing the features from the stage before: - Early layers detect simple, local patterns: edges (places where brightness changes sharply) and small spots. - Middle layers combine edges into textures and parts: a curve, a corner, a strap, a sole. - Later layers combine parts into whole objects: "boot" is a sole, plus a tall shaft, plus a heel. This layered structure is called a hierarchical representation. It is powerful because simple features can be reused: the same edge detector helps recognise a boot, a bag and a dress, so the network does not need to learn a separate template for every object in every position. Language works the same way: characters combine into words, words into phrases, phrases into meaning. Figure 5.1.3. A conceptual hierarchy from local edges to larger combinations. These are explanatory illustrations, not measured filters from the notebook experiment. You will see this hierarchy directly in Note 5.2, where a convolutional network learns edge detectors in its first layer without being told to. Key terms - Hidden unit (neuron): one output of a hidden layer; a weighted sum of its inputs passed through an activation function. - Dead unit: a ReLU unit whose output is 0 for every input, so it never contributes or learns. - Hierarchical representation: a representation built in stages, where each layer combines the simpler features of the layer before it. Check yourself. 1. Our one-layer encoder learned whole-garment templates. Give one reason why a template like this might fail if the same bag appeared slightly smaller or shifted to one side of the image. Worked answer The template lines up with particular pixel positions. If the bag is smaller or shifted, its outline falls on different pixels, so the weighted sum changes and the unit may not switch on. A hierarchical network that detects edges and parts wherever they appear is much less sensitive to this.

title: Why Representation Quality Matters for Downstream Tasks
text: So far we have compared representations when the downstream classifier had plenty of labelled data: 10,000 examples. In real projects, labelled data is often the scarcest resource. Labels cost money, time and expert attention. So the most practical question about a representation is: how much labelled data does it save you? To find out, we repeat the linear-probe experiment while giving the classifier fewer and fewer labelled examples: 20, 100, 500, 2,000 and 10,000. With very small samples the result depends heavily on which images happen to be chosen, so for every size below 10,000 we draw 5 different random samples and average the results. We also record the gap between the best and worst of the 5 draws, to see how noisy each estimate is. Read the table row by row, then column by column. - With only 20 labelled examples (about two per class), the learned representation reaches 0.562, against 0.414 for raw pixels and 0.404 for handcrafted features. But look at the spread row: the 5 draws differ by up to 0.161 to 0.199. With so few examples, a single lucky or unlucky draw moves the result a lot, which is exactly why we averaged. - With 100 labelled examples, the learned representation reaches 0.794. Raw pixels need 2,000 labelled examples to reach the same accuracy (0.794). In other words, on this task the learned representation does the job with about one twentieth of the downstream labels, after the encoder used its separate 40,000 labelled examples. - With 10,000 examples, the handcrafted features level off at 0.694. Adding more labels hardly helps, because seven numbers simply cannot describe the differences between a shirt and a pullover. The representation, not the amount of data, has become the limit. The plot shows the same results. The grey dashed line is chance level. This is the practical heart of representation learning. A good representation: 1. reaches higher accuracy with the same simple classifier; 2. needs far fewer labels to get there; 3. can be reused: we trained the encoder once, and could now attach many different heads to it for different tasks. The third point is the foundation of modern AI engineering. In Module 7 you will use encoders that were trained on billions of examples, and attach your own small head, which is the same experiment as this one at a vastly larger scale. Common mistake: trusting a single small-sample result. With 20 labelled examples, the accuracy of one draw varied by close to 0.2 depending on which images were picked. Whenever your training set is small, repeat the experiment with different samples and report the average and the spread. Check yourself. 1. The handcrafted curve is almost flat between 2,000 and 10,000 labelled examples. What does that tell you about where its errors are coming from? Worked answer The errors are no longer caused by a lack of labelled examples; they are caused by the representation itself. Seven numbers cannot capture the differences between some classes (for example, shirt vs. pullover), so no amount of extra labels lets the classifier separate them. The representation has become the bottleneck.

title: The Big Picture: From Pixels to Visual Understanding
text: Think about how you would describe the way you recognise a sneaker. You don't examine each point of the photo separately. You notice edges where the shoe meets the background, the curve of the sole, the stripes on the side, the laces. Those local details are found wherever they appear in the picture, and then combined into the overall shape that says "sneaker". A CNN is built to work in the same spirit. It has three big ideas: 1. Look locally. Instead of connecting every pixel to every unit, a CNN slides a small window, typically 3×3 pixels, across the image and asks the same question at every position: "Is my pattern here?" The small window of weights is called a filter (or kernel). 2. Reuse the same detector everywhere. The filter's weights are the same at every position. A vertical-edge detector that works in the top-left corner also works in the bottom-right. This is called weight sharing. 3. Build up in stages. The output of one layer of filters, a set of feature maps showing where each pattern was found, becomes the input to the next layer. Early layers find simple patterns such as edges; later layers combine them into parts and shapes. Every so often, a pooling layer shrinks the maps so that later layers see a wider area. At the end, a small fully connected head, exactly the kind of head you met in Note 5.1, turns the final feature maps into a prediction. Figure 5.2.1. The exact lesson architecture: 1×28×28 → 16×28×28 → 16×14×14 → 32×14×14 → 32×7×7 → 1,568 features → a classifier. Batch dimension is omitted; feature-map appearance is schematic. Keep this picture in mind. Sections 2 and 3 explain the input and the problem CNNs solve; Sections 4 to 7 examine each part; Sections 8 and 9 put the whole thing to work.

title: Representing Images as Tensors
text: Before any network can process an image, the image has to be stored as a tensor: a multi-dimensional array of numbers, which you have used throughout the course. For images, the shape of that tensor follows a convention that you need to know well, because most bugs in vision code are shape bugs. Let's load Fashion-MNIST again. This time we also download its separate test set: 10,000 images that we will touch only once, at the very end of the note. The raw arrays have shape (60000, 28, 28) and (10000, 28, 28): number of images, height, width. PyTorch's convolution layers expect one more dimension, the number of channels. A channel is one "layer" of values per pixel. A greyscale image has 1 channel (brightness). A colour image has 3 channels (red, green and blue), so every pixel is described by three numbers. PyTorch's standard layout for a batch of images is therefore: The cell below adds the channel dimension with unsqueeze(1), scales the values from 0–255 to 0–1, and splits the 60,000 training images into 50,000 for training and 10,000 for validation. A single image is now [1, 28, 28]: 1 channel, 28 rows, 28 columns. The training set is [50000, 1, 28, 28]. Values run from 0.0 to 1.0, stored as 32-bit floats, which is what PyTorch layers expect. During training we feed the network batches (small groups of images processed together), so a batch of 64 images has shape [64, 1, 28, 28]. A colour image of 32×32 pixels would be [3, 32, 32]. Notice the last line. PyTorch puts channels first (C, H, W), but most image libraries, including matplotlib, put channels last (H, W, C). permute(1, 2, 0) reorders the dimensions, turning [3, 32, 32] into [32, 32, 3]. Common mistake: passing a [3, H, W] tensor straight to plt.imshow, or passing an [H, W, 3] image straight into a PyTorch convolution. The first gives an error or a garbled picture; the second makes PyTorch treat the image's height as if it were the number of channels. Whenever an image looks wrong or a layer complains about channels, print .shape first. Key terms - Channel: one value per pixel of a particular kind, such as brightness, or the red, green or blue component. Greyscale images have 1 channel; colour images have 3. - Channels-first / channels-last: the order of dimensions. PyTorch uses (N, C, H, W); matplotlib and many image libraries use (H, W, C). - Batch: a group of examples processed together; it adds a leading dimension N. Check yourself. 1. A batch of 16 colour photos, each 224 pixels tall and 224 pixels wide, is stored for PyTorch. What is its shape? Worked answer (16, 3, 224, 224): 16 images, 3 colour channels, 224 rows, 224 columns.

title: Flattening Images: Preserved Values, Lost Explicit 2D Layout
text: The MLP from Note 5.1 begins with nn.Flatten(), which turns each [1, 28, 28] image into a list of 784 numbers. That seems harmless. Let's see what it does to neighbouring pixels. The pixel at row 10, column 10 lands at position 290. Its right-hand neighbour is at 291, but its equally close neighbour below is at 318. Flattening removes the explicit 2D layout, not the underlying pixel information. Every value remains in a fixed order. If we know the original dimensions, we can reshape the vector and reconstruct the image exactly. The disadvantage appears when this vector enters a dense layer. That layer gives each input position its own weights. It does not explicitly treat nearby pixels as neighbours or reuse a local detector across positions. It can learn spatial patterns, but must discover useful relationships from data, often with more parameters. A CNN builds locality and weight sharing into its architecture. We can investigate this difference by applying one fixed random permutation of the pixel positions to every image. The experiment changes which pixels appear adjacent while preserving all values and their consistent identities: physical pixel positions still map to fixed vector indices. The shuffled images are unrecognisable to us. But nothing has been lost from the MLP's point of view. Every image still contains exactly the same 784 values, just in a consistently different order, and the dense architecture has no built-in preference for the original image neighbourhoods. To test this, we need a model and a training loop. The MLP below is the same shape as in Note 5.1. We also write two helper functions that we will reuse throughout this note: - evaluate returns the accuracy and the predictions. It switches the model to evaluation mode with model.eval() and turns off gradient tracking, then switches back. - train is the familiar training loop, with an optional list snapshots that stores a copy of the weights after every epoch, so that we can later pick the best epoch. Now we train two identical MLPs, with the same starting weights, for 2 epochs each: one on the original images, one on the shuffled images. The two accuracies are 0.8528 and 0.8527, essentially identical. But are they really the same, or is a small difference hiding behind the rounding? With a validation set of 10,000 images, one image is worth 0.0001 of accuracy, so the two models differ by a single image overall. A more careful check is the sign test. We ignore the images that both models get right or both get wrong (they tell us nothing about which model is better) and count the disagreements. If the two models were truly equally good, each disagreement would be a coin flip. The original-pixel MLP was correct on 90 examples where the shuffled one was wrong; the reverse happened on 89. The paired binomial test returns p = 1: these observations provide no evidence of an accuracy difference under its null hypothesis. This does not prove exact equivalence. A dense layer can accommodate a fixed pixel permutation by learning a correspondingly permuted set of input weights. The experiment illustrates its lack of a built-in spatial preference; it does not show that the model cannot learn spatial relationships. In Section 8 we compare this with a CNN's explicit local connections. Key terms - Spatial structure: the arrangement of pixels in two dimensions. - Permutation: a rearrangement of positions, applied consistently here. - Paired sign test: compare the cases on which exactly one classifier is correct, using a binomial test with probability 0.5 under equal accuracy. It concerns these fitted models on these evaluation examples, not variation across training seeds. Check yourself. 1. Why did we apply the same permutation to every image, instead of a different random shuffle for each one? Worked answer Using the same permutation keeps the task learnable and fair: a given pixel position still means the same thing in every image, just at a different place in the list. If each image were shuffled differently, the pixel values would carry no consistent positional meaning, and no model could learn much. That would not test whether the model uses spatial structure; it would just destroy the information. Visual walkthrough: Follow a grid into a vector. Watch the same values move in row order. Reshaping with the original dimensions recovers the image grid. These supplied numbers illustrate the calculation. The web app adds a paused, step-by-step animation of the same example.

title: Convolutional Neural Networks: The Complete Picture
text: We have seen the problem: a dense MLP does not build in local spatial connections. Here is the full CNN we will use in this note, before we examine its pieces. Read the comments on the right: they show the shape of the data after each layer, for a batch of N images. The two networks are almost the same size: 101,770 parameters for the MLP and 105,866 for the CNN. So any difference in how they behave is about how the parameters are arranged, not how many there are. The CNN is organised exactly as the encoder–head split from Note 5.1: - features (the encoder) contains two rounds of convolution → ReLU → pooling. Throughout this part, the data stays in the 2D shape (channels, height, width), so spatial structure is preserved. - head flattens the final feature maps and classifies them with two fully connected layers. By this point, the encoder has already turned "where is everything" into "which patterns are present", so the head combines learned local features; flattening itself still preserves every feature-map value. The best way to understand a network's shapes is to watch data flow through it. The cell below passes a dummy batch of 8 images through each layer and prints the shape after every step. Follow the numbers down the list: - Conv2d (first): 1 channel in, 16 out. The image stays 28×28, but we now have 16 feature maps per image, one for each filter. - MaxPool2d: height and width halve to 14×14; the number of channels does not change. - Conv2d (second): 16 channels in, 32 out, still 14×14. - MaxPool2d: down to 7×7. - Flatten: 32 × 7 × 7 = 1,568 numbers per image. - Linear layers: 1,568 → 64 → 10 class scores. Notice the trade the encoder makes as data flows through it: the maps get smaller (28 → 14 → 7) while the number of channels gets larger (1 → 16 → 32). The network gives up fine positional detail in exchange for a richer description of what is present. Every piece in this list is examined in the next three sections: the filters and feature maps produced by Conv2d (Section 5), the size changes caused by padding and pooling (Section 6), and why stacking layers builds hierarchical features (Section 7). Check yourself. 1. If we removed the second MaxPool2d, what would the shape after Flatten become? Worked answer The maps would stay at 32 channels × 14 × 14, so Flatten would produce 32 × 14 × 14 = 6,272 numbers per image. The first nn.Linear would then need in_features=6272, otherwise PyTorch raises a shape error.

title: Convolutional Filters and Feature Maps
text: The central operation of a CNN is convolution. The idea is simple: take a small grid of weights, the filter, place it over a patch of the image, multiply each weight by the pixel underneath it, and add everything up. That sum is one output value. Then slide the filter one step and repeat, until you have covered the whole image. The grid of outputs is a feature map. 5.1 A convolution you can check by hand Let's do this on a tiny 5×5 image, so that every number is visible. The image is dark (0) in its two left columns and bright (1) in its three right columns, so it contains one vertical edge. Our filter has −1 in its left column, 0 in the middle and +1 on the right. In words, the filter asks: "Is it brighter on my right than on my left?" Take the top-left output value. The filter covers rows 0–2 and columns 0–2 of the input. The left column of that patch is 0, 0, 0 (multiplied by −1 gives 0); the middle column is 0, 0, 0 (multiplied by 0 gives 0); the right column is 1, 1, 1 (multiplied by +1 gives 3). The total is 3. The filter has found an edge. Now take the top-right output value. The patch covers columns 2–4, which are all bright. The left column gives −3, the right column gives +3, and they cancel to 0. No edge there, so no response. Our hand calculation and PyTorch's F.conv2d agree exactly. Two facts about this output are worth noticing: - The 5×5 input produced a 3×3 output. A 3×3 filter only fits in 3 positions across a 5-wide image. We'll return to this in Section 6. - The filter's weights add up to zero. So on a perfectly uniform patch, whether all dark or all bright, it outputs 0. It responds only to change. That is what makes it an edge detector. A note on the name: strictly, what deep-learning libraries compute is called cross-correlation; mathematical convolution also flips the filter first. Because the filter's weights are learned anyway, the flip makes no practical difference, and everyone in deep learning simply calls it convolution. 5.2 Filters on a real image Now apply two classic hand-designed edge filters to the ankle boot. The first is a stronger version of the vertical-edge filter above; the second is the same filter turned on its side, which detects horizontal edges. Notice that we stack the two filters into one tensor of shape [2, 1, 3, 3] (2 filters, each looking at 1 input channel, each 3×3), and F.conv2d produces one feature map per filter. Each feature map is a picture of where the filter's pattern occurs. In the vertical-edge map, the left side of the boot is red (dark on the left, bright on the right) and its right side is blue (bright on the left, dark on the right). In the horizontal-edge map, the top edges and the sole light up instead. One filter, slid across the whole image, has produced a full map of one kind of feature. In a CNN, nobody designs these filters by hand. The first Conv2d layer of our network has 16 filters whose weights start random and are learned by backpropagation, just like the weights of any other layer. The network discovers which patterns are worth detecting. We will look at what it learns in Section 9. 5.3 Why sharing one filter everywhere is so efficient Because each filter is reused at every position, a convolution layer needs remarkably few parameters. Compare our first convolution layer with a fully connected layer that produces the same number of outputs: Our first convolution layer has 160 parameters: 16 filters × 9 weights, plus 16 biases. It produces 12,544 output values (16 maps of 28×28). A fully connected layer mapping the same 784 inputs to the same 12,544 outputs would need 9,847,040 parameters, 61,544 times as many. That saving comes from two assumptions built into convolution: - Locality: each output depends only on a small neighbourhood of the input, because nearby pixels matter most. - Weight sharing: the same pattern is worth detecting anywhere in the image. Assumptions like these are called an inductive bias: knowledge about the problem that is built into the architecture rather than learned from data. When the assumptions are true, as they are for images, the network learns faster from less data. When they are false, they can hurt. You will see both outcomes in Section 8. Key terms - Filter (kernel): a small grid of learnable weights that is slid across the input. - Convolution: sliding a filter over the input and, at each position, computing the sum of weights × inputs. - Feature map: the grid of outputs a filter produces; it shows where the filter's pattern appears. - Weight sharing: using the same filter weights at every position. - Inductive bias: an assumption about the problem built into a model's design. Check yourself. 1. A filter has the weights [[1, 1, 1], [1, 1, 1], [1, 1, 1]]. What does its feature map show, and would it be a good edge detector? Worked answer All the weights are positive and equal, so it adds up the brightness in each 3×3 patch. Its feature map is a slightly blurred copy of the image. It is not a good edge detector: its weights do not cancel out (its balance is 1), so it responds to brightness, not to change. Visual walkthrough: Slide one shared filter. Step through nine exact dot products. Notice which values change and which filter weights stay fixed. These supplied numbers illustrate the calculation. The web app adds a paused, step-by-step animation of the same example.

title: Stride, Padding, and Pooling
text: In Section 5.1 a 3×3 filter shrank a 5×5 image to 3×3. If every layer shrank the image like that, a deep network would quickly run out of image, and the pixels near the border would be used less than those in the middle. Three settings control what happens to the size of the data: padding, stride and pooling. 6.1 Padding and stride - Padding adds a border of zeros around the input before the filter is applied. With a 3×3 filter, adding one pixel of padding on every side (padding=1) keeps the output the same size as the input. That is why our CNN's convolutions keep 28×28 as 28×28. - Stride is how far the filter moves at each step. With stride=1 it visits every position; with stride=2 it skips every other position, roughly halving the output size. These combine into one formula for the output size along each dimension: The brackets ⌊ ⌋ mean "round down to a whole number". Let's check the formula against PyTorch for several settings on a 28×28 input: The formula and PyTorch agree in every case. Take the first line: (28 + 0 − 3) / 1 + 1 = 26. Without padding, a 3×3 filter loses one pixel on each side. Add padding=1 and the result is 28 again. With stride=2 as well, the output drops to 14. Common mistake: getting the input size of the first nn.Linear after Flatten wrong. It must equal channels × height × width of the last feature maps (here 32 × 7 × 7). If you change any padding, stride or pooling setting, recompute it with the formula, or simply pass a dummy batch through the encoder and print the shape, as we did in Section 4. 6.2 Pooling Pooling shrinks a feature map by summarising small blocks of it. A 2×2 pool with stride 2 splits the map into non-overlapping 2×2 blocks and replaces each block by one number: - Max pooling keeps the largest value: "was the pattern found anywhere in this block?" - Average pooling keeps the mean value: "how strongly, on average, was it found here?" Here is a 4×4 grid pooled both ways: The top-left block contains 1, 3, 4 and 6. Max pooling keeps 6; average pooling gives (1 + 3 + 4 + 6) / 4 = 3.5. The bottom-right block contains 9, 5, 3 and 7, which gives 9 and 6. Max pooling is the usual choice inside CNNs because of what it throws away. If an edge shifts by one pixel within a block, the maximum hardly changes. So the network becomes a little less sensitive to exactly where a pattern appears, which is usually what we want for recognising objects. Pooling also has no learnable parameters at all. Key terms - Padding: extra values (usually zeros) added around the input's border. - Stride: the step size of the filter as it slides. - Pooling: summarising small blocks of a feature map (by max or average) to make it smaller. Check yourself. 1. Use the formula to find the output size of a convolution with kernel size 7, stride 2 and padding 3, applied to a 224×224 image. Worked answer ⌊(224 + 2 × 3 − 7) / 2⌋ + 1 = ⌊223 / 2⌋ + 1 = 111 + 1 = 112. The output is 112×112.

title: Hierarchical Feature Learning: From Edges to Objects
text: A single 3×3 filter can only see 3×3 pixels. That is enough for an edge, but not for a sole, let alone a whole boot. So how does a CNN ever recognise large shapes? The answer is stacking. The second convolution layer does not look at pixels; it looks at the feature maps from the first layer. Each of its outputs covers a 3×3 block of those maps, and each of those values already summarised a 3×3 block of pixels. Pooling in between makes the reach grow faster still. The region of the original image that can influence one output value is called its receptive field. We can measure the receptive field directly. We pass an image through the encoder, pick the output value at the centre of the final map, and use backpropagation to ask: which input pixels have any effect on it? Pixels whose gradient is not zero are inside the receptive field. (For this measurement we use average pooling instead of max pooling, because max pooling passes the gradient only to the single winning pixel in each block, which would hide part of the window. The receptive field is the same size either way.) We also compute the same quantity with a simple formula: each layer adds (kernel size − 1) × (the combined stride of all earlier layers). Measured and calculated agree: the receptive field grows from 3×3 after the first convolution, to 4×4 after the first pool, to 8×8 after the second convolution, and to 10×10 after the second pool. In a 28×28 image, a 10×10 window is large enough to cover a whole heel, a strap or the toe of a shoe. This growth is the mechanism behind hierarchical feature learning: - First layer, small receptive field: can only detect simple local patterns, such as edges, spots and changes of brightness. - Second layer, larger receptive field: combines several edge maps, so it can detect corners, curves and textures: the parts of an object. - Deeper layers in larger networks: keep combining, so later units can respond to whole objects. The networks that classify ordinary photos have dozens of layers and receptive fields covering most of the image. Figure 5.2.2. For this model, receptive-field widths grow from 3 after conv1 to 4 after pool1, 8 after conv2, and 10 after pool2. This describes theoretical input coverage, not a measured activation map. Key terms - Receptive field: the region of the input image that can affect one particular output value. - Hierarchical features: features organised in levels, with each level combining the simpler features of the level below. Check yourself. 1. Our network's receptive field after the second pool is 10×10, yet the network classifies whole 28×28 garments. How can the head still use information from the whole image? Worked answer The head is fully connected: after flattening, every one of the 1,568 values (covering all 7×7 positions of all 32 maps) feeds into the head. Each value describes a different 10×10 region, and together those regions cover the whole image, so the head can combine evidence from every part of the garment.

title: CNNs in Practice with PyTorch
text: We have now seen every part of the CNN. Let's train the whole thing and test whether its built-in assumptions pay off. 8.1 Training and choosing the epoch on validation We train for 5 epochs with the Adam optimizer and a learning rate of 0.001, using the train function from Section 3. After each epoch we record the training loss and the validation accuracy, and keep a snapshot of the weights. At the end, we pick the epoch with the best validation accuracy. We never use the test set to make this choice; it stays untouched until the final evaluation. The training loss falls every epoch, from 0.678 to 0.283, and validation accuracy rises every epoch, from 0.8392 to 0.8929. The best epoch on validation is therefore the last one, epoch 5, and those are the weights we keep. The plot shows both curves. Validation accuracy is still rising at epoch 5, so we have not trained to the point of overfitting; a few more epochs would probably help a little. We stop here to keep the notebook quick to run. 8.2 Does the CNN really use spatial structure? In Section 3, the MLP did just as well on shuffled pixels as on real ones. If the CNN truly relies on neighbourhoods, it should lose accuracy when the pixels are shuffled, because its filters will be looking at "neighbours" that are not really neighbours. To keep the comparison fair, we train a fresh CNN on shuffled images for 2 epochs, with the same starting weights, and compare it with our main CNN's snapshot after the same 2 epochs. This time the difference is large. After 2 epochs, the CNN reaches 0.8643 on real images but only 0.8341 on shuffled ones. The paired sign test gives strong evidence of a difference for these fitted models: the real-image CNN was right on 557 images that the shuffled one got wrong, against only 255 the other way round, with a p-value of 1.14e-26. Such an imbalance is very unlikely under the equal-accuracy null; repeat training seeds to assess training variability too. Notice also that the CNN on shuffled pixels (0.8341) did worse than the MLP on shuffled pixels (0.8527). When the CNN's built-in assumption, that neighbouring pixels belong together, is false, it becomes a handicap. This is the inductive bias from Section 5.3 in action. It helps when it matches reality and hurts when it does not. 8.3 Final evaluation on the test set Now, once and only once, we evaluate the chosen model on the 10,000 test images. The test accuracy is 0.8903, very close to the final validation accuracy of 0.8929. That closeness is reassuring: it suggests we did not accidentally tune our choices to the validation set. Out of 10,000 test images, 1,097 are misclassified. The per-class accuracies are far from equal. Bags (0.970), sneakers (0.964), trousers and sandals (0.959 each) are easy. Shirts (0.694) and pullovers (0.767) are hard. To see why, let's find the most common mistakes. The four most common mistakes are all between upper-body garments: 121 pullovers predicted as coats, 119 shirts predicted as T-shirts, and 105 each of T-shirts predicted as shirts and shirts predicted as coats. At 28×28 greyscale, these items have nearly the same outline, and the details that separate them (buttons, collars, fabric texture) occupy only a few pixels. These are mistakes that a person squinting at the same tiny images would also make. Common mistake: reporting only the overall accuracy. An accuracy of 0.8903 hides the fact that the model is right on only 0.694 of shirts. Always look at per-class results and the most common confusions; they tell you where the model needs to improve and whether its errors are acceptable for your application. Check yourself. 1. Why did we pick the best epoch using the validation set rather than the test set, given that the test set is also data the model never trained on? Worked answer Choosing the epoch is a decision based on data. If we made that decision using the test set, the test score would no longer be an honest estimate of performance on new data, because we would have picked the epoch that happened to suit those particular test images. The validation set exists to absorb those decisions; the test set is kept for one final, unbiased measurement.

title: Visualising Learned Filters and Feature Maps
text: In Section 5, we used filters designed by hand. Our trained CNN designed its own. Let's open it up and look. 9.1 The learned filters Each of the 16 filters in the first convolution layer is a 3×3 grid of weights. Looking at 3×3 pictures and deciding which ones "look like edges" is very subjective, so we first measure something objective. Recall from Section 5.1 that an edge detector's weights add up to roughly zero, so that it ignores uniform brightness and responds only to change. We define a filter's balance as: A balance near 0 means the positive and negative weights cancel, so the filter responds to change (edge-like). A balance near 1 means the weights all have the same sign, so the filter responds to overall brightness or darkness. To know whether training changed anything, we compare the learned filters with the same filters at their random starting values. Training has pushed many filters towards balanced, contrast-sensitive weights. Balance alone does not prove that a filter detects a particular edge orientation. The median balance fell from 0.30 at the random start to 0.06 after training, and 9 of the 16 learned filters have a balance below 0.2. A few filters went the other way: filter 15 has a balance of 1.00 and filter 3 has 0.93, meaning their weights all share one sign. These respond to brightness or darkness itself rather than to edges. Here are all 16 filters, labelled with their balance: The low-balance filters contain both strong red and strong blue weights, often on opposite sides or corners of the grid, at various angles. That is the signature of an edge or contrast detector. They are rougher and less symmetric than the hand-designed filters of Section 5.2, which is typical of learned filters, but the network has arrived at the same kind of tool purely from the training signal. Filters 3 and 15, by contrast, are almost entirely one colour. 9.2 The feature maps Filters are easier to understand by what they produce. Let's pass the ankle boot through the trained network and look at the feature maps after each convolution layer (after ReLU, which sets negative values to 0). The first-layer maps (top row, 28×28) are easy to read. Some light up along particular edges of the boot, such as the sole or the front. Others light up across the whole boot or, like map 3, across the background, which matches filter 3's same-sign weights. Each map is a different "view" of the same image. The second-layer maps (bottom row, 14×14) are coarser and harder to interpret, which is normal: each value now combines 16 first-layer maps across an 8×8 window of the original image. They respond to combinations, such as a particular edge in a particular region. The numbers back this up. In the first layer, 0.38 of the values are zero; in the second layer, 0.50 are. On this one image, the deeper features are more sparse: each one switches on for fewer locations, because it responds to a more specific combination of patterns. Common mistake: over-reading feature-map pictures. A map that "looks like" it detects heels may be responding to something else entirely, such as overall brightness in that region. Pictures are a starting point for questions, not proof; back them up with measurements, as we did with the balance score and the zero fractions. Check yourself. 1. Filter 15 has a balance of 1.00. Would you expect its feature map for the boot to highlight edges, or something else? Why? Worked answer Something else. With a balance of 1.00, its weights all share one sign, so on a uniform patch they do not cancel. It responds to overall brightness (if the weights are positive) or darkness (if they are negative) across each patch, so its map looks like a filled-in silhouette or its inverse, rather than a set of outlines.

title: The Big Picture: From Text to Numerical Representations
text: Here is the whole journey a piece of text takes before a network can learn from it. Every later section explains one step of it. 1. Raw text: "This movie wasn't GOOD. It was great!" 2. Tokenisation: split the text into units called tokens, here words: this, movie, wasn't, good, it, was, great. 3. Token IDs: look each token up in a fixed vocabulary (a numbered list of all known tokens) and replace it with its number. 4. Embeddings: replace each ID with a learned vector, for example 32 numbers per word. Similar words should get similar vectors. 5. Model: combine the vectors and make a prediction, for example "positive review". Figure 5.3.1. Token IDs are arbitrary vocabulary indices. An embedding lookup turns each index into a learned vector. The displayed IDs are an example vocabulary, not the recorded IDs of this experiment. The first three steps are fixed preprocessing. Step 4 is where the learning happens, and it is the focus of this note. We will work with IMDb movie reviews: 50,000 reviews from the Internet Movie Database, each labelled positive or negative. It is one of the most widely used datasets for learning about text, and we will return to it in Modules 7 and 8. The download happens only the first time you run the cell. The file has 50,000 rows with two columns, review and sentiment. But 418 rows are exact duplicates: the same review text with the same label, appearing more than once. Duplicates are dangerous: if one copy lands in the training set and another in the validation set, the model is tested on a review it has already seen, and its score looks better than it really is. So we remove them, leaving 49,582 reviews (24,884 positive and 24,698 negative, almost perfectly balanced), and shuffle the order. Common mistake: splitting a dataset into training and validation sets before removing duplicates. Copies of the same example then end up on both sides of the split, and validation accuracy is inflated. Deduplicate first, then split. You will meet this issue again, in more depth, in Module 8. To keep this notebook fast, we use 20,000 reviews for training and 5,000 for validation. Here is the start of the first training review:

title: Why Neural Networks Cannot Process Raw Text Directly
text: Look closely at that review and think about it from a network's point of view. Three problems stand out. Problem 1: text is made of symbols, not numbers. A network can only do arithmetic. Every character does have a numeric code (its Unicode code point), but those codes are arbitrary labels. The capital O that begins the review is stored as 79 and the r after it as 114. Nothing about 79 or 114 relates to meaning. By that numbering, "good" and "food" differ by one letter and would look almost identical, while "good" and "great" would look quite different. Arithmetic on character codes is arithmetic on spelling, not meaning. Problem 2: texts have different lengths. The shortest training review has 10 words, the median has 173 and the longest has 2,470. But the networks you have built expect inputs of a fixed shape, such as a batch of shape (64, 784). Text needs a way to be cut and padded to a common shape. Problem 3: the same meaning can be written in many ways. "GOOD", "Good" and "good." are the same word to a reader but different strings to a computer. The review also contains HTML line-break tags, , left over from the web page it was copied from. The rest of this note solves these problems one at a time: tokenisation deals with Problem 3 and prepares for Problem 1; token IDs and embeddings solve Problem 1; padding and truncation solve Problem 2. Check yourself. 1. Why would it be a poor idea to represent each word by the sum of its characters' code points? Worked answer The sum of code points depends only on spelling, and different words can share the same sum: "dog" and "god" have identical letters, so identical sums, but very different meanings. And words with similar meanings ("good", "great") would get unrelated sums. The number would carry no information about meaning.

title: Tokenisation and Token IDs
text: 3.1 Splitting text into tokens Tokenisation means splitting text into the units the model will treat as its basic building blocks: the tokens. The simplest idea, splitting on spaces, already runs into trouble: Splitting on spaces produces tokens such as 'GOOD. It', which mix words with punctuation and HTML. Our small tokenize function does three things instead: it lowercases the text, removes the tags, and keeps only runs of letters and apostrophes. The result, ['this', 'movie', "wasn't", 'good', 'it', 'was', 'great'], is much cleaner. Every tokeniser involves choices like these, and they matter. Lowercasing means "Apple" (the company) and "apple" (the fruit) become the same token. Dropping punctuation throws away the difference between "great!" and "great?". There is no perfect tokeniser, only one that suits the task. In this note we use whole words. In Module 6 you will meet subword tokenisers, which split rare words into common pieces, and which are widely used by modern language models. 3.2 Building a vocabulary Next we tokenise all 20,000 training reviews and count how often each word appears. The training reviews contain 4,617,067 tokens but only 79,754 distinct words. The counts are extremely uneven: the 1,000 most common words cover 76.3% of all the tokens, and the 10,000 most common cover 94.3%. The most common words are tiny "function words" such as the, and, a and of. The plot below shows this unevenness. Each point is one word, ranked from most common to least common, plotted against how often it occurs. Both axes are logarithmic (each step is a factor of 10). The curve falls steadily: a handful of words occur hundreds of thousands of times, while the 10,000th most common word occurs only 24 times, and 32,674 words, about 40% of all distinct words, occur exactly once. This pattern, where a word's frequency falls roughly in proportion to its rank, is called Zipf's law, and it holds for almost every language and every large body of text. It also tells us how to build a sensible vocabulary. Words that appear only once or twice are too rare for a model to learn anything reliable about. So we keep the 10,000 most common words and add two special tokens: - (ID 0): a filler token used to make short texts as long as long ones (Section 9.1). - (ID 1): "unknown", used for every word that is not in the vocabulary. We then build two lookup tables: itos ("integer to string") maps an ID to its word, and stoi ("string to integer") maps a word to its ID. Our example sentence has become the list of numbers [11, 17, 291, 49, 9, 13, 80]. Common words get small IDs because we numbered the vocabulary by frequency: the is ID 2 (right after the two special tokens), and great is ID 80. On the validation reviews, 6.0% of tokens are not in the vocabulary and become . That is the price of a fixed vocabulary: the model will see in place of rare names, misspellings and unusual words. Key terms - Token: one unit of text the model works with; here, a word. - Tokenisation: splitting text into tokens. - Vocabulary: the fixed list of tokens the model knows, each with a number. - Token ID: the number of a token in the vocabulary. - / : special tokens for unknown words and for padding. Token IDs solve the "symbols are not numbers" problem, but only on the surface. An ID is just a label, like a seat number. Word 80 is not "bigger" than word 49 in any meaningful way, and words 49 and 50 are not similar just because their numbers are close. Feeding the raw IDs into a network as if they were measurements would make it treat these arbitrary labels as quantities. We need a better way to give the network each word. Check yourself. 1. Our vocabulary covers 94.3% of training tokens. Why is the share of tokens on the validation reviews (6.0%) slightly higher than the 5.7% you might expect from that figure? Worked answer The vocabulary was chosen using the training reviews. Words that are common in training are, by construction, in the vocabulary; the validation reviews contain some words that were rare or absent in training (new names, rare words, typos), so slightly more of their tokens fall outside the vocabulary. This is a small, honest example of the gap between training data and new data.

title: One-Hot Encoding and Its Limitations
text: The classic way to give a network a categorical value without implying any order is one-hot encoding, which you have probably used for categorical columns in classical machine learning. Each word becomes a vector as long as the vocabulary, filled with zeros except for a single 1 at the word's ID. Each one-hot vector has 10,002 entries, and exactly 1 of them is non-zero. One-hot vectors solve the ordering problem, since no word is "bigger" than another. But they create two new problems. They are huge and wasteful. A single 200-token review becomes 200 × 10,002 = 2,000,400 numbers, almost all zeros. They make every word equally different from every other word. A standard way to measure how similar two vectors are is their dot product: multiply matching entries and add them up. For one-hot vectors, the 1s are always in different places, so the dot product between any two different words is 0. As the output shows, "good" is exactly as similar to "great" (0.0) as it is to "terrible" (0.0). One-hot vectors carry no notion of meaning at all, so a model cannot transfer anything it learns about "great" to "excellent". What we would like is a short vector for each word, made of ordinary numbers rather than mostly zeros, arranged so that similar words have similar vectors. That is exactly what an embedding is. Check yourself. 1. If we doubled the vocabulary to 20,000 words, what would happen to the length of each one-hot vector, and to the similarity between "good" and "great"? Worked answer Each one-hot vector would grow to about 20,000 entries (plus the special tokens). The similarity between "good" and "great" would still be exactly 0, as for any two different words. More words make one-hot vectors more wasteful, not more meaningful.

title: Word Embeddings and Embedding Layers
text: An embedding layer is, at heart, a lookup table: a matrix with one row per word in the vocabulary. Row 49 holds the vector for "good", row 80 holds the vector for "great", and so on. To embed a token, you simply fetch its row. In PyTorch this is nn.Embedding(num_embeddings, embedding_dim), where num_embeddings is the vocabulary size and embedding_dim is the length of each vector. The crucial point is that the table's entries are ordinary learnable parameters. They start random and are adjusted by backpropagation, like any other weights, so that the vectors become useful for the task. Our table has shape (10002, 8): one row of 8 numbers for each of the 10,002 tokens, which makes 80,016 parameters. Looking up "good" and "great" returns their two rows. The numbers are random, because nothing has been trained yet. The last line of the output reveals what an embedding layer really is. Multiplying a one-hot vector by the table picks out exactly one row, so an embedding lookup gives the same result as one-hot encoding followed by a linear layer, and PyTorch confirms the two are identical (True). The embedding layer just skips the wasteful multiplication by thousands of zeros and fetches the row directly. Figure 5.3.2. Selecting row 49 is equivalent to multiplying a one-hot vector by the table, without materialising that dense one-hot vector. Both table entries and the chosen row are illustrative. Embedding layers work on whole batches of token IDs at once. A batch of shape (B, T) (B texts, each T tokens long) becomes a tensor of shape (B, T, D), adding one dimension of size D for the vector. Two sentences of 4 tokens each, shape (2, 4), become (2, 4, 8): each of the 8 tokens has been replaced by its 8-number vector. Common mistake: passing token IDs with a floating-point dtype to an embedding layer. Embedding layers need integer IDs (torch.long), because an ID is a row number, not a quantity. Key terms - Embedding: a learned vector of numbers that represents a token. - Embedding layer: a learnable lookup table with one vector per vocabulary entry (nn.Embedding). - Embedding dimension: the length of each vector (embedding_dim).

title: Embedding Dimensions and Vector Representations
text: How long should each word's vector be? The output above shows the parameter cost for our 10,002-word vocabulary: 80,016 parameters with 8 dimensions, 640,128 with 64, and 3,000,600 with 300. It helps to think of each dimension as one "axis of meaning" that the model can use to tell words apart. With only 2 dimensions you could perhaps separate positive words from negative words, and formal words from casual ones, and nothing else. More dimensions allow more distinctions: tone, topic, grammar, whether a word is about people or objects, and so on. But nobody tells the network what each axis should mean. The axes are learned, and usually no single dimension corresponds neatly to a human concept; the meaning is spread across all of them together. The trade-off is familiar from Module 3: - Too few dimensions: the vectors cannot hold enough distinctions, and the model underfits. - Too many dimensions: many more parameters to learn, which needs more data and invites overfitting, especially for rare words. Word embeddings trained on their own typically use somewhere between tens and a few hundred dimensions; the embeddings inside large language models are much longer. In this note we use 32 dimensions for the sentiment model and 50 for the second model in Section 9. Check yourself. 1. A vocabulary has 50,000 tokens and an embedding dimension of 512. How many parameters does the embedding table have? Worked answer 50,000 × 512 = 25,600,000 parameters.

title: Semantic Similarity and Cosine Similarity
text: If embeddings are supposed to place similar words close together, we need a way to measure "close". For word vectors, the standard measure is cosine similarity. Imagine each vector as an arrow pointing out from the origin. Cosine similarity looks only at the angle between two arrows, not at their length: Here a · b is the dot product from Section 4, and ‖a‖ is the length (or norm) of vector a, the square root of the sum of its squared entries. Dividing by both lengths removes the effect of size, so only direction counts. The result always lies between −1 and +1: - +1: the arrows point in exactly the same direction. - 0: they are at a right angle; the vectors are unrelated. - −1: they point in exactly opposite directions. Let's check this on small 2D vectors whose angles we can picture: [1, 1] and [2, 2] point the same way (one is just longer), so their cosine is 1.000, even though they are not equal. [1, 0] and [0, 1] are at a right angle: 0.000. [1, 0] and [1, 1] are 45° apart: 0.707. And [1, 1] and [−1, −1] point in opposite directions: −1.000. Figure 5.3.3. Cosine similarity compares directions rather than lengths: 1 for the same direction, 0 for perpendicular vectors, and −1 for opposite directions. It is undefined for a zero vector without a numerical convention. Now apply cosine similarity to the untrained embedding table from Section 5: These numbers mean nothing. "Good" comes out more similar to "great" (−0.081) than to "terrible" (−0.682) or "the" (−0.714), but that is pure luck: the table is random. With only 8 dimensions, random vectors can easily have large positive or negative cosines by chance. An embedding table becomes meaningful only after it has been trained, and, as Section 9 will show, what it becomes depends entirely on what it was trained to do. Key terms - Dot product: multiply matching entries of two vectors and add the results. - Norm (length): the size of a vector, the square root of the sum of its squared entries. - Cosine similarity: the dot product divided by both norms; it measures the angle between two vectors, from −1 to +1. Check yourself. 1. Two word vectors have a cosine similarity of 0.98, but one is three times as long as the other. Are they similar, according to cosine similarity? Worked answer Yes. Cosine similarity ignores length and looks only at direction. A cosine of 0.98 means the vectors point in almost the same direction, so they count as very similar, regardless of one being longer.

title: Static vs. Contextual Representations
text: Before we train anything, there is one limitation of embedding layers that is important to understand, because it explains why the field moved on to the Transformers of Module 6. Consider the word "bank" in these two sentences: - She sat by the bank of the river. - He deposited cash at the bank. To a reader, these are two different meanings. But an embedding layer is a lookup table, and "bank" has only one row. So it must receive exactly the same vector in both sentences: The cosine similarity is 1.0: the two vectors are identical. This is called a static representation: each word gets one fixed vector, whatever its surroundings. The lookup table alone cannot change the vector of "bank" with context. A model that simply averages these vectors also loses word order and struggles with negation. An order-aware model can instead build contextual representations from the same static starting vectors. A contextual representation, by contrast, gives each word a vector that depends on the words around it. "Bank" near "river" and "bank" near "cash" would get different vectors. Producing contextual representations requires a model that lets words exchange information with one another. Sequence models (Note 5.4) and, above all, Transformers (Module 6) do exactly this. They still begin with an embedding layer like ours, and then transform those static vectors into contextual ones. Figure 5.3.4. A static table returns the same vector for a token type in every sentence. A contextual model produces different output vectors as surrounding tokens change; a static vector can still encode multiple usages. Key terms - Static representation: one fixed vector per word, the same in every context. - Contextual representation: a vector for a word that depends on the surrounding words. Check yourself. 1. A sentiment model averages static word embeddings to represent a review. Why might it struggle with the review "not good at all"? Worked answer The average of the static vectors for "not", "good", "at" and "all" contains the strongly positive vector for "good". Averaging cannot express that "not" reverses the meaning of "good", so the review may be scored as positive. We measured exactly this: "the movie was not good" was still scored 0.569 positive.

title: Text Embeddings in Practice with PyTorch
text: Now we train embeddings for real, in two different ways, and compare what they learn. 9.1 Turning reviews into a fixed-size tensor Reviews have different lengths, but a batch must be a rectangular tensor. The standard solution has two parts: - Truncation: cut every review to at most MAX_LEN tokens; we use 200. - Padding: fill shorter reviews up to 200 with the token (ID 0). The training set is now a tensor of shape (20000, 200): 20,000 reviews, each exactly 200 token IDs. Truncation affects 40.4% of training reviews, which are longer than 200 tokens, and 20.9% of all positions in the tensor are padding. Truncating that many reviews loses information, because the end of a review often contains its verdict. It is a deliberate trade-off between accuracy and speed. Padding, meanwhile, must not influence the prediction: a review should not become more negative just because it is short. We deal with that next. 9.2 Objective 1: learning embeddings for sentiment Our first model is deliberately simple. It is a bag of embeddings: look up the vector for every token, average the vectors of the real (non-padding) tokens, and feed that one average vector to a linear layer that outputs a single score. A positive score means "positive review". The loss is BCEWithLogitsLoss, the binary cross-entropy loss for two-class problems. The line that handles padding is the mask: it is 1 for real tokens and 0 for padding, so that padding vectors are multiplied by zero and excluded from the average. We also pass padding_idx=PAD to the embedding layer, which keeps the vector fixed at zero and never trains it. The embedding table is trained only through the sentiment loss. The words' vectors are free to become whatever helps tell positive reviews from negative ones. We train for 4 epochs and keep the epoch with the best validation accuracy. Validation accuracy rises to 0.8646 at epoch 3, then slips to 0.8632 at epoch 4 while the training loss keeps falling. That is the first sign of overfitting, so we keep the epoch 3 weights. Not bad for a model that ignores word order completely. Now the interesting part: what did the embedding table learn? For a few words, we find the nearest neighbours: the vocabulary words whose vectors have the highest cosine similarity to that word's vector. The sentiment words have very sensible neighbours. "Excellent" sits next to wonderfully, best and fantastic; "awful" sits next to poorly, dull, waste and worst. But look at the neutral words. "Husband" is next to betray, aimed and crude; "music" is next to testament, ida and evokes; "actor" is next to characterization and diane. These neighbours are less clearly related in meaning, and their similarities (around 0.55 to 0.79) are noticeably lower than those of the sentiment words (around 0.85). This makes perfect sense once you remember what the table was trained for. The sentiment loss only ever asked one question: does this word push a review towards positive or negative? So the embeddings organised themselves along that single question. Words with no sentiment, like "husband" and "music", received no direct supervision for general semantic similarity. 9.3 Objective 2: learning embeddings from context (skip-gram) Can we learn embeddings that capture general meaning instead? A famous idea from linguistics says yes: "You shall know a word by the company it keeps." Words that appear in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings. "Husband" and "wife" both appear near "married", "her", "his" and "divorce"; "music" and "soundtrack" both appear near "score", "songs" and "beautiful". Skip-gram turns this idea into a training objective. It needs no labels at all, only raw text: 1. Take a word in the text, the centre word. 2. Look at the words up to a few positions on either side, the context words. Each (centre, context) pair is a positive example: "these two words appeared together". 3. Also pick a few random words from the vocabulary, called negative samples or "noise" words. Each (centre, random word) pair is a negative example: "these probably did not appear together". 4. Train two embedding tables so that the dot product of a centre word's vector with a true context word's vector is high, and with a noise word's vector is low. This is the training method behind word2vec, one of the most influential models in natural-language processing. Because it learns from text alone, it is an example of self-supervised learning: the training labels ("did these words appear together?") come from the data itself. First we build the training pairs. We also randomly drop many occurrences of very frequent words such as "the", a step called subsampling, because very frequent words dominate the pair counts. We build each window within one review, so the end of one review never becomes the context of another. From 15,000 training reviews, with a window of up to 5 words on each side, subsampling keeps 1,307,513 tokens, which produce 12,625,140 (centre, context) pairs. Now we train, for one pass over all the pairs. Inside the loop, pos is the dot-product score for each true pair and neg holds the scores for the 5 noise words of each pair. The loss uses logsigmoid, the logarithm of the sigmoid function, to push pos up and neg down. It is the same idea as binary cross-entropy, with the true pairs labelled 1 and the noise pairs labelled 0. The loss falls from an average of 3.407 over the first 100 steps to 2.598 over the last 100. Now the same nearest-neighbour test, on the skip-gram embeddings: The neutral words now have more clearly related neighbours. "Husband" sits next to wife, mother and daughter; "music" next to soundtrack, sound, songs and score; "actor" next to comedian and talented, as well as actors' names. The sentiment words also have plausible neighbours: "excellent" next to superb, flawless and exceptional, and "awful" next to terrible, bad and horrendous. These are observations from this run, rather than guaranteed semantic groupings. 9.4 Backing the comparison with numbers Nearest-neighbour lists are easy to cherry-pick, so let's measure the difference more systematically. We take three sets of word pairs: - related pairs, which a reader would call similar in meaning, such as husband–wife, music–soundtrack and film–movie; - opposite pairs with opposite sentiment, such as excellent–awful and love–hate; - 200 random pairs drawn from the 2,000 most common words, as a baseline. We compute the average cosine similarity within each set, for three embedding tables: a random untrained one, the sentiment one and the skip-gram one. Always read these numbers against the random column, which tells you what "no relationship" looks like in each table. - Untrained: all three averages are close to zero (−0.076, 0.085 and 0.011). As expected, random vectors encode nothing. - Sentiment: related pairs average only 0.141, barely above random (−0.001). But opposite pairs are strongly negative, at −0.609. This table has learned one thing very well, positive versus negative, and little else. - Skip-gram: related pairs average 0.830, far above its random baseline of 0.408. Notice the baseline itself is high: skip-gram vectors tend to share a common overall direction, which is why comparing against random pairs matters. The surprise is the opposite pairs: 0.495, above the random baseline. To skip-gram, "excellent" and "awful" are somewhat similar, because they appear in the same kinds of contexts ("the acting was ___", "an ___ film"). Within the 20 words of the picture below, the same story shows up group by group: the family words average −0.06 under the sentiment objective and 0.87 under skip-gram, while the positive words are tightly grouped in both (0.77 and 0.83). Here is a 2D picture of 20 words from four groups in each table. Each panel is a PCA projection (principal component analysis, a method that finds the two directions along which the points vary most and flattens everything onto them). A 2D picture of 32- or 50-dimensional vectors always loses information: these pictures keep 58% and 67% of the variation in the 20 vectors, so treat them as illustrations of the numbers above, not as proof. In the sentiment panel, positive and negative words form two tight clusters at opposite sides, while family and music words are scattered without structure. In the skip-gram panel, family and negative words form clear groups, while positive and music words also show structure but partly overlap in this 2D projection. The full-dimensional cosine measurements provide the stronger comparison. This is the key lesson of this note: an embedding learns whatever its training objective rewards. Both demonstrations use learnable embedding tables and the same vocabulary, but they are not an objective-only controlled experiment: sentiment uses 32 dimensions and 20,000 reviews, while skip-gram uses 50 dimensions and 15,000 reviews, with a different prediction head and training procedure. The results illustrate task-shaped representations; they do not isolate the objective as the only cause of every difference. A sentiment objective builds a "sentiment axis". A context objective builds a map of how words are used, which captures topic and meaning but cannot, by itself, tell good from bad. Neither is "the true meaning" of a word; each is a representation shaped for a purpose. You saw the same idea with images in Note 5.1: a representation is good for a task. 9.5 The limit of static embeddings Finally, let's go back to Section 8 and test our sentiment model on four short sentences. "The movie was good" gets a probability of 0.982 of being positive, and "the movie was bad" gets 0.000. So far, so good. But "the movie was not good" still gets 0.569, more likely positive than negative, and "the movie was not bad" gets 0.000, as negative as "bad" itself. The model cannot understand negation. It sees each word's static vector, averaged together, with no idea that "not" changes the meaning of the word after it. Averaging also throws away word order completely. Fixing this needs a model that processes the words in relation to one another, which is exactly where Note 5.4 begins. Common mistake: judging embeddings by a few hand-picked neighbour lists. As you saw, a sentiment table gives perfect neighbours for "awful" and nonsense for "husband". Always test several kinds of words, and compare against a random baseline. Check yourself. 1. According to the skip-gram embeddings, "excellent" and "awful" are more similar than two random words. Why would using those embeddings, unchanged, for sentiment analysis be risky? Worked answer Skip-gram places "excellent" and "awful" relatively close together (average opposite-pair cosine 0.495, above the random baseline of 0.408), because they appear in similar contexts. A sentiment classifier built on these vectors would start from a representation in which positive and negative words are hard to tell apart, so it would need to learn that distinction from labelled data. Embeddings from one objective are not automatically right for a different task.

title: Why Sequence Order Matters
text: Consider two sentences: "dog bites man" and "man bites dog". They contain exactly the same words, but one is ordinary and the other is news. Any representation that treats a sentence as a bag of words, simply counting which words occur, cannot tell them apart: The two bags are identical. And if we average the embedding vectors of the words, as our sentiment model did in Note 5.3, the result is also identical, whatever the embeddings are: A cosine similarity of 1.0 means the two sentences get exactly the same representation. Averaging is order-blind: adding up the same vectors in a different order always gives the same total. The same problem appears everywhere in sequences. "Not good" and "good, not" mean different things. In a sensor reading, a temperature that rises then falls is different from one that falls then rises. What we need is a way of combining a sequence that depends on the order of its items. Key terms - Sequence: an ordered list of items, such as words in a sentence or readings over time. - Bag of words: a representation that records which words appear (and how often) but not their order. - Order-blind: giving the same result whatever order the inputs come in. Check yourself. 1. Name one other everyday example (not language) where two sequences contain the same items but mean different things because of their order. Worked answer Many answers work. For example: the steps of a recipe (mix then bake is not the same as bake then mix), a phone number or PIN, a sequence of moves in a game, or a patient's symptoms appearing in a particular order.

title: Recurrent Neural Networks: The Complete Picture
text: Think about how you read this sentence. You don't hold every previous word separately in mind. You keep a running sense of "what this is about so far", and update it as each new word arrives. A recurrent neural network (RNN) does exactly that. It reads a sequence one item at a time, in order, and keeps a vector called the hidden state, its running memory. At each step it combines two things: the new input and its previous hidden state. Its output is a new hidden state, which is carried forward to the next step. The update rule at each step t is: where: - x_t is the input at step t (for example, the embedding of word t); - h_(t−1) is the hidden state from the previous step (it starts as all zeros); - W_x and W_h are weight matrices, and b is a bias; the same weights are used at every step; - tanh (the hyperbolic tangent) squashes each value into the range −1 to +1, so the hidden state cannot grow without limit. Figure 5.4.1. One recurrent update with shared weights reads dog → bites → man. Each hidden state depends on the current token and previous state; the final state is a finite-dimensional sequence summary. The second term, W_h h_(t−1), is what makes the network recurrent: the output of the network feeds back into itself. Let's write this loop by hand, with tiny sizes so that every number is visible: 4 numbers per input word and 3 numbers in the hidden state. After reading "dog", the hidden state is [0.999, −0.681, 0.204]. After "bites" it has changed to [−0.941, 0.98, 0.626], and after "man" to [0.672, 0.388, 0.319]. Every value stays between −1 and +1, because of tanh. The final hidden state is the network's summary of the whole sentence. PyTorch provides the same thing as nn.RNN. If we copy our weights into it, it should give identical results: It matches. Note the two outputs of nn.RNN: out holds the hidden state at every step, shape (batch, T, hidden) = (1, 3, 3), and h_last holds only the final hidden state, shape (layers, batch, hidden) = (1, 1, 3). With batch_first=True, PyTorch expects inputs as (batch, T, features). Common mistake: forgetting batch_first=True. Without it, PyTorch's recurrent layers expect (T, batch, features), and will silently treat your batch dimension as time if the shapes happen to fit. Now the key test. Does the RNN tell "dog bites man" from "man bites dog"? Yes. The final states are very different, with a cosine similarity of only 0.2831, compared with 1.0 for averaging. Because each step depends on everything before it, the same words in a different order produce a different memory. The RNN is order-aware. Key terms - Recurrent neural network (RNN): a network that processes a sequence one step at a time, carrying a hidden state forward. - Hidden state: the RNN's running memory; a vector updated at every step. - Unrolling: drawing (or computing) an RNN as one copy of the cell per step, connected by the hidden state. Check yourself. 1. An RNN has a hidden state of 32 numbers. How many numbers does it carry forward after reading a sequence of 5 words? After 5,000 words? Worked answer 32 numbers in both cases. The hidden state has a fixed size, whatever the length of the sequence. That is the information bottleneck of Section 5.

title: Why Standard RNNs Struggle with Long-Term Dependencies
text: Order-awareness is a good start. But consider this sentence: "The film, which was shot over three years in four countries with a cast of hundreds and a famously difficult director, was a triumph." To know that "was" (singular) is correct, the network must connect it to "film", many words earlier. A connection like this, between items far apart in a sequence, is a long-term dependency. Can an RNN learn one? 3.1 Measuring how far the gradient reaches The RNN learns, like every network, through backpropagation. Recall from Module 1 that backpropagation is credit assignment: it works out how much each input and weight contributed to the error. For an RNN, the gradient has to travel backwards through every step, from the final output back to the early inputs. Let's measure how much of it arrives. We feed a random sequence of 60 inputs into an untrained RNN, take its final output, and backpropagate. The size of the gradient at each input position tells us how strongly the final output depends on that input, and so how much that input can be "learned from". We average over 3 random starting weights. The gradient shrinks dramatically with distance: about 1.9 for the very last input, 0.055 five steps back, 0.0029 ten steps back, 0.0000023 twenty steps back, and 8.8e-12 forty steps back. (The notation 8.8e-12 means 8.8 × 10⁻¹², a decimal point followed by eleven zeros and then 88.) For practical purposes, an input 40 steps back has no influence on learning at all. This is the vanishing gradient problem, which you met in Module 3. In an RNN it is especially severe, because the "depth" of the network is the length of the sequence. 3.2 Why it vanishes: repeated multiplication Every step backwards multiplies the gradient by the same kind of factor: the recurrent weights W_h, times the slope of tanh. If that factor is a little less than 1, repeating it many times drives the result towards zero; if it is a little more than 1, the result explodes. Multiplying by 0.9 forty times leaves 0.0148; multiplying by 0.5 forty times leaves 9.1e-13, essentially nothing. Multiplying by 1.1 forty times gives 45.3: the opposite problem, an exploding gradient. A factor of exactly 1 at every step is almost impossible to maintain. The tanh function makes vanishing more likely. Its slope is 1.0 at zero but drops quickly away from zero: 0.42 at ±1, 0.071 at ±2 and 0.01 at ±3. So whenever the hidden state is pushed towards ±1, which tanh does to large values, the gradient flowing back through that step is multiplied by a small number. Here is the measurement from Section 3.1 as a plot. On a logarithmic scale, a constant shrinking factor per step shows up as a straight downward line. A vanishing gradient is a warning sign, but the real question is whether the network can still learn a long-range task. So let's set it one. Each sequence is a list of random tokens. The first token is a clue, 0 or 1, and the label is simply that clue. Everything after it is noise.
