To succeed, the network must remember the first token all the way to the end, and it classifies using only its final hidden state. By changing the sequence length, we control exactly how far the information has to travel. The two example sequences start with 0 and 1, and their labels are 0 and 1. Now we train an RNN at four lengths, with 3 different random seeds each, and measure accuracy on 1,000 validation sequences. Guessing would score about 0.5, and each validation sequence is worth 0.001 of accuracy. At length 10, every seed solves the task perfectly (1.0). At length 30, only one of the three seeds succeeds; the other two score 0.475 and 0.461, no better than guessing. At lengths 50 and 100, every seed fails, with accuracies between 0.494 and 0.533. The task itself is trivial: "repeat the first token". The RNN fails not because the task is hard, but because the error signal from the end of the sequence cannot reach the first step to teach it what to remember. This is the long-term-dependency problem, measured directly. Key terms - Long-term dependency: a relationship between items far apart in a sequence. - Vanishing gradient: a gradient that shrinks towards zero as it travels back through many steps, so early inputs cannot be learned from. - Exploding gradient: a gradient that grows uncontrollably as it travels back. Check yourself. 1. Why does the RNN succeed at length 10 but fail at length 50, when the rule to learn ("output the first token") is exactly the same? Worked answer The rule is the same, but the distance the learning signal must travel is not. At length 50, the gradient from the final output must pass back through 49 steps before reaching the first token, and it shrinks at every step, so almost nothing arrives to teach the network what it should have stored. At length 10, enough of the gradient survives.

title: LSTM and GRU: The Intuition Behind Gating Mechanisms *(Extension)*
text: This section goes a little deeper than the rest of the note. The key idea, that gates let a network choose what to keep, is worth understanding; the details are optional. The vanilla RNN overwrites its entire memory at every step: the new hidden state is a fresh tanh of a mix of input and old memory. The Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, designed specifically to solve the problem we just measured, changes this. It keeps a separate memory, the cell state, and controls it with gates. A gate is a set of numbers between 0 and 1, produced by a sigmoid function, that is multiplied element by element with some other vector. A gate value of 1 lets everything through; 0 blocks everything. The LSTM has three: - the forget gate decides how much of the old cell state to keep; - the input gate decides how much new information to write; - the output gate decides how much of the cell state to reveal as the hidden state. The crucial change is in how memory is carried forward. Instead of being squashed through tanh at every step, the cell state is updated mostly by multiplying by the forget gate and adding new information. If the forget gate stays close to 1, the memory, and the gradient flowing back along it, passes from step to step almost unchanged. Figure 5.4.2. The forget gate retains old cell state, the input gate admits a candidate, and the output gate exposes tanh of the new state. A near-one forget gate helps preserve the direct memory path; it does not guarantee perfect long-range learning. 4.1 The catch: the gate must start open Here is a detail that is easy to miss. The forget gate is computed with a sigmoid of a weighted sum plus a bias. PyTorch starts all biases at around zero, so at the start of training the forget gate sits at about sigmoid(0): In this zero-logit illustration, the forget gate is 0.500, retaining half the old cell state per step along this direct path. Actual gates vary with the inputs, previous state, random weights and biases; PyTorch does not fix them all at exactly 0.5. After 40 steps that leaves 9.1e-13, the same vanishing as a plain RNN. If instead we set the forget-gate bias so that the gate starts at sigmoid(3) = 0.953, the memory kept after 40 steps is 0.143, enormously more. (Each LSTM has two bias vectors that are added together, so setting each to 1.5 gives a total of 3.) Starting the forget gate open is a well-known practical technique. Let's test both versions of the LSTM on the same memory task. The results are striking: - The default LSTM does no better than the vanilla RNN. It solves length 10, but fails at length 30 on all three seeds (0.471 to 0.502), and at every longer length. - The LSTM with its forget gate open scores 1.0 on every seed, at every length, all the way to 100. The plot shows all three models; each line is the average over seeds, and the faint dots are individual seeds. Forty steps back, the gradient is 8.8e-12 for the RNN, 6.1e-09 for the default LSTM, and 0.30 for the open-gate LSTM. The open forget gate keeps the gradient path alive. So the honest summary is: gates make long-term memory possible, but they have to be used that way. An LSTM's architecture allows memory to persist; whether it does depends on the gate values, which are learned, and which need a good starting point. The Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) is a simplified relative of the LSTM. It merges the cell state and hidden state and uses two gates instead of three, so it is a little cheaper. With an input size of 16 and a hidden size of 32, a vanilla RNN has 1,600 parameters, a GRU 4,800 and an LSTM 6,400: each gate needs its own weights. Key terms - LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory): a recurrent network with a protected cell state controlled by forget, input and output gates. - GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit): a simpler gated recurrent network with two gates. - Gate: a vector of values between 0 and 1 (from a sigmoid) that scales another vector, letting information through or blocking it. - Cell state: the LSTM's long-term memory line. Check yourself. 1. The default LSTM failed the length-30 task even though its architecture is designed for long memory. In one sentence, why? Worked answer Its forget gate started at about 0.5, so it kept only half its memory per step, and the memory (and gradient) vanished almost as fast as in a plain RNN, before the gates could learn to stay open. Visual walkthrough: Inspect one LSTM memory update. Follow one scalar coordinate through the forget, input and output gates. The values are a worked example. These supplied numbers illustrate the calculation. The web app adds a paused, step-by-step animation of the same example.

title: The Limitations of Recurrent Processing
text: If an LSTM with a well-set forget gate can carry a fact across 100 steps, why did the field move on? Because remembering one fact is not the only requirement. Real language tasks expose two deeper limitations that no choice of gates can remove. Limitation 1: everything must squeeze through one fixed-size memory. However long the sequence is, the RNN carries forward only its hidden state. With a hidden size of 32, the RNN carries forward a (1, 1, 32) state after 10 steps, and exactly the same 32 numbers after 1,000 steps. Every fact from a 1,000-word document (names, dates, who did what to whom) must be compressed into those 32 numbers before the end. Adding facts means overwriting others. This is called the information bottleneck. Limitation 2: the steps must run one after another. To compute the hidden state at step 1,000, the RNN needs the state at step 999, which needs step 998, and so on: 1,000 steps that cannot be done at the same time. Modern hardware such as GPUs is fast precisely because it does thousands of calculations in parallel. A sequential loop wastes most of that power, which makes RNNs slow to train on large datasets. Compare the last line of the output. Comparing every position with every other position, for all 1,000 positions, is a single matrix multiplication producing a (1000, 1000) grid of scores. All of it can be computed at once. That operation is the core of attention.

title: From Sequential Processing to Attention
text: Attention takes a completely different approach. Instead of passing information along a chain, step by step, it lets each position look directly at every other position and decide how much to take from each one. Here is the idea in one picture. To build its representation, the last word in a sentence asks a question, its query. Every word in the sentence offers a key, a description of what it contains, and a value, the information it can contribute. The query is compared with every key to produce a score; the scores are turned into weights that sum to 1 (with softmax); and the result is a weighted average of the values. A word that is relevant to the query gets a large weight, however far away it is. Figure 5.4.3. Recurrent information follows sequential updates; attention can directly mix allowed context positions. Connection strengths are illustrative. A causal model can consult only the current and earlier positions. Let's build the smallest possible version of this, a single attention step in which the last position attends to all 60 positions, and run the same gradient measurement as in Section 3.1. We will study queries, keys and values properly in Module 6; for now, watch what happens to the gradient. Through attention, the gradient reaching an input 59 steps back is 3.9e-02, about the same as for an input 10 steps back (5.2e-02). Through the RNN, the input 59 steps back receives 7.3e-17. The most recent position gets a larger gradient under attention (2.4e-01) only because it also supplies the query. Here are all four measurements together: The picture summarises this whole note: - The vanilla RNN (blue) and default LSTM (orange) fall in straight lines: their gradients shrink by a constant factor per step. - The open-gate LSTM (green) keeps its gradient, and even grows slightly towards the far past, but it still has the fixed-size bottleneck and still has to process one step at a time. - Attention (red) is flat: every input is one step away from the output, so distance simply does not matter. Attention solves all three problems at once: 1. No long chain: every position connects directly to every other, so gradients do not have to survive many multiplications. 2. No single bottleneck: each position keeps its own vector, and any position can draw on any other, so information does not all have to fit into one hidden state. 3. Parallel computation: all the comparisons are matrix multiplications that run at once on a GPU. It also gives us what Note 5.3 was missing: contextual representations. When "bank" attends to "river", or "good" attends to "not", its new vector reflects its surroundings. Attention has a price. Comparing every position with every other means the number of comparisons grows with the square of the sequence length. For 1,000 positions, that was a (1000, 1000) grid, a million scores. You will meet this cost, and how it is managed, in Module 6. Common mistake: concluding that RNNs "cannot remember". As you measured, a well-initialised LSTM carried a fact across 100 steps perfectly. The reasons attention replaced recurrence for language are the fixed-size bottleneck and sequential computation, together with attention's direct access to every position. Key terms - Attention: a mechanism in which each position computes a weighted average of other positions' information, with weights based on relevance. - Query, key, value: what a position is looking for, what each position offers as a description, and the information each position contributes. - Information bottleneck: forcing all information through a fixed-size representation. - Parallel computation: performing many calculations at the same time instead of one after another. Check yourself. 1. Give two reasons, other than vanishing gradients, why processing a 10,000-word document with an RNN is difficult. Worked answer First, everything must be compressed into a fixed-size hidden state, so facts from early in the document are overwritten by later ones (the information bottleneck). Second, the 10,000 steps must be computed one after another, which makes training slow and wastes the parallel power of modern hardware.

title: What Does It Mean to Represent Different Modalities?
text: A modality is a type of data, defined by how it is recorded: images, text, audio, video, sensor readings. Each modality has its own structure. Images are 2D grids of pixels where neighbours matter; text is a sequence of discrete symbols where order matters. That is why we used different encoders for them: a CNN for images, an embedding layer for text. Each encoder produces a vector, but there is no reason for the vectors from two separately trained encoders to be comparable. Imagine two people describing the same building, one in French using metres and one in Japanese using feet. Each description is accurate, but you cannot compare them number by number until you agree on a shared language and shared units. A shared representation space is that agreement: a single space in which an image of a bag and the text "a photo of a bag" land in the same place. Figure 5.5.1. Separate encoders do not automatically align their coordinates. Joint contrastive training can make projected image and text vectors comparable in a shared space. Cluster positions here are schematic. We start by loading the images. We will create the text ourselves in Section 2.

title: Mapping Different Modalities into a Shared Representation Space
text: 2.1 Our image–text dataset A shared space is learned from pairs: an image together with text that describes it. Real systems learn from enormous collections of images and captions gathered from the internet. We will make simple captions ourselves from the class names, using four sentence patterns called templates, so that each class can be described in several different ways. Each class gets 4 captions, which makes 40 distinct captions in total, built from a vocabulary of only 21 words. The four captions for class 7 are shown: "a photo of a sneaker", "a picture of a sneaker", "an image showing a sneaker" and "a sneaker on a plain background". During training, every image will be paired with one of its class's captions, chosen at random. 2.2 Two encoders and two projections The recipe for a shared space has three parts: 1. An image encoder that turns an image into a vector. We use the same small CNN as in Note 5.2. 2. A text encoder that turns a caption into a vector. We use the bag-of-embeddings idea from Note 5.3: look up each word's embedding and average them. 3. A projection at the end of each encoder: a linear layer that maps the encoder's output into the shared space. Both projections output vectors of the same length, 32 numbers, and we normalise each vector to length 1, so that their dot product equals their cosine similarity. The CNN on its own produces 1,568 numbers per image, while the text encoder's word embeddings have 32 numbers. Those two cannot be compared at all. After the projections, both produce vectors of shape (batch, 32), and each has length 1.0. Now an image and a caption can be compared, with a single dot product. But being comparable is not the same as being meaningful. Let's test the untrained encoders. For each validation image, we compute its similarity with the 10 descriptions "a photo of a t-shirt", "a photo of a trouser" and so on, and pick the most similar. If the space were meaningful, this would classify images correctly using only text. With untrained encoders, the accuracy is 0.100: exactly what random guessing among 10 classes would give. The two encoders produce vectors of the same size, but they have no reason to agree. We need to train them so that matching images and captions end up close together. Key terms - Modality: a type of data, such as images, text or audio. - Shared representation space: a single vector space in which data from different modalities can be compared directly. - Projection: a layer, usually linear, that maps an encoder's output into the shared space. - Normalise (to unit length): divide a vector by its length so that its length becomes 1; then dot product equals cosine similarity. Check yourself. 1. Why do the image and text projections have to output vectors of the same length? Worked answer Comparing an image with a caption means computing a dot product (or cosine similarity) between their vectors, which is only defined for vectors of the same length. The projections are what translate both modalities into the same "coordinates".

title: Contrastive Learning: The Core Intuition
text: How do we train two encoders so that matching pairs are close? We cannot simply tell the network "the correct vector for a bag is this one", because nobody knows what the right vectors are. What we do know is which image goes with which caption. Contrastive learning uses exactly that. Take a batch of images, each with its own caption. Compute the similarity of every image with every caption in the batch. The training goal is: - pull together each image and its own caption (the positive pair); - push apart each image and all the other captions in the batch (the negative pairs). Think of a seating chart at a wedding. You don't know the exact coordinates where each guest should sit, but you know who belongs with whom. Moving partners together and strangers apart, again and again, gradually produces a sensible arrangement of the whole room. Figure 5.5.2. In this toy batch each image has one designated matching caption. Contrastive loss raises matched scores relative to other batch entries; semantically similar off-diagonal pairs can be false negatives. 3.1 The contrastive loss, by hand Here is the loss on a tiny made-up example with 4 images and 4 captions. S[i, j] is the similarity between image i and caption j, and the correct matches are on the diagonal. We read the matrix row by row: each row asks "which of the 4 captions belongs to this image?". That is a 4-way classification problem, so we can use the ordinary softmax and cross-entropy loss from classification, with the correct answer being the diagonal entry. We then do the same column by column ("which image belongs to this caption?") and average the two. Before the softmax, the similarities are multiplied by a scale, here 10, which controls how sharply the softmax separates the scores. (In CLIP it is described as dividing by a temperature, which is the same thing.) In this example, the diagonal entries are clearly the largest in each row, so after scaling and softmax, each image puts almost all its probability on its own caption: 0.999, 0.996, 0.977 and 0.973. The loss is correspondingly small: 0.014 for the rows, 0.012 for the columns, and 0.013 on average. If an off-diagonal similarity were higher than the diagonal one, the probability on the correct caption would drop and the loss would rise sharply. That is the signal that drives learning. 3.2 Training our toy model The contrastive_loss function below does exactly this for a whole batch. In every training step, we draw 128 random training images, give each one a random caption from its own class, embed both, and minimise the contrastive loss. We train for 400 steps. The training function also records a floor for the loss, which needs explaining. Each batch contains about 12.8 images of each class, and many of their captions are identical or nearly so. Our model is supposed to map all bag images to the same place, so it cannot tell which of the roughly 13 bag images in the batch belongs to a particular bag caption. The best it can do is spread the probability evenly among them, and that gives a loss of about the logarithm of their number. These same-class "negatives" are called false negatives: pairs that the loss treats as wrong, even though they are a perfectly good match. The starting loss is close to ln(128) = 4.852, which is what you get when every one of the 128 captions looks equally likely: the untrained model has no idea which caption fits. Over the first 20 steps the loss averages 4.886, and over the last 20 steps it has fallen to 2.934. The floor caused by same-class items is 2.584, so the model has closed most of the possible gap. The plot shows the loss approaching, but not reaching, the floor. Now we repeat the test from Section 2: match each of the 10,000 validation images to the most similar of the 10 descriptions "a photo of a ...". No classifier head was trained for this; we are classifying images purely by comparing them with text. The accuracy is now 0.875, against 0.100 before training. Classes with distinctive shapes are easiest: bags (0.974), trousers (0.973) and sandals (0.960). Coats are hardest (0.671), followed by pullovers (0.790) and shirts (0.796), the same family of similar upper-body garments that troubled the CNN in Note 5.2. The text side is genuinely flexible, within limits. Because the text encoder averages word embeddings, any combination of words it knows produces a valid description. Let's try different wordings: All four training templates give similar accuracies, from 0.868 to 0.875, and even the bare class name '{}', a description the model never saw on its own during training, scores 0.865. But the prompt "this is a {}" fails completely, because "this" is not one of the 21 words in the vocabulary. Our text encoder can only understand words it was trained on, a limitation we return to in Section 4. To see the shared space more directly, we average the vectors of all validation images of each class and compare each average with each of the 10 class descriptions. A meaningful shared space should produce a bright diagonal. Images and the description of their own class have an average cosine of 0.888; images and other classes' descriptions average 0.203. The brightest off-diagonal cells all involve the hard upper-body classes: T-shirt images against "a photo of a shirt" (0.71), coat images against "shirt" (0.69), pullover images against "shirt" (0.68), and coat images against "pullover" (0.61). The model's confusions in the space are the confusions you would expect. Finally, a picture of the space itself. We project 1,000 validation images (dots) and the 10 descriptions (stars) together onto two dimensions with PCA. This 2D picture keeps only 50% of the variation in the 32-dimensional vectors, so treat it as an illustration of the numbers above, not a measurement. The images form clusters by class, and each description sits near its own class's cluster. Two details are worth noticing. The stars lie near their clusters rather than in their centres: images and text occupy slightly different regions of the shared space, which is consistent with the matching cosine of 0.888 being high but below 1. And the "coat" and "shirt" stars sit almost on top of each other in the crowded upper-body region, which matches the high coat–shirt similarity of 0.69. Common mistake: expecting the contrastive loss to go to zero. With false negatives in every batch, it cannot. Judge a contrastive model by what it can do (matching accuracy, retrieval quality), not by how low the loss goes. Key terms - Contrastive learning: training by pulling matching pairs together and pushing non-matching pairs apart. - Positive / negative pair: a matching image–caption pair / a non-matching one. - Contrastive loss: cross-entropy over the image–caption similarity matrix, in both directions, with the matches on the diagonal. - Temperature (scale): a number that controls how sharply the softmax separates similarity scores. - False negative: a pair treated as non-matching by the loss even though it is actually a valid match. Check yourself. 1. If we trained with a batch size of 1,024 instead of 128, would the loss floor caused by same-class items go up or down? Why? Worked answer It would go up. With 1,024 items and 10 classes, each batch would contain about ten times as many same-class items, so each image would have more indistinguishable "correct" captions to spread its probability over. The floor is roughly the logarithm of that number, so a larger batch means a higher floor. (Real systems like CLIP use very diverse captions, so true duplicates in a batch are rare, and large batches mainly help by providing more, and harder, negatives.)

title: CLIP as an Example of Joint Image–Text Representation Learning
text: What we have built is a miniature version of CLIP (Contrastive Language–Image Pre-training), a model released by OpenAI that showed how powerful this idea becomes at scale. CLIP has exactly the same structure as our toy: - an image encoder (in CLIP, a large CNN or a Vision Transformer, which you will meet in Module 6); - a text encoder (in CLIP, a Transformer that reads the whole sentence, not an average of word vectors); - projections into a shared space, with normalised vectors; - the contrastive loss over large batches of image–caption pairs, with a learned temperature. The big difference is the data. Our toy learned from 40 template captions about 10 kinds of clothing. CLIP learned from an enormous collection of real images paired with the text that appeared next to them on the internet: captions, titles, descriptions. That variety is what gives CLIP its most famous ability, zero-shot classification: classifying images into categories it was never explicitly trained on, simply by writing a description of each category. Figure 5.5.3. Training aligns image–caption pairs. At inference, compare a new image with candidate text descriptions. Bars are illustrative similarities, not measured confidence or calibrated probabilities. 4.1 Why our toy cannot do true zero-shot classification Our model did classify images using text, but only for the 10 classes whose captions it was trained on. Is that really "zero-shot"? Let's test it properly. We train a fresh model without any sneaker images or sneaker captions, then ask it to recognise sneakers using the description "a photo of a sneaker". The model trained without sneakers still reaches 0.796 overall on the validation images, but it recognises none of the sneakers (0.000). It matches 721 of them to "sandal", 233 to "ankle boot" and 1 to "bag": all visually similar shoes, or nearly. It has learned sensible things about the images, since sneakers land near other footwear, but the word "sneaker" never appeared in any training caption, so its embedding is still random. Text it has never learned from carries no meaning. This is precisely why CLIP's scale matters. CLIP can recognise categories that no one explicitly labelled because, during training, it saw those words in many real captions, alongside many images. Its text encoder has learned what words like "sneaker", "zebra" or "lighthouse" refer to. Zero-shot classification is not magic: it is reuse of what was learned from text during training. Check yourself. 1. Our model, trained without sneakers, matched sneaker images mostly to "sandal" and "ankle boot". What does that tell you about what its image encoder learned, even without sneakers in training? Worked answer Its image encoder learned general visual features of footwear, such as a low, wide outline with a sole, even without seeing sneakers. Sneaker images landed near sandal and ankle-boot images in the shared space. What was missing was the text side: the word "sneaker" had no learned meaning to match them to.

title: Applications: Image Search, Text-to-Image Retrieval, and Multimodal AI
text: A shared image–text space is useful far beyond classification. Because images and text are now comparable, we can search in either direction. 5.1 Text-to-image search To search a collection of images with a sentence, embed every image once and store the vectors. To answer a query, embed the text and rank all the stored images by cosine similarity. Here are the top 8 validation images for three queries, with the cosine similarity above each one: Every result in all three rows is from the requested class, with cosine similarities between 0.91 and 0.93. Let's measure this more broadly: for each class, we search with "a photo of a ..." and check what fraction of the top 100 results really belong to that class. This fraction is called precision at 100. Precision at 100 is 1.00 for trousers, sandals and ankle boots, and at least 0.95 for every class, averaging 0.976. Even coats, the hardest class to classify, reach 0.95: the very best matches for a query are much more reliable than the average match. Notice something about this search: no image was ever tagged with keywords. The ranking came entirely from the shared space. That is how modern photo libraries let you search your own pictures by typing what you remember. 5.2 Other applications The same shared space powers several other kinds of system: - Image-to-text retrieval: find the captions, products or documents that best match an image (the reverse direction of the search above). - Zero-shot classification: as in Section 4, classify images into categories described in words, without training a new classifier. - Duplicate and similarity search: find images similar to a given image by comparing image vectors directly. - Guiding image generation: some text-to-image generators use a CLIP-style shared space to check how well a generated image matches the prompt. - Multimodal assistants: models that answer questions about images often begin with an image encoder trained in a shared image–text space, whose vectors are then passed to a language model. You will load a real pretrained CLIP model and use it for zero-shot classification and search in Module 7. Key terms - Retrieval: finding the items in a collection that best match a query. - Precision at k: the fraction of the top k results that are correct. - Zero-shot classification: classifying into categories using descriptions only, without training on labelled examples of those categories. Check yourself. 1. In the search above, we embedded all 10,000 validation images once and reused their vectors for every query. Why is this important for a real search system with millions of images? Worked answer Embedding an image requires running the image encoder, which is expensive. If we re-embedded millions of images for every query, each search would take far too long. By embedding the collection once and storing the vectors, each new query costs only one text embedding plus fast dot products, which can be done for millions of stored vectors very quickly.

title: Comparing Raw Inputs and Learned Features
text: 1.1 The experimental setup To compare representations fairly, we reuse the three-way split from Note 5.1. Each group of images has one job, and no image is used for more than one job: - 40,000 images are used only to train the two encoders, so that they learn their representations. - 10,000 images are used to train the downstream classifiers (the linear probes) and as the reference set for nearest neighbours. - 10,000 images are held out, and every accuracy in this note is measured on them. 1.2 Learning the two representations We train two encoders, each with a 10-class head on top, for 3 epochs each: - an MLP encoder: flatten, then one hidden layer of 128 units, the same as in Note 5.1; - a CNN encoder: the two convolution blocks from Note 5.2, followed by a fully connected layer of 64 units. After training, we keep only the encoders and discard the heads, exactly as in Note 5.1. Both encoders learn normally: the MLP's average training loss falls from 0.649 to 0.404, and the CNN's from 0.742 to 0.357. Now we pass every image through each encoder and collect the representations. Each image now has three descriptions: 784 raw pixel values, 128 MLP features and 64 CNN features. The CNN's description is the most compact of the three. 1.3 Linear probes As in Note 5.1, we measure each representation by training the same simple classifier on top of it: a standardised logistic regression, trained on the 10,000 probe images and evaluated on the 10,000 validation images. Any difference in accuracy comes from the representation. The ranking is clear: raw pixels reach 0.803, MLP features 0.867 and CNN features 0.882. The CNN's representation is the most useful and the smallest. But a difference of 0.015 between the MLP and the CNN is only 150 images out of 10,000. Could it be luck? We use the sign test from Note 5.2: look only at the images where two classifiers disagree, and ask whether the split could plausibly be a coin flip. For these fitted classifiers, the paired tests provide strong evidence of accuracy differences on this validation sample; they do not establish that every retraining will have the same ranking. Against raw pixels, the CNN-feature classifier was right on 1,143 images that the raw-pixel classifier got wrong, against only 351 the other way round (p = 6.9e-98). Against MLP features the margin is smaller but still convincing: 477 against 319 (p = 2.4e-08). With 10,000 validation images, each image is worth 0.0001 of accuracy, so even modest accuracy gaps rest on hundreds of images. 1.4 Where does the gain come from? An overall accuracy hides a lot. Let's compare raw pixels and CNN features class by class. The gains are very uneven. Trousers barely change (+0.012): their long two-legged shape is already obvious in raw pixels, so there is little left to gain. The biggest gains are for coats (+0.122), pullovers (+0.114), dresses and shirts (+0.112 each) and T-shirts (+0.110), the classes that look alike in outline and differ in details such as sleeves, collars and texture. Those are exactly the local patterns that convolution filters are designed to pick up. Notice also what the learned representation did not fix. Shirts remain by far the hardest class, at 0.640 even with CNN features. We will look at why in Section 1.6. 1.5 With very few labels In Note 5.1 we saw that good representations shine when labelled data is scarce. Let's check that the CNN representation holds up here too: we train each linear probe on just 100 labelled images, about 10 per class, repeated with 5 random draws. With 100 labels, CNN features reach 0.838 on average, against 0.792 for MLP features and 0.669 for raw pixels. The spread across the 5 draws is narrower for the CNN, too (0.826 to 0.850), than for raw pixels (0.613 to 0.698). With only 100 labels, the CNN representation already beats raw pixels trained with all 10,000 labels (0.803). 1.6 Are similar images close together? A representation is a kind of map in which every image has a position. A good map should place images of the same kind close together. We can check this directly with nearest neighbours: for a query image, find the images whose representations are closest to it (here, by straight-line distance). Let's start with the first four validation images, chosen by position, not because they make any representation look good: For these four queries, an ankle boot, a pullover, a pair of trousers and a T-shirt, both spaces find almost entirely correct neighbours. The one mistake shown is a CNN neighbour of the ankle boot that is actually a sneaker. Easy images are easy in any reasonable representation. To see a difference, we need harder cases. Shirts were the hardest class, so here are the first four validation shirts, again chosen by position, not by outcome: This picture is humbling. For the first shirt, both spaces find shirts. But look at the second "shirt": it looks much more like a dress, and both spaces return dresses. The fourth looks like a T-shirt, and both spaces return T-shirts. Some of these mistakes say more about the data than about the representation. At 28×28 pixels, some shirts genuinely look like other garments, and no representation learned from these pixels can recover a distinction that the pixels do not contain. The numbers below the picture put the four examples in context. Across 2,000 validation images, 0.782 of the 5 nearest neighbours share the query's class in raw-pixel space, against 0.841 in CNN space. For shirts alone the agreement is far lower in both spaces, 0.542 and 0.576. Four examples could have suggested that the CNN space is worse for shirts. The measurement over 200 shirts says it is slightly better, and that shirts are hard for everyone. We can turn this neighbour idea into a classifier: k-nearest neighbours (k-NN) predicts a validation image's class by majority vote among its 5 nearest probe images. Its accuracy summarises how well each representation groups classes together. The ranking is the same as for the linear probes: 0.828 for raw pixels, 0.850 for MLP features and 0.877 for CNN features. Two very different ways of using a representation, a linear classifier and a neighbour vote, agree about which one is best. These full-dimensional k-NN numbers are our reference point for the pictures that follow. Common mistake: judging a representation from a handful of examples. Four shirts could have suggested the opposite of what 200 shirts show. Always back examples with a measurement over many cases.

title: Visualising Learned Representations
text: People love to look at representations, and pictures can be genuinely illuminating. But a representation with 64 or 784 dimensions cannot be drawn on a flat page without throwing information away. The question is always: how much does the picture distort? Here we answer it with the same k-NN measurement: if a 2D picture preserved the neighbourhoods of the full representation, k-NN in the picture would be about as accurate as k-NN in the full space. 2.1 PCA Principal component analysis (PCA) finds the two directions along which the data varies most and projects everything onto them. It is a linear projection: like casting a shadow of a 3D object onto a wall, it keeps the overall shape but flattens everything else. The 2D PCA view keeps 47% of the variance (spread) of the raw pixels and 69% of the CNN features. More importantly, look at what happens to the neighbourhoods. In 2D, k-NN accuracy drops to 0.504 for raw pixels (from 0.828 in full dimensions) and to 0.617 for CNN features (from 0.877). The flat picture loses a large part of the structure in both cases, so we should read it with care. The CNN panel looks more organised: trousers, bags and footwear form clear separate groups, while all the upper-body garments are piled together in one corner. The raw-pixel panel looks like a blurred ring. That impression is consistent with the numbers: CNN features are better organised. But neither picture is a faithful map. The heavy overlap in the CNN corner does not mean those classes are inseparable; in the full 64 dimensions, a linear classifier separates them far better than the picture suggests. 2.2 t-SNE t-SNE (t-distributed stochastic neighbour embedding) takes a different approach. Instead of projecting, it moves points around on the page, trying to keep each point's nearest neighbours near it. It does not try to preserve large distances. It is widely used because it produces striking, clustered pictures. t-SNE is slower than PCA and cannot place new points without re-running, so we apply it to 2,000 validation images, and we measure k-NN on those same 2,000 images with 5-fold cross-validation (train on four-fifths, test on the remaining fifth, five times), both in the t-SNE picture and in the full representation. Note that this full-dimensional k-NN uses only 2,000 images as its reference set instead of 10,000, so its accuracies are lower than in Section 1.6. That is fine: what matters is comparing the picture with the full space on the same images. This is a very different story from PCA. In the t-SNE pictures, k-NN accuracy is almost as high as in the full space: 0.769 against 0.783 for raw pixels, and 0.841 against 0.846 for CNN features. Here, t-SNE retains class information useful to k-NN. Similar classification accuracy does not prove that the identities of individual neighbours are preserved. This is a transductive visualisation diagnostic: t-SNE was fitted to all 2,000 points before cross-validation, so this is not an estimate of performance on unseen points. To measure neighbour preservation directly, use neighbour overlap or trustworthiness. The CNN picture shows tight, well-separated clusters for trousers, bags, sandals, sneakers and ankle boots, with the upper-body classes closer together and partly mixed. But notice that the raw-pixel picture also looks quite organised, much more so than its PCA picture. t-SNE is very good at making clusters visible. That is its strength, and also a reason for care: a clustered t-SNE picture on its own is not evidence that a representation is good. Here the numbers tell us which exposes more class information for this full-dimensional k-NN diagnostic (0.846 against 0.783), and the pictures only illustrate it. 2.3 What t-SNE does not preserve If t-SNE keeps neighbourhoods, can we read the rest of the picture too, such as which clusters are far apart? Let's re-run t-SNE on the same CNN features with different random starting points and see what changes. The class-prediction scores are similar across these runs: k-NN in the picture stays at 0.845 and 0.838, close to the 0.841 of the first run. But the global layout is not. The two classes whose cluster centres end up farthest apart are trousers and sandals in one run, trousers and bags in another, and coats and ankle boots in the picture above. The same data, with a different random start, gives a different arrangement of clusters. So the rule for reading t-SNE pictures is: - Use as hypotheses: local groupings that remain stable across settings; verify important neighbours in the full representation. - Do not trust: distances between clusters, the sizes of clusters, or the empty space between them. Figure 5.6.1. Conceptual projection analogy. PCA retains directions of greatest variance; t-SNE emphasises local neighbourhoods. Both can distort structure, so validate claims using appropriate measurements in the full representation space. Common mistake: concluding from a t-SNE plot that "class A is very different from class B because their clusters are far apart". t-SNE does not preserve distances between clusters, and the layout changes between runs. Compare distances in the full representation instead. Key terms - k-nearest neighbours (k-NN): classifying an item by majority vote of the k most similar items. - PCA: a linear projection onto the directions of greatest variance. - Explained variance: the share of the data's spread that a PCA projection keeps. - t-SNE: a non-linear method that arranges points in 2D to preserve each point's nearest neighbours. - Cross-validation: repeatedly splitting data into training and test parts and averaging the results. Check yourself. 1. In Section 2.1, PCA of the CNN features kept 69% of the variance, but k-NN accuracy fell from 0.877 to 0.617. How can a picture keep most of the variance yet lose so much of the neighbourhood structure? Worked answer Variance measures overall spread, which is dominated by the biggest differences in the data, such as "footwear vs. trousers vs. tops". PCA keeps those large directions, which accounts for most of the variance. But the finer distinctions that decide which class a point's nearest neighbours belong to, such as shirt vs. pullover, live in the many smaller directions that PCA throws away. So the picture keeps the big shape while scrambling many local neighbourhoods.

title: Summary: What Changes When a Network Learns Representations?
text: Let's step back and answer the question that has run through all of Module 5. The description changes, and the description decides what is easy. Raw data such as pixels and characters is complete but unhelpful: individual values mean little, and important patterns are spread across many of them. A learned representation re-describes each example in terms of features that matter for a task. In this note, the same linear classifier went from 0.803 on raw pixels to 0.882 on 64 CNN features, a difference confirmed by a sign test (p = 6.9e-98). The architecture shapes what can be learned. The CNN's representation beat the MLP's (0.882 against 0.867, p = 2.4e-08) while using half as many numbers, because convolution builds in the knowledge that nearby pixels matter. That same idea runs through the module: CNNs for images, embeddings for words, recurrence and then attention for sequences. Each design encodes an assumption about the data. The objective shapes what is learned. In Note 5.3, the same embedding layer learned a sentiment axis or a map of word usage depending purely on the training objective. In Note 5.5, contrastive learning shaped two encoders so that images and text shared a space. A representation is always good for something. Good representations save labels. With 100 labels, CNN features (0.838) beat raw pixels with 10,000 labels (0.803). This is the reason pretrained models matter so much: someone else has already spent the data and compute to learn a good representation, and you can reuse it. Not everything can be learned away. Some shirts look like dresses or T-shirts at this resolution, and no representation could fix that (5-NN agreement for shirts: 0.542 raw, 0.576 CNN). Representation learning extracts what is in the data; it cannot invent what is not. Evaluate with numbers, illustrate with pictures. Linear probes, k-NN, per-class breakdowns and sign tests told us what was true. PCA pictures lost much of the structure (k-NN 0.617 against 0.877), and t-SNE retained similar class-prediction scores in this transductive diagnostic (0.841 against 0.846) but not the layout between clusters, which changed from run to run. Figure 5.6.2. Module 5 connects representation learning for images, text and sequences with shared spaces and measurement. A learned representation need not be compact or have individually interpretable coordinates. Where this leads. Module 6 takes the attention idea from Note 5.4 and builds it into the Transformer, the architecture that produces contextual representations for text, and, as Vision Transformers, for images too. Modules 7 and 8 then show how to reuse and adapt representations that have already been learned at enormous scale.

title: The Big Picture: What Is a Transformer?
text: A Transformer is a network that takes a sequence of tokens and produces a new vector for every token, where each new vector has been enriched with information from the other tokens in the sequence. Stack enough of these enrichment steps, add a final layer that turns vectors into predictions, and you have a model that can classify text, translate it, or generate it one token at a time. It helps to think of a Transformer as a meeting. Each token arrives with its own notes (its embedding). In each round of the meeting, every token gets to listen to the others, decide who is relevant to it, and update its notes accordingly. That listening is attention. Between rounds, each token also takes a moment to think privately about what it has heard: that is the feed-forward network. After several rounds, each token's notes describe not just itself, but its role in the whole sequence. Throughout this module, we work with Tiny Shakespeare: about a million characters of Shakespeare's plays in one text file. Our models will read and write it one character at a time, which keeps the vocabulary tiny and lets us train on a CPU. The file contains 1,115,394 characters, built from just 65 distinct characters: letters, digits, punctuation, the space and the newline. Each character gets a number, its token ID; "First Citizen" becomes [18, 47, 56, 57, 58, 1, 15, 47, 58, 47, 64, 43, 52]. (We look at tokenisation properly in Note 6.2.) Now here is a complete, working Transformer. We build it from PyTorch's ready-made nn.TransformerEncoderLayer, so it fits in a few lines. Don't worry about every argument yet: by the end of the module you will have rebuilt each piece yourself. For now, read it as a list of stages: 1. tok_emb turns each token ID into a vector of 64 numbers. 2. pos_emb adds a vector that encodes each token's position in the sequence. 3. blocks is a stack of 3 Transformer blocks, each containing attention and a feed-forward network. 4. ln_f is a final normalisation step. 5. head turns each token's final vector into a score for every token in the vocabulary: a prediction of what comes next. Our tiny Transformer has 162,561 parameters. That is minuscule by modern standards, but it has all the essential parts of the models behind today's chat assistants. Figure 6.1.1. The lesson’s causal decoder-only Transformer adds token and position embeddings, applies three blocks, then normalises and predicts 65 next-character logits per position. The short row illustrates part of a 64-token context.

title: What Problem Were Transformers Designed to Address?
text: In Note 5.4 we found three problems with recurrent networks: - A long chain: information, and the learning signal, has to pass through every step between two distant tokens, and fades along the way. - A fixed-size bottleneck: everything read so far must be squeezed into one hidden state. - Sequential computation: step 1,000 cannot start until step 999 has finished, so the parallel power of modern hardware is wasted. The Transformer removes all three. Every token can attend directly to every other token, so the chain has length one. Every token keeps its own vector, so there is no single bottleneck. And because no token has to wait for the previous one, the whole sequence is processed at once. Let's see that last point concretely. For our 32-character input, a single forward pass of the Transformer produces 32 predictions at once: one at every position, each saying what character should come next at that point. An RNN reading the same input would need 32 steps, one after another. This matters most during training. With one forward pass, we get a prediction, and therefore a training signal, at every position of every sequence in the batch. That is a key reason Transformers can be trained on enormous amounts of text. We return to this idea, called parallel training, in Note 6.6. The price, as you saw at the end of Note 5.4, is that comparing every token with every other token costs work proportional to the square of the sequence length. We measure that cost in Note 6.3.

title: The Transformer as a Complete Information-Processing System
text: Let's follow one input all the way through our model, and print the shape of the data after each stage. We use the first 32 characters of the play as input. Read the shapes from top to bottom: - The input is (1, 32): a batch of 1 sequence, 32 token IDs long. - After the embeddings it is (1, 32, 64): each of the 32 tokens is now a vector of 64 numbers. This size, called d_model or the model dimension, is the "width" of the Transformer. - After each of the 3 blocks it is still (1, 32, 64). Blocks never change the shape; they change the content of each token's vector, by mixing in information from other tokens. - After the output head it is (1, 32, 65): at every one of the 32 positions, one score for each of the 65 characters in the vocabulary. These scores are called logits. That constant shape inside the stack is one of the Transformer's most useful properties. Because each block takes (batch, tokens, d_model) and returns the same shape, you can stack as many blocks as you like, and the same block design works for any length of input up to the maximum context. What does the untrained model predict? Let's turn the logits at the last position into probabilities with softmax and look at its best guesses for the character after "proceed". The untrained model's favourite guess is 'i' with probability 0.065, followed by 'N', 'R', a space and '-'. These are random preferences, not knowledge. The entropy of the distribution, a measure of how spread out it is, is 4.024. The maximum possible, for a perfectly uniform guess among 65 characters, is ln(65) = 4.174. So the untrained model is close to "no idea at all", which is exactly where training will start from in Note 6.6. Key terms - Transformer: a network built from stacked blocks of attention and feed-forward layers that processes all tokens of a sequence in parallel. - Model dimension (d_model): the length of each token's vector inside the Transformer. - Transformer block: one round of attention plus feed-forward processing; input and output have the same shape. - Logits: the raw scores the output head produces, one per vocabulary entry; softmax turns them into probabilities. - Entropy: a measure of how uncertain a probability distribution is; highest when every outcome is equally likely. Check yourself. 1. If we fed our model a batch of 8 sequences, each 50 characters long, what would be the shape of the logits? Worked answer (8, 50, 65): 8 sequences, 50 positions each, and 65 scores (one per character) at every position.

title: The Roles of Tokens, Embeddings, Attention, and Feed-Forward Networks
text: Each stage of the pipeline has one job. Here they are in the order the data meets them: - Tokens. The text is split into units and each unit gets an ID. The model only ever sees IDs. (Note 6.2.) - Token embeddings. A lookup table turns each ID into a vector, exactly as in Note 5.3. This vector describes the token on its own, with no context. - Positional information. Attention, as you will see in Note 6.3, has no built-in sense of order. So we add a second vector that encodes where each token sits. (Notes 6.2 and 6.3.) - Attention. Each token gathers information from other tokens, weighted by relevance. This is the only place where tokens exchange information. (Note 6.3.) - Feed-forward network (FFN). A small two-layer MLP applied to each token's vector separately. It processes what attention gathered. (Note 6.4.) - Output head. A linear layer that turns each final vector into one score per vocabulary entry. (Note 6.5.) A useful slogan: attention moves information between tokens; the feed-forward network processes information within each token. Where do the parameters live? Let's count them by component. The feed-forward networks hold the most parameters: 99,264, or 61.1% of the model. Attention holds 49,920 (30.7%). The embeddings, output head and layer norms together hold well under a tenth. The roughly two-to-one ratio between feed-forward and attention follows from a standard design choice: each feed-forward network expands every vector to 4 × d_model numbers and back, which needs about twice as many weights as attention's four d_model × d_model projections. Large language models keep a similar balance, which is one reason researchers think of the feed-forward layers as the place where much of a model's "knowledge" is stored. Check yourself. 1. In one sentence each, what is the job of attention, and what is the job of the feed-forward network? Worked answer Attention moves information between tokens, letting each token gather what is relevant from the others. The feed-forward network processes the information within each token's vector, separately for every token.

title: Encoder, Decoder, and Encoder–Decoder Architectures
text: All Transformers share the blocks we have just seen. What distinguishes the three main families is which tokens each token is allowed to look at, and that is controlled by a mask: a grid that says, for every pair of positions, whether attention between them is allowed. The three grids show the three patterns. Each row is a position doing the looking; each column is a position being looked at; blue means "allowed". Encoder-only (bidirectional). Every token may look at every other token, before and after it (left grid). This gives the richest possible understanding of a complete input, so encoders are used to understand text: classify it, extract information from it, or produce embeddings for search. The best-known example is BERT. An ordinary bidirectional encoder is not trained for the left-to-right autoregressive generation loop we build here. It can predict masked tokens, and encoder architectures can be adapted for other generation procedures; "encoder" does not mean that text generation is fundamentally impossible. Decoder-only (causal). Each token may look only at itself and the tokens before it (middle grid). This is called a causal mask, because the output at each position can only depend on what came earlier, just as a writer can only build on what has already been written. This is exactly what you need to generate text one token at a time. GPT-style language models, including the chat assistants you may have used, are decoder-only. So is the model we build in this module. Encoder–decoder. An encoder reads the whole input bidirectionally; a decoder generates the output causally, and at every layer it also looks at the encoder's output through cross-attention (right grid: every output position may look at every input position). This suits tasks that turn one sequence into another, such as translation or summarisation. The original Transformer was of this kind; T5 is a well-known modern example. We can verify the difference between bidirectional and causal attention directly. Below, two inputs differ only in their last character: "the king is dead" and "the king is deaf". We run both through our model with and without the causal mask, and check whether the output at the first position changes. With bidirectional attention, changing the last character changes the output at position 0 (by up to 0.095371): the first token can "see" the end of the sentence. With the causal mask, the change is exactly 0.000000: the first token cannot see anything after it. The mask does exactly what it promises. For completeness, here is PyTorch's full encoder–decoder nn.Transformer, with a source sequence of 10 tokens (say, an English sentence) and the first 7 tokens of a target sequence (its translation, generated so far): The decoder produces one vector per target position, (1, 7, 64), each informed by all 10 source tokens through cross-attention. To generate the 8th target token, a head would turn the last of these vectors into scores over the target vocabulary. Key terms - Mask: a grid that allows or blocks attention between each pair of positions. - Bidirectional attention: every token can attend to every other token (encoders). - Causal attention: each token can attend only to itself and earlier tokens (decoders). - Cross-attention: attention from the decoder's tokens to the encoder's output. - Encoder-only / decoder-only / encoder–decoder: the three Transformer families, used respectively for understanding, generating, and transforming one sequence into another. Check yourself. 1. Which family would you choose for each task: (a) deciding whether an email is spam; (b) a chatbot; (c) translating German into English? Worked answer (a) Encoder-only: you need to understand a complete email, not generate text. (b) Decoder-only: a chatbot generates its reply one token at a time. (c) Encoder–decoder: an encoder reads the whole German sentence and a decoder generates the English one, using cross-attention to consult the German. (Large decoder-only models can also translate, by treating the German text and its translation as one long sequence.)

title: How Information Flows Through a Transformer
text: There is a powerful way to picture what happens inside the stack of blocks. Think of each token's vector as a stream that flows upward through the model. This is often called the residual stream. Each block does not replace the stream; it adds something to it: first whatever attention gathered from other tokens, then whatever the feed-forward network computed. (This "adding" is the residual connection, which you will meet properly in Note 6.4.) So a token's vector starts as "this is the character d at position 8", and after each block it carries a little more about its surroundings. Let's watch this happen. We take two inputs with the same ending, "good lord" and "evil lord". Their final character, d, has the same ID and sits at the same position in both, so before any block their vectors must be identical. Do they stay identical? Before any block, the cosine similarity of the two d vectors is 1.000: identical, as expected. After block 1 it is 0.997, after block 2 0.989, and after block 3 0.978. Because each block mixes in information from earlier tokens, the d in "good lord" and the d in "evil lord" gradually become different vectors. This is a contextual representation, the thing that static embeddings could not provide in Note 5.3. The effect is small here because the model is untrained: its attention is essentially random, so it mixes in context weakly and without purpose. After training, the context will matter far more. Figure 6.1.2. A schematic residual stream: the same character can acquire different context-dependent representations. The coloured updates are an analogy, not measured semantic coordinates or guaranteed attention behaviour. Check yourself. 1. Why must the two d vectors be identical before the first block? Worked answer Before the first block, a token's vector is just its token embedding plus its position embedding. Both d tokens have the same ID and the same position (8), so they get exactly the same two vectors and the same sum. No information from other tokens has been mixed in yet.

title: The Original Transformer vs. Modern Transformer Architectures
text: This section is included in class. It connects our teaching model to refinements used in research papers and model documentation. The Transformer in "Attention Is All You Need" has been refined in several ways since it was published, mostly to make large models train more reliably: - Where normalisation goes. The original placed layer normalisation after each attention and feed-forward step ("post-norm"). Most modern models place it before each step ("pre-norm"), which trains more stably in deep stacks. You will measure this difference yourself in Note 6.4. - Activation function. The original feed-forward network used ReLU; modern models usually use smoother functions such as GELU or gated variants. - Positional information. The original added fixed sine-and-cosine patterns. Many models instead learn position vectors, as ours does, and many large models use methods such as rotary position embeddings (RoPE) that encode relative positions inside attention itself. - Families. The original was an encoder–decoder for translation. The most prominent models today are decoder-only. These are refinements, not a different architecture. PyTorch builds both styles from the same layer class, with exactly the same number of parameters: Both layers have 49,984 parameters. The only differences are the order of operations (norm_first) and the activation function: the same components, arranged slightly differently.

title: Beyond Text: Vision Transformers and Multimodal Models
text: Nothing in a Transformer block is specific to text. A block only needs a sequence of vectors. So if you can turn something into a sequence of vectors, you can process it with a Transformer. The Vision Transformer (ViT) does exactly this for images. It cuts an image into a grid of small square patches, flattens each patch into a list of pixel values, and passes each through a linear layer to make a vector. Those patch vectors are then treated just like word embeddings. Here is the idea applied to a 28×28 Fashion-MNIST image, cut into 7×7 patches: The 28×28 image becomes a 4×4 grid of patches, (4, 4, 7, 7), which we flatten into a sequence of 16 "tokens" of 49 numbers each, (16, 49). A linear layer turns each into a 64-number vector, giving (1, 16, 64): exactly the shape of a 16-token text sequence. We can then pass it through the same kind of Transformer block we used for Shakespeare, and get back (1, 16, 64). (In a real ViT, a position embedding is added too, so the model knows where each patch came from.) Notice how this connects back to Module 5. A CNN builds in the assumption that nearby pixels belong together. A ViT does not: from its first layer, any patch can attend to any other patch. With enough training data, this flexibility pays off, which is why many modern vision models are Transformers. The same trick powers multimodal models. Turn image patches, audio frames or video frames into vectors, put them in the same sequence as text tokens, and one Transformer can attend across all of them. That is how assistants that "see" an uploaded image work: the image becomes a set of vectors placed alongside the words of your question. Check yourself. 1. A 224×224 image is cut into 16×16 patches. How many patch tokens does the Vision Transformer receive? Worked answer 224 / 16 = 14 patches along each side, so 14 × 14 = 196 patch tokens.

title: The Big Picture: From Raw Text to Transformer Inputs
text: Here is the full journey, from a text file to what a Transformer receives in training: 1. Split the data into a training part and a validation part. 2. Tokenise: cut the text into tokens and build a vocabulary. 3. Encode: replace every token with its ID, giving one long sequence of integers. 4. Cut into windows: take chunks of fixed length, the context window, from that long sequence. 5. Make targets: for each window, the target is the same window shifted one token to the left, because the model's job is to predict the next token. 6. Batch: stack many windows into a tensor of shape (batch, context). The embedding layers then turn that integer tensor into vectors inside the model. Let's start with step 1. For text that tells a continuous story, like a play, we split by position rather than at random: the first 90% of the file for training and the last 10% for validation. A random split would scatter neighbouring lines across both sets, so the model would be validated on text it had effectively seen, just shifted by a few characters. Of the 1,115,394 characters, 1,003,854 go to training and 111,540 to validation. The validation text begins in the middle of a scene from The Taming of the Shrew. Figure 6.2.1. Split the data without crossing the boundary, tokenise and encode, then sample windows. For next-token learning y is x shifted one position forward in the source stream. The real batch shape is (32, 64); the short example is illustrative.

title: Tokenisation and Subword Tokenisation
text: There is no single correct way to cut text into tokens. Let's compare three, and measure what each costs. 2.1 Characters The simplest choice treats every character as a token. The training text uses 65 distinct characters, and "To be, or not to be" becomes 19 IDs, which decode back perfectly. Character tokenisation has two great strengths: the vocabulary is tiny, and every validation character is covered in this dataset. Every character in the validation text is already in the vocabulary (0 missing). Its weakness is length. One token per character makes every sequence as long as possible, and the model must learn from scratch that t, h, e in a row form a common word. 2.2 Words The opposite choice treats every word as a token. Here we split text into words, single punctuation marks and single whitespace characters, so that spaces and newlines are kept and the text could be rebuilt exactly. The training text now becomes 424,883 tokens, less than half as many as with characters. But the vocabulary explodes to 12,571 distinct tokens, and 2.6% of the validation tokens never appeared in training at all: words like "affability", "petitioners" and the name "Licio". A word-level model has no way to read such words; they would all become one token. (The share is fairly low only because spaces and punctuation, which are never unknown, count as tokens too.) 2.3 Subwords: byte-pair encoding Is there a middle path, with a modest vocabulary, shorter sequences than characters, and no unknown tokens? Yes: subword tokenisation, where common words become single tokens but rare words are spelled out from smaller pieces. The most widely used method is byte-pair encoding (BPE). Its training algorithm is surprisingly simple: 1. Start with every word split into single characters. 2. Count every pair of adjacent pieces across the whole training text. 3. Merge the most frequent pair into a new, single piece, everywhere it occurs. 4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 for a chosen number of merges. The list of merges, in order, is the tokeniser. To tokenise new text, you start from characters and apply the same merges in the same order. Let's train one with 200 merges. The first merge joins t and h into th, the most common pair of characters in the text. Then come ou, er, in and an; the 6th merge combines th and e into the whole word the. Each merge shortens the text: the training text needs 1,003,854 tokens with no merges, 778,195 after 50 merges, 715,298 after 100 and 654,024 after 200. The first merges help the most, because they capture the most frequent pairs. Now let's use the trained merges to tokenise some phrases. Common words such as "To", "be", "not", "the" and "king" have become single tokens. "Villain" is split into v, ill, ain: the tokeniser has not merged the whole word, but it reuses common pieces. And "Zounds", an old oath that the merges never formed into a word, is spelled from Z, ou, nd, s. An unseen word made from known characters can fall back to those characters. Our character-based vocabulary cannot encode a genuinely new character without an unknown-token or byte fallback. Here are the three schemes side by side: BPE with 200 merges sits between the extremes. Its vocabulary of 265 tokens is only four times the character vocabulary, it needs 654,024 training tokens instead of 1,003,854 (each token covers 1.53 characters on average), and it has no unknown tokens. Real language models use the same algorithm with tens of thousands of merges, usually working on bytes rather than characters so that any text in any language can be encoded. The plot shows the trade-off: as the vocabulary grows, sequences get shorter. For the rest of this module we use characters. With 65 tokens the output head stays tiny, every pattern the model learns is visible letter by letter, and our small model can learn spelling as well as style. Keep the trade-off in mind, though: in Module 7, the pretrained models you load all come with their own subword tokenisers. Common mistake: using a model with a different tokeniser from the one it was trained with. Token ID 300 means one piece of text to one tokeniser and something completely different to another. A model and its tokeniser are a pair; always load them together. Key terms - Character / word / subword tokenisation: splitting text into single characters, whole words, or pieces in between. - Byte-pair encoding (BPE): a subword method that repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair of pieces. - Merge: one BPE step, joining a pair of pieces into a new piece; the ordered list of merges defines the tokeniser. - Out-of-vocabulary (OOV): a token that never appeared in the training vocabulary. Check yourself. 1. Why can a BPE tokeniser always encode a word it has never seen, while a word-level tokeniser cannot? Worked answer A BPE tokeniser starts every word from single characters and only then applies merges, so any word made of known characters can be encoded, at worst one character at a time. A word-level tokeniser only knows whole words it saw in training, so a new word has no entry at all.

title: Token IDs and Embedding Layers
text: With a tokeniser chosen, the whole text becomes one long sequence of integer IDs. Inside the model, an embedding layer turns each ID into a vector of d_model numbers, exactly as in Note 5.3. The training text is now one tensor of 1,003,854 integers (int64, which PyTorch calls torch.long, the type embedding layers require). The first 10 IDs become a (10, 64) tensor of vectors. The choice of tokeniser also sets the size of the embedding table, and of the output head, which needs one score per vocabulary entry. With d_model = 64, the character vocabulary needs a table of only 4,160 parameters; BPE with 200 merges needs 16,960; the word vocabulary would need 804,544, several times more than the entire model we built in Note 6.1. For large models with vocabularies of tens of thousands, the embedding table and output head are a significant share of all parameters. Check yourself. 1. If we switched our model from characters to the 12,571-word vocabulary, which two parts of the model would grow, and why? Worked answer The token embedding table and the output head. Both have one row (or one output) per vocabulary entry, so going from 65 to 12,571 entries would multiply their size by almost 200. With d_model = 64, the embedding table alone would grow from 4,160 to 804,544 parameters.

title: Context Windows and Sequence Length
text: A Transformer reads a fixed maximum number of tokens at once: its context window (also called context length or block size). Anything outside the window is invisible to the model when it makes a prediction. We use a context of 64 tokens. How much text fits in 64 tokens depends on the tokeniser: With characters, 64 tokens hold 64 characters, about one line of verse: "Second Citizen:" plus the start of the next line. With BPE (200 merges), the same 64 tokens hold about 98 characters, and with words, about 151. This is a major practical reason to use subword tokenisers: the same context window, and the same computational cost, covers more text. Why not simply use a huge context? Because attention compares every token with every other token in the window, so its cost grows with the square of the context length. You will measure this in Note 6.3. Choosing a context length is a trade-off between how much the model can see and how much each training step costs. The context window also fixes the size of the position embedding table: one learned vector for each position from 0 to 63. Adding it to the token embedding gives each token a different vector depending on where it sits: In "to be or not to be", the two t characters (positions 0 and 13) have identical token embeddings (True), but after adding their position embeddings, their vectors have a cosine similarity of only 0.628. The model can now tell them apart. The position table costs 4,096 parameters (64 positions × 64 numbers). Note 6.3 explains why attention needs this information. Key terms - Context window: the maximum number of tokens the model can read at once. - Position embedding: a learned vector for each position in the context window, added to the token embedding. Check yourself. 1. Our model's context is 64 characters. What happens to information that appeared 100 characters earlier when it predicts the next character? Worked answer It is invisible. The model only receives the 64 most recent characters, so anything earlier cannot influence the prediction at all, however important it was.

title: Constructing Transformer Inputs with PyTorch
text: Now we can build training examples. A decoder-only language model learns one task: predict the next token. So every training example is a pair: - x, the input: a window of 64 consecutive token IDs from the text; - y, the target: the same window shifted one position to the left, so that y[t] is the token that follows x[t]. To make a batch, we pick random starting points in the training text and cut a window at each. The batch has x and y of shape (32, 64). Reading the first example as text shows the shift clearly: x[0] starts with 't, for his purpose' and ends with 'no', while y[0] starts one character later, ', for his purpose', and ends with 'nor'. There are 1,003,789 possible starting points in the training text, and sampling is with replacement: repeated windows are possible and become increasingly likely over many training steps. A single window holds 64 training examples, not one. Because of the causal mask, the prediction at position t can only use x[0] to x[t], so each position is a separate next-character question with its own amount of context: At position 0, the model has seen only 't' and must predict ','. At position 7 it has seen 't, for h' and must predict 'i'. And so on, up to position 63, where it has the full window. One forward pass answers all 64 questions at once, and in a batch of 32 windows that is 2,048 predictions, each contributing to the loss. This is the parallel training that Note 6.1 promised; we use it in Note 6.6. Finally, because the starting points are random, we draw them from a seeded torch.Generator so that results can be reproduced: The same seed gives exactly the same batch (True). In Note 6.6, this lets us compare different training settings on identical sequences of batches. Common mistake: shifting the targets the wrong way, or not at all. If y equals x, the model learns to copy its input, which the causal mask makes trivially easy: the loss falls to almost zero and the model learns nothing useful. If your language model's loss looks too good to be true, check the shift first. Check yourself. 1. In a batch of shape (32, 64), how many next-token predictions contribute to the loss? Worked answer 32 × 64 = 2,048. Every position in every window is a separate next-token prediction.

title: The Big Picture: How Attention Helps a Model Focus on Relevant Information
text: Imagine reading the sentence "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired." To understand "it", you look back over the sentence and decide that "animal" is the relevant word, not "street". If the sentence ended "...because it was too wide", you would pick "street" instead. Understanding a word means gathering information from the right other words, and which words are right depends on the context. Attention gives every token a way to do exactly that. For each token, it works out how relevant every other token is, then builds a new vector for the token from a relevance-weighted mix of the others. The token's new vector now carries context. Figure 6.3.1. Bidirectional illustration with invented attention weights. Later tired or wide can affect an earlier position only when the mask permits it. A causal model at it cannot see those future words. Attention mixes projected values and is not a guaranteed explanation of a decision. The rest of this note explains how a network computes "how relevant", and how it uses the answer.

title: The Limitations of Processing Tokens Independently
text: First, let's see precisely why we need a mechanism like this. Most layers you know, such as linear layers, activation functions and the feed-forward network inside a Transformer block, process each token's vector on its own. Whatever the surrounding tokens are, the same input vector produces the same output vector. Here is the word "bank" in two sentences, "the river bank" and "money in the bank", passed through such a per-token layer: The two outputs for "bank" are identical (True). However many per-token layers we stack, "bank" by the river and "bank" with the money will always be processed identically, because no information ever flows between positions. This is the static-representation problem from Note 5.3, seen from inside a network. To build context, tokens must be able to read from each other. That is the one job of attention.

title: Self-Attention: The Complete Picture
text: Here is the whole mechanism for a sequence of T tokens, each represented by a vector. We call it self-attention because the tokens attend to other tokens of the same sequence. 1. Project. From each token's vector, compute three new vectors with three different learned linear layers: a query q, a key k and a value v. 2. Score. For every pair of tokens (i, j), compute a relevance score: the dot product of token i's query with token j's key. 3. Scale.
