Divide every score by √d, where d is the length of the query and key vectors. 4. Mask (decoders only). Block the scores for pairs that are not allowed, such as future tokens. 5. Normalise. Apply softmax across each row, so that each token's weights over all the tokens are positive and add up to 1. 6. Mix. Each token's output is the weighted average of all the value vectors, using its weights. Written compactly, with the queries, keys and values for all tokens stacked as rows of matrices Q, K and V: Don't worry if the formula looks dense: Sections 4 to 8 take it apart one step at a time, with numbers you can check by hand. Figure 6.3.2. Project Q, K and V; compare queries with keys; scale by √dₖ; apply the mask before row-wise softmax; then mix values. Each output is a weighted sum of projected value vectors.

title: Queries, Keys, and Values: An Intuitive Introduction
text: Why three different vectors per token? Think of a library search. - The query is what you are looking for: the search you type. - Each book has a key: the label or catalogue entry that describes it, used only for matching. - Each book also has its value: the actual content you take away once you decide it is relevant. Matching uses queries against keys; what you collect is values. Separating them lets a token look for one thing while offering something different. For example, a verb might look for its subject (its query), describe itself as an action (its key), and pass on information about tense (its value). In a Transformer, all three are produced by learned linear layers from the token's vector, so the network learns what to look for, how to describe itself and what to pass on. To keep the arithmetic visible, we will use a hand-made example with 4 tokens, "the cat sat down", and query, key and value vectors of just 2 numbers each. The numbers are chosen so that "sat" and "down" look for something that "cat" offers, as a verb might look for its subject.

title: Computing Attention Scores
text: The score between token i and token j is the dot product of i's query with j's key: multiply matching entries and add. A large score means "j's key matches what i is looking for". We compute all 16 scores with two loops, then check against the single matrix product Q Kᵀ. Read the score grid row by row; each row is one token asking "who is relevant to me?". - The row for "sat" is [0, 4, 1, 0]. Its query [2, 0] matches the key of "cat", [2, 0], strongly: 2 × 2 + 0 × 0 = 4. The other keys match much less. - The row for "down" is similar, [0.5, 4, 1.25, 0.25]: it is also most interested in "cat". - "the" and "cat" share the query [0, 1], so their rows are identical: [1, 0, 0.5, 0.5]. The loops and Q @ K.T give exactly the same grid (True). In practice we always use the matrix product: one operation computes every score at once, which is exactly the parallelism that makes Transformers fast. Check yourself. 1. A query is [1, 2] and a key is [3, −1]. What is their score? Worked answer 1 × 3 + 2 × (−1) = 3 − 2 = 1.

title: Scaling and Softmax
text: Scores can be any size, but we want weights: positive numbers that add up to 1 for each token, so that each token divides 100% of its attention among the others. Softmax does exactly that. But before softmax, the scores are divided by √d. Why? 6.1 Why divide by √d A dot product adds up d products. If the entries of queries and keys are random numbers with a typical size of about 1, then the more numbers you add, the larger the typical result: its spread grows like √d. Let's measure that with 10,000 random query–key pairs. The spread (standard deviation) of the raw dot products is 1.99 for d = 4, 8.01 for d = 64 and 22.45 for d = 512, growing like √d (√4 = 2, √64 = 8, √512 ≈ 22.6). After dividing by √d, it is 1.00, 1.00 and 0.99: the same at every size. Why does the size of the scores matter? Because softmax exaggerates differences. If scores are large, the largest one swallows almost all the weight. Here are 8 scores with d = 512, passed through softmax with and without scaling: Without scaling, softmax puts a weight of 1.000 on a single key and 0.0 on the other seven: the entropy is 0.000, which means no uncertainty and no blending at all. With scaling, the largest weight is 0.442 and the rest is shared among several keys, with an entropy of 1.480 (the maximum possible for 8 keys is 2.079). This matters for learning, not just for the output. When softmax is that extreme, small changes to the scores barely change the weights, so the gradients flowing back through the softmax are close to zero, and the queries and keys stop learning. Dividing by √d keeps scores at a sensible size however wide the vectors are, so attention can stay soft and trainable. Now we apply both steps to the "the cat sat down" scores. Here d = 2, so we divide by √2 ≈ 1.414. Every row now adds up to 1. "Sat" gives 0.808 of its attention to "cat" and spreads the rest thinly. "Down" gives 0.771 to "cat". "The" and "cat", with their weak, similar scores, spread their attention more evenly: their largest weight is only 0.345. Common mistake: applying softmax over the wrong dimension. The weights for one query must sum to 1 across the keys, so softmax goes over the last dimension (dim=-1) of the score matrix. If the weights for one token add up to something other than 1, check the dimension.

title: Weighted Sums and Contextual Representations
text: The final step uses the weights to mix the values. Each token's output is the weighted average of every token's value vector, using that token's row of weights. In matrix form, it is simply weights @ V. The output for "sat" is [0.168, 0.928]. Our hand calculation, 0.048 × the value of "the" + 0.808 × the value of "cat" + 0.097 × the value of "sat" + 0.048 × the value of "down", gives the same vector. Since the value of "cat" is [0, 1], the output for "sat" has become mostly "cat": the verb has pulled in information about its subject. "The" and "cat", whose weights are more evenly spread, get a more blended output, [0.709, 0.534]. This is how attention creates contextual representations. Each output vector is no longer a description of a token on its own, but of the token together with what it found relevant. In a real Transformer, this output is added back into the token's residual stream (Note 6.1), so the token carries this context into the next layer. Check yourself. 1. If a token's weights were [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25], what would its output be? Worked answer The plain average of all four value vectors: each contributes exactly a quarter. Visual walkthrough: Mix values with causal attention. Choose each query position in turn. Masked future tokens receive zero weight; allowed weights sum to one. These supplied numbers illustrate the calculation. The web app adds a paused, step-by-step animation of the same example.

title: Causal Attention vs. Bidirectional Attention
text: So far, every token could attend to every other token, including the ones after it. That is bidirectional attention, used in encoders. A decoder that generates text must not let a token see the future, because during generation the future has not been written yet. If it could peek during training, it would learn to "predict" the next token by simply reading it, and would fail completely when generating. The fix is the causal mask from Note 6.1. Before softmax, we replace every score where the key comes after the query with −∞ (minus infinity). Since e to the power of −∞ is 0, softmax gives those positions exactly zero weight, and the remaining weights still add up to 1. The masked score grid has −∞ above the diagonal, and the weights there are exactly 0. Each row still sums to 1. Notice how the rows change: - "the" (position 0) can only see itself, so it gives itself all of its attention: 1.000. - "cat" (position 1) can see "the" and itself: 0.670 and 0.330. - "sat" (position 2) still gives most attention to "cat" (0.848), because "cat" comes before it. - "down" (position 3) can see everything, so its row is unchanged from the unmasked version. Key terms - Self-attention: attention in which a sequence's tokens attend to tokens of the same sequence. - Query, key, value: three learned projections of each token: what it looks for, how it is matched, and what it passes on. - Attention score: the dot product of a query with a key, divided by √d. - Attention weights: the softmax of the scores; each token's weights sum to 1. - Causal mask: setting scores for future positions to −∞ so their weights become 0. Check yourself. 1. In a causal model, how many tokens can position 0 attend to, and what is its weight on each? Worked answer One: itself. With only one allowed position, softmax gives it a weight of 1.

title: Multi-Head Attention
text: A single attention pattern can only express one kind of relevance at a time. But a token often needs several kinds of information at once: the previous word, the subject of the sentence, an earlier mention of the same name, the matching opening bracket. Multi-head attention runs several attention operations, called heads, side by side, each with its own query, key and value projections, so that each can learn a different kind of relationship. To keep the cost the same, the model's vector is split between the heads rather than copied. With d_model = 64 and 4 heads, each head works with 16 numbers: A (1, 10, 64) tensor is viewed as (1, 4, 10, 16): 4 heads, each seeing all 10 tokens with 16 numbers per token. Each head computes its own (10, 10) grid of weights. Afterwards, the heads' outputs are put back side by side into (1, 10, 64), and a final linear layer combines them. Reshaping back and forth loses nothing (True). To see why several heads help, let's build two heads by hand, each designed to capture a different relationship, for the words "to be or not to be". Each token's input vector contains two parts: which word it is, and which position it is at. We set the query and key weights directly: - Head A turns each token's position into a query for the previous position. - Head B turns each token's word into a query for the same word. The rows confirm the designs. Head A's row for "not" (position 3) puts 0.98 of its weight on position 2, the previous word "or". Head B's row for the second "be" (position 5) splits its weight between itself and the earlier "be" at position 1, 0.493 each: it found the previous copy of its own word. Here are both heads as heatmaps: Head A forms a clear diagonal one step below the main diagonal: every token looks at its predecessor (the first token, having no predecessor, looks at itself). Head B lights up only where a word matches an earlier copy of itself. The two heads read the same sentence and gather completely different information, and the model receives both. In a real Transformer, nobody designs the heads. Their weights are learned, and trained models do develop specialised heads like these. Patterns very much like Head A, "attend to the previous token", are among the most commonly found in trained language models. We will look at the heads of our own trained model in Note 6.6. Key terms - Head: one attention operation with its own query, key and value projections. - Multi-head attention: several heads running in parallel on slices of the model vector, combined by a final linear layer. - d_head: the vector length per head, d_model / n_heads. Check yourself. 1. A model has d_model = 512 and 8 heads. What is d_head? Worked answer 512 / 8 = 64.

title: Attention Is Order-Blind: Positional Information
text: Look back at the formula in Section 3. Nothing in it refers to where a token sits. Scores depend only on the vectors themselves. So if you shuffle the input tokens, every token still finds exactly the same partners with exactly the same weights, and the outputs are simply shuffled in the same way. Let's verify that with PyTorch's own attention layer: Without position information, shuffling the 5 input tokens gives exactly the same outputs, in the shuffled order (True). To attention alone, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would be the same bag of words, as in Note 5.4. But when we add a vector for each position before attention (and the positions stay put while the tokens move), shuffling the tokens changes the outputs (False). The position vectors have broken the symmetry: the model can now tell orderings apart. Transformers generally supply position through learned vectors, sinusoidal encodings, or mechanisms inside attention such as RoPE. The causal mask also carries some ordering information, so the unmasked permutation argument does not apply unchanged to causal attention. There are two common ways: - Learned position embeddings: a table with one learnable vector per position, as in Note 6.2. This is what our model uses. - Sinusoidal positional encodings: fixed vectors made from sine and cosine waves of many different frequencies, as in the original Transformer. Each dimension oscillates at its own speed, so every position gets a unique pattern. Let's compute the sinusoidal version for 64 positions and look at it. In the left panel, each column is one position's 64-number vector. The top dimensions oscillate quickly from position to position, and the lower ones slowly, rather like the hands of a clock: the second hand tells you small differences, the hour hand large ones. Together they give every position a distinct pattern. The right panel shows a useful property: nearby positions get similar vectors. The cosine similarity of position 10 with itself is 1.0, with position 11 it is 0.966, with position 15 it is 0.734, and it tends to fall further with distance (0.59 at position 30, 0.49 at position 60), although not perfectly smoothly. So the encoding carries a sense of "near" and "far", which attention can use. Common mistake: forgetting positional information when building a Transformer from scratch. The model will still train, but unmasked attention is permutation-equivariant, while causal attention has only the ordering information supplied by its mask, and it will plateau at a much worse loss than it should. Check yourself. 1. If attention by itself ignores order, why does a decoder with a causal mask still know something about order, even without position vectors? (Hint: think about what each position is allowed to see.) Worked answer The causal mask itself carries some order information: position 0 can attend only to one token, position 1 to two tokens, and so on. A token can partly infer where it is from how many tokens it can see. This is weak and indirect, so models still add explicit positional information.

title: The Cost of Attention: Why It Grows with Sequence Length Squared
text: Attention's great strength, that every token compares itself with every other token, is also its main cost. With T tokens, each head computes a T × T grid of scores. Double the sequence length and that grid becomes four times larger. With our context of 64 tokens, each head's score grid has 4,096 entries and needs 16 KB of memory at 32-bit precision. At 1,024 tokens it has 1,048,576 entries (4 MB): 256 times as many as at 64. At 8,192 tokens it needs 256 MB, per head, per layer, per sequence. At 131,072 tokens a single grid would need 65,536 MB, 64 GB, more memory than most GPUs have, and that is for just one head of one layer. This quadratic cost is the main reason context windows were limited for many years, and a great deal of engineering goes into managing it. Two key ideas are worth knowing by name: - Memory-efficient attention (for example FlashAttention) computes the same result in small tiles without ever storing the full T × T grid. PyTorch's F.scaled_dot_product_attention, which you will use in Section 12, can use such methods automatically. - Restricted attention patterns let each token attend to only part of the sequence, such as a sliding window of recent tokens, trading some reach for a cost that grows more slowly. Check yourself. 1. A model's context is increased from 4,096 to 16,384 tokens. By what factor does the size of each attention score grid grow? Worked answer 16,384 / 4,096 = 4 times as many tokens, so 4² = 16 times as many entries in each score grid.

title: Implementing Scaled Dot-Product Attention with PyTorch
text: Now we can put everything together into the attention module that our model will use in Note 6.5. It takes a batch of shape (B, T, d_model) and returns the same shape. Read the comments beside each line for the shapes. - One linear layer produces queries, keys and values at once (3 d_model outputs), which we split into three. - view and transpose split the model vector into heads: (B, T, D) becomes (B, H, T, d_head). - The core is the formula from Section 3: scores, scaling, causal mask, softmax, weighted sum of values. All heads are computed at once, because the head dimension is treated just like the batch dimension. - Merge and project: the heads are put back side by side, and the output projection proj combines them. Input and output are both (2, 12, 64), and the weights have shape (2, 4, 12, 12): for each of 2 sequences and 4 heads, a 12 × 12 grid. The module has 16,640 parameters: 64 × 192 + 192 for the combined query–key–value layer, plus 64 × 64 + 64 for the output projection. Any implementation from scratch should be checked against a trusted one. PyTorch provides F.scaled_dot_product_attention, which computes the core of attention (in a fast, memory-efficient way) given queries, keys and values. We feed it the same queries, keys and values as our module and compare: Our implementation matches PyTorch's (True), with a maximum difference of 1.2e-07, which is just floating-point rounding. And no weight sits above the diagonal (True), so the causal mask works. In real projects you would normally call F.scaled_dot_product_attention directly, because it is faster and uses less memory; writing it yourself once is how you understand what it does. Finally, let's look at the weights our untrained module produces for the opening of Romeo's famous line, "ROMEO:\nBut, soft! what light", using random untrained embeddings. The triangle shape is the causal mask at work: nothing above the diagonal. Within the triangle, the patterns are noisy and unfocused. For the last position, head 0's largest weight is 0.168, compared with 0.036 if the weight were spread evenly over all 28 positions. There is some structure, from the random weights, but nothing meaningful: an untrained module has not yet learned what to look for. In Note 6.6 we will draw the same kind of picture for the trained model and compare.

title: The Big Picture: How a Transformer Block Works
text: A Transformer block takes a sequence of token vectors and returns a sequence of the same shape, (batch, tokens, d_model), with each vector improved. It does that in two sub-layers, each wrapped in the same pattern: 1. Attention sub-layer: normalise the vectors, let tokens exchange information with multi-head self-attention, and add the result back to the input. 2. Feed-forward sub-layer: normalise again, process each token separately with a small two-layer network, and add the result back. So the four ingredients are multi-head self-attention, a feed-forward network, residual connections (the "add back" steps) and layer normalisation (the "normalise" steps). In code, the modern version of the block is just two lines: Figure 6.4.1. The pre-norm block adds attention and feed-forward updates to the residual stream, with LayerNorm on each branch. Every stage preserves (B, T, 64). The feed-forward network is shared across positions. Here is the block in PyTorch, built from the attention module of Note 6.3. It has two switches that we will use for experiments later: pre_norm chooses where layer normalisation goes, and residual lets us remove the "add back" steps. The block maps a (2, 10, 64) input to a (2, 10, 64) output. Its 49,984 parameters split into 16,640 for attention, 33,088 for the feed-forward network and 256 for the two layer norms. Notice that this attention module calls F.scaled_dot_product_attention directly: we checked in Note 6.3 that it computes exactly what our own code did.

title: Multi-Head Self-Attention
text: The first sub-layer is the attention module from Note 6.3, unchanged. Within the block, its role is to gather: each token pulls in a weighted mix of information from the earlier tokens it finds relevant. What attention does not do is much processing. Its output for each token is essentially a weighted average of value vectors, followed by one linear projection: a good way to collect information, but a fairly simple operation. Making sense of what was gathered is left to the second sub-layer.

title: Feed-Forward Networks
text: The feed-forward network (FFN) is a small multilayer perceptron, just like the MLPs you built in Module 2: a linear layer that expands each token's 64 numbers to 256, a non-linear activation, and a linear layer that brings it back to 64. Its job is to process each token's vector after attention has gathered context into it, computing new features from the combination. The FFN is applied to every token separately and identically: the same weights, no information passing between positions. We can check that processing all tokens together gives exactly the same result as processing them one at a time: Token by token or all at once, the outputs are the same (True). Inside, each token's vector briefly becomes 256 numbers wide, (1, 5, 256), before being projected back. This "expand, transform, contract" shape gives the FFN room to compute many intermediate features, and it is why the FFN holds about two-thirds of the block's parameters: 33,088 of 49,984. The activation in the middle is GELU (Gaussian Error Linear Unit), a smooth relative of ReLU used in most modern Transformers: For large positive inputs, the two are almost the same. The difference is near zero: ReLU has a sharp corner and outputs exactly 0 for every negative input, while GELU curves smoothly and lets small negative values through (at −1, ReLU gives 0.0 and GELU gives −0.1587). The smooth shape gives gradients for slightly negative inputs too, which tends to make training a little easier. Check yourself. 1. The FFN never lets tokens exchange information. Why can a Transformer still produce contextual representations? Worked answer Because the attention sub-layer, which comes first in every block, has already mixed information from other tokens into each token's vector. The FFN then processes that context-rich vector. Attention gathers; the FFN processes what was gathered.

title: Residual Connections
text: A residual connection (or skip connection) adds a sub-layer's input to its output: instead of x = f(x), we compute x = x + f(x). The sub-layer only has to learn a change to apply to the vector, not a complete new vector. This matters for two reasons. - Information is preserved. The original token information flows straight up the stack. Each sub-layer adds to it rather than replacing it. This is the "residual stream" picture from Note 6.1. - Gradients have a direct path. During backpropagation, the derivative of x + f(x) with respect to x includes a plain "+1" from the x term. So the gradient can flow from the loss back to the early layers along an uninterrupted highway, however deep the stack, instead of being multiplied through every sub-layer in turn, which, as Note 5.4 showed, makes gradients shrink. Let's measure the second point. We build stacks of 1, 4, 12 and 24 blocks, with and without residual connections, pass a random input through, and measure the size of the gradient that arrives back at the input. With residual connections, the gradient reaching the input is 3.33e-02 for one block and grows to 1.54e-01 for 24 blocks. Without them, it is much smaller at every depth, between 4.37e-03 and 5.31e-03, about 8 times smaller with one block and about 29 times smaller with 24. The deeper the stack, the more the residual path matters. In Section 7 we will see what this means for actual training. Key terms - Residual (skip) connection: adding a layer's input to its output, x + f(x). - Residual stream: the sequence of token vectors that flows up through the model and that each sub-layer adds to. Check yourself. 1. If a sub-layer learns to output all zeros, what does a block with residual connections do to its input? Worked answer It passes the input through unchanged: x + 0 = x. This is one reason residual blocks are easy to train: a block that has not learned anything useful yet does no harm.

title: Layer Normalisation
text: As a vector flows up through many blocks, each adding something to it, its numbers can drift to very different sizes. Large values make later layers behave erratically, and they make the best learning rate hard to choose. Layer normalisation (LayerNorm) keeps every token's vector at a standard scale. For each token separately, LayerNorm: 1. computes the mean and variance of that token's numbers; 2. subtracts the mean and divides by the square root of the variance (plus a tiny number, 1e-5, to avoid dividing by zero), so the vector has mean 0 and standard deviation 1; 3. multiplies by a learnable scale and adds a learnable shift, so the model can choose a different scale if that helps. Let's do it by hand for a 4-number vector: The vector [2, −1, 4, 3] has mean 2.0 and variance 3.5. Subtracting the mean and dividing by √3.5 gives [0.0, −1.6036, 1.069, 0.5345], exactly what nn.LayerNorm returns. The learnable scale starts at 1 and the shift at 0, so at the start of training LayerNorm is pure standardisation. Here is its effect on tokens of wildly different sizes: Before normalisation, the five tokens' standard deviations range from 0.1 to 853.7. After it, every token has a standard deviation of 1.0 and a mean of 0.0. At initialisation this gives a predictable scale. After training, the learned per-coordinate scale and shift can change the output mean and standard deviation; they need not remain exactly 0 and 1. Note what LayerNorm normalises over: the 64 numbers within one token. It does not mix information between tokens or between examples in a batch, unlike the batch normalisation used in many CNNs. So it behaves identically in training and inference, and for any batch size. Key terms - Layer normalisation: rescaling each token's vector to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, followed by a learnable scale and shift. Check yourself. 1. LayerNorm is applied to a token vector whose 64 numbers are all equal to 5. What problem arises, and how does the small constant 1e-5 help? Worked answer All 64 numbers equal the mean, so the variance is 0, and dividing by √0 would mean dividing by zero. Adding 1e-5 inside the square root keeps the division safe; the result is simply a vector of zeros (before the learnable shift). Visual walkthrough: Normalise one token, coordinate by coordinate. Follow centring, scaling and the learned affine transformation. The coordinates remain different. These supplied numbers illustrate the calculation. The web app adds a paused, step-by-step animation of the same example.

title: The Order of Operations Within a Transformer Block
text: There are two ways to combine normalisation with the residual connections. - Post-norm (the original Transformer): transform, add, then normalise: x = LayerNorm(x + sublayer(x)). The normalisation sits on the residual stream itself. - Pre-norm (most modern Transformers): normalise the sub-layer's input, transform, then add: x = x + sublayer(LayerNorm(x)). The residual stream is never normalised; it is a clean highway from bottom to top. Figure 6.4.2. Post-norm puts normalisation on the residual path after each addition. Pre-norm puts it at each branch input, leaving an identity route within the block. A final model-level norm may still follow the stack; training behaviour depends on the full setup. The difference looks cosmetic. Let's find out whether it is. We train a 6-block language model on Tiny Shakespeare, predicting the next character, with a fairly high learning rate of 0.01, for 250 steps, in three versions, each with two random seeds: - post-norm, with no warmup; - pre-norm, with no warmup; - post-norm, with a 100-step learning-rate warmup: the learning rate starts near zero and rises linearly to 0.01 over the first 100 steps. The training function also records the gradient norm at every step: the overall size of all the gradients combined, a useful health check. The results split sharply. - Post-norm, no warmup fails on both seeds: its loss is stuck at 3.341 and 3.317. With seed 1, its gradient norm spiked to 117.6 at one point. - Pre-norm, no warmup trains well on both seeds: 2.133 and 2.146. - Post-norm with warmup trains on both seeds too, 2.229 and 2.232, although a little behind pre-norm after the same number of steps. What does a loss of about 3.3 mean? Let's compute two reference points: A model that ignores the input and always predicts the overall frequency of each character (how often e, space, t and so on appear) gets a loss of 3.309. A completely uniform guess gets ln(65) = 4.174. The failed post-norm runs, at 3.317 and 3.341, have collapsed to the character-frequency baseline: the model has learned how common each character is, and nothing else. The plot shows it happening. The post-norm run (red) drops quickly, then falls onto the dashed baseline within about ten steps and never leaves it. The pre-norm run (blue) and the warmed-up post-norm run (green) keep improving throughout. Why does post-norm break? In post-norm, every gradient travelling down the residual stream must pass through a LayerNorm in every block, and early in training, with random weights and a large learning rate, the first updates can be large enough to knock the model into a state from which it does not recover. Warmup avoids those damaging first steps by keeping the early updates small, and pre-norm avoided this failure in our experiment by keeping the residual path free of normalisation. This is why almost every modern Transformer uses pre-norm, and why warmup is standard practice whenever post-norm (or any fragile setup) is used. The original Transformer paper also trained with a learning-rate warmup. Common mistake: concluding that a model or dataset "doesn't work" because a loss curve flattens at a baseline. A loss stuck at the character-frequency (or class-frequency) baseline usually means training has collapsed, often because of an unstable setup. Before changing anything else, compare against simple baselines, then try a lower learning rate, warmup or pre-norm. Key terms - Post-norm / pre-norm: layer normalisation applied after the residual addition / to each sub-layer's input. - Learning-rate warmup: gradually increasing the learning rate from near zero at the start of training. - Gradient norm: the overall size of all gradients combined; a sudden spike is a warning sign. - Training collapse: training that gets stuck at a trivial solution, such as predicting only class frequencies. Check yourself. 1. A colleague's post-norm Transformer is stuck at a loss equal to the character-frequency baseline. Suggest two changes, each supported by the experiment above. Worked answer Either switch to pre-norm blocks, which trained well with the same learning rate, or add a learning-rate warmup, which rescued post-norm on both seeds. Lowering the learning rate is a third reasonable option.

title: Stacking Transformer Blocks: Why Depth and Residual Connections Matter
text: A single block lets each token gather information once and process it once. Stacking blocks lets the model build on what earlier blocks found. One block might connect each character to the one before it; a later block can then use that to recognise whole words; later still, which speaker is talking. Each block's attention works on vectors that already contain context from the blocks below, so the reach and complexity of what the model can represent grows with depth: the same hierarchy idea as CNN layers in Note 5.2. Depth costs parameters, but each block adds the same amount: Each extra block adds 49,984 parameters (for example, 60,545 for one block, 160,513 for three and 310,465 for six; the rest is the embeddings, final norm and output head). Large language models stack dozens of much wider blocks. But depth only helps if the stack can be trained. In Section 4 we saw that removing residual connections makes the gradient reaching the input much smaller. Here is what that means in practice: the same 6-block pre-norm model, trained for 200 steps at a learning rate of 0.003, with and without residual connections. With residual connections, the model reaches a loss of 2.267. Without them, it reaches 3.296: almost exactly the character-frequency baseline of 3.309. Without the residual highway, this 6-block model learns essentially nothing about context in 200 steps. This experiment shows how important residual connections are for this deep stack and training budget; it does not prove that every non-residual architecture is untrainable. Check yourself. 1. Why might a 1-block model without residual connections still train reasonably, while a 6-block model without them fails? Worked answer With one block, the gradient has only one sub-layer pair to pass through, so enough of it reaches the embeddings. With six blocks and no residual path, the gradient must pass through twelve sub-layers in turn and arrives much weaker, so the early layers barely learn, and the input information is replaced rather than refined at every step.

title: The Big Picture: Assembling the Components
text: A decoder-only language model is a stack of the pieces you already know, in this order: 1. Token embedding: each character ID becomes a 64-number vector. 2. Position embedding: a learned vector for each position (0 to 63) is added. 3. Transformer blocks × 3: pre-norm blocks with causal multi-head self-attention and a feed-forward network, exactly as in Note 6.4. 4. Final layer norm: with pre-norm blocks, the residual stream itself is never normalised, so we normalise it once at the end. 5. Output head: a linear layer from 64 numbers to one score per vocabulary entry. First we load the data and the batch function from Note 6.2. Now the model. The attention and block classes are the ones from Notes 6.3 and 6.4, written compactly. The GPT class assembles them. Two details are worth noticing: - forward accepts optional targets. If they are given, the model also computes the cross-entropy loss, comparing its predictions at every position with the true next characters. This keeps the training loop in Note 6.6 short. - The assert refuses sequences longer than the context window, because there is no position embedding for position 64 or beyond. A clear error message here saves a confusing one later. The complete model has 162,561 parameters, exactly the same as the version we built from PyTorch's ready-made layers in Note 6.1. Same design, same size; the difference is that now we have written every part ourselves. Figure 6.5.1. The untied reference model has 162,561 parameters. A 64-token input produces logits of shape (B, 64, 65). Cross-entropy consumes raw logits during training; softmax converts them to probabilities for inspection or sampling.

title: From Input Tokens to Output Predictions
text: Let's pass a batch of 4 training windows through the model one stage at a time and print the shape after each stage. The journey is short: - 4 windows of 64 token IDs, (4, 64), become token embeddings of shape (4, 64, 64). - The position embeddings have shape (64, 64), one vector per position. PyTorch's broadcasting (Module 2) adds the same position vectors to every sequence in the batch, so the sum is still (4, 64, 64). - The three blocks and the final layer norm keep the shape (4, 64, 64). - The output head turns each 64-number vector into 65 scores: logits of shape (4, 64, 65). So for every one of the 4 × 64 = 256 positions in the batch, the model produces a full set of scores for what comes next. Common mistake: confusing the two 64s. In (4, 64, 64), the first 64 is the number of positions (the context) and the second is d_model, the vector size. They are equal in our model by coincidence. If you change one, the other must not change with it. When shapes look ambiguous, print them with descriptive labels, or choose different sizes while debugging so that every dimension is distinguishable.

title: Output Projections and Probability Distributions
text: The output head is a single linear layer, but it carries a whole idea: it compares each token's final vector against a learned vector for every entry in the vocabulary and produces a score for each. Higher score, more likely next token. Softmax turns the 65 scores at each position into a probability distribution: 65 positive numbers that add up to 1. Let's look at the prediction at position 10 of the first window. The probabilities have shape (4, 64, 65), and each set of 65 sums to 1.0. At position 10, the model has seen 't, for his ' and the true next character is 'p' (the text continues "purpose"). The untrained model's top guesses are 'h', 'A', '!', 'u' and 's', each with only about 0.03 to 0.05 probability, and it gives the correct 'p' just 0.013. As expected, it knows nothing yet. 3.1 What loss should an untrained model have? The cross-entropy loss is the average of −log(probability given to the true next token) over all positions. If the model gave every character the same probability, 1/65, the loss would be −log(1/65) = ln(65). So before training, the loss should be close to that value. The untrained model's loss is 4.301, a little above the uniform-guess value of 4.174. The reason is that its random logits are not all equal: they have a spread of 0.582, so its guesses are slightly confident in random directions, which costs a bit more than guessing uniformly. Close to ln(vocabulary size), and a little above it, is exactly what a healthy, freshly initialised model should show. This is the first sanity check for any classifier or language model. If the starting loss is far above ln(vocabulary size), something is wrong, usually initial logits that are far too large, or labels that do not match the outputs. 3.2 Weight tying The token embedding table (65 × 64) and the output head's weights (65 × 64) both hold one vector per vocabulary entry: one is used to read tokens in, the other to score tokens out. Many language models tie them, using the same matrix for both, which saves parameters and often helps a little. Tying removes 4,160 parameters, the size of one 65 × 64 matrix: 162,561 becomes 158,401. In large models with vocabularies of tens of thousands of tokens, the saving is substantial. We keep our model untied for simplicity. Key terms - Output head: the final linear layer that turns each vector into one score (logit) per vocabulary entry. - Probability distribution: a set of non-negative numbers that sum to 1, one per possible outcome. - Cross-entropy loss: the average of −log(probability of the correct token). - Weight tying: using the same matrix for the token embedding and the output head. Check yourself. 1. A language model with a vocabulary of 50,000 tokens reports a loss of 10.8 before any training. Is that plausible? (ln(50,000) ≈ 10.82.) Worked answer Yes. A loss of 10.8 is almost exactly ln(50,000) ≈ 10.82, the loss of a uniform guess, which is what an untrained model should produce. A value far higher, say 30, would suggest a problem.

title: Implementing a Simplified Transformer with PyTorch: Checking It Works
text: A new model can have bugs that produce no error message at all: a mask that does not mask, a shift in the wrong direction, a layer that never receives gradients. The model will still train, just badly, and you may lose days wondering why. So before training, we run two quick checks. 4.1 Check 1: the model cannot see the future If the causal mask works, the prediction at position t must depend only on tokens 0 to t. So if we change the token at position 40, the logits at positions 0 to 39 must not change at all, while the logits from position 40 onwards may. The largest change at positions 0 to 39 is exactly 0. From position 40 onwards, every position changes, by between 8.28e-03 and 1.36e+00. The biggest change is at position 40 itself, whose own input changed. The later changes are small because the untrained model mixes in context only weakly, but they are there. The causal mask works: no information flows backwards from the future. If this test ever shows changes before the edited position, the model is leaking future information. During training it would learn to "predict" tokens by reading them, reach a suspiciously low loss, and then generate nonsense. 4.2 Check 2: can the model learn at all? Overfit one batch The second check is a classic: take one small batch and train on it repeatedly. A model with enough capacity, a working loss and correctly flowing gradients should be able to memorise a single batch almost perfectly. If it cannot, something is broken in the training pipeline, and there is no point training on the full dataset yet. On the single batch, the loss falls from 4.301 to 0.01 by step 100 and 0.007 by step 300: the model has memorised it almost perfectly, so gradients are flowing and every part can learn. But look at the last line. On a different batch, the same model's loss is 7.281, far worse than an untrained model's 4.301. It has not learned Shakespeare; it has memorised 8 windows and become confidently wrong about everything else. This is overfitting in its most extreme form, and it is exactly what the check is designed to produce. A sanity check, not a training method. 4.3 Generating text from the untrained model Finally, let's see what the model writes before training. Generation works one token at a time: run the model on the text so far, take the probability distribution at the last position, draw the next character from it, append it, and repeat. (We keep at most the last 64 characters, the context window.) Note 6.6 covers this process, and better ways to choose the next token, in detail. After the prompt "ROMEO:", the untrained model produces random characters: capitals, punctuation and letters with no structure at all. Every piece of the model works; it simply has not learned anything yet. That is the starting point for Note 6.6. Common mistake: skipping sanity checks to save time. Checking the initial loss, the causal mask and the overfit-one-batch behaviour takes seconds. Discovering a broken mask after hours of training wastes far more time, and a silent bug may never be discovered at all. Check yourself. 1. A colleague's overfit-one-batch test gets stuck at a loss of 3.3 and never goes lower. Name two things that might be wrong. Worked answer Possible causes include: the targets are not aligned with the inputs (for example, not shifted, or shifted the wrong way); gradients are not reaching the parameters (for example, optimizer.zero_grad(), loss.backward() or optimizer.step() is missing, or the optimizer was given the wrong parameters); the learning rate is far too high or too low; or the model has collapsed to predicting character frequencies, which is what a loss of about 3.3 suggests on this dataset.

title: How Encoders, Cross-Attention and Encoder–Decoder Models Differ
text: Our model is decoder-only. Here is how the other two families from Note 6.1 would differ from what we built, in terms of code: - An encoder-only model uses the same blocks without the causal mask: in our attention class, is_causal=True becomes False. Every token then sees the whole input. The output head is usually replaced too: for classification, the token vectors are pooled into one vector and a small head predicts the class. - An encoder–decoder model has two stacks. The encoder is a stack of unmasked blocks that reads the source sequence. The decoder is a stack like ours, but each decoder block has a third sub-layer, between self-attention and the feed-forward network: cross-attention. In cross-attention, the queries come from the decoder's tokens, while the keys and values come from the encoder's output. So each target token asks "which parts of the source are relevant to me?" and gathers information from them. No causal mask is needed there, because the whole source is known in advance. Seven decoder tokens attend over ten encoder outputs. The output has one vector per decoder token, (1, 7, 64), and the weights have shape (1, 7, 10): for each of the 7 target tokens, a distribution over the 10 source tokens, each summing to 1.0. Translating "the cat sat" into French, the token being generated for "chat" would, after training, place most of its weight on "cat". Figure 6.5.2. Decoder queries attend to keys and values from encoded source tokens. Target self-attention is causal; source self-attention is bidirectional apart from any padding mask. Residual connections and norms are omitted for clarity. Key terms - Cross-attention: attention in which queries come from one sequence (the decoder's) and keys and values from another (the encoder's output). Check yourself. 1. Why does cross-attention not need a causal mask, while the decoder's self-attention does? Worked answer During translation, the entire source sentence is available from the start, so letting every target token see all of it is legitimate. The decoder's self-attention looks at the target sequence itself, which is being generated one token at a time; during training, a target token must not see the target tokens after it, or it could simply read the answer.

title: The Big Picture: From Training Examples to Language Generation
text: Here is the whole story in two loops. The training loop (repeated many times): 1. Take a batch of real text windows, and their targets: the same windows shifted one character left. 2. Run the model once; it predicts the next character at every position. 3. Measure how wrong it was with cross-entropy loss. 4. Backpropagate and update the weights. The generation loop (repeated once per new character): 1. Run the model on the text so far. 2. Take its probability distribution for the next character. 3. Choose one character from that distribution. 4. Append it to the text and repeat. Figure 6.6.1. Teacher forcing compares every position with its true next character in one masked pass. Generation samples from the last position, appends the choice, and repeats with fixed weights. ↵ denotes a newline; the sample text is illustrative. The first half of this note (Sections 2–7) is about training; the second half (Sections 8–10) is about generation. The model and data are exactly as before: 1,003,854 training characters, 111,540 validation characters, a 65-character vocabulary, and a model with 162,561 parameters.

title: Next-Token Prediction
text: A language model is trained on one deceptively simple task: given the text so far, predict the next token. No labels are needed beyond the text itself; every character in the training data is the answer to the question "what comes after the characters before it?". This makes language modelling self-supervised, like the skip-gram objective in Note 5.3, and it is why language models can learn from enormous amounts of raw text. Why should such a simple task produce anything impressive? Because predicting the next character well requires a lot of knowledge. To predict that "KING RICH" continues with "A", the model must have learned character names. To predict a line break followed by a speaker's name in capitals, it must have learned the layout of a play. To predict the end of a word it has never seen in exactly that context, it must have learned spelling patterns. Every regularity in the text becomes a way to reduce the loss. Large language models are trained on exactly this task, with subword tokens and vastly more text, and the knowledge they show is a by-product of predicting the next token very well.

title: Training Targets and Label Shifting
text: As we set up in Note 6.2, each training example is a window of text x and a target y that is the same window shifted one position to the left, so that y[t] is the character that follows x[t]. The input begins 't, for his purpose in th' and the target begins one character later, ', for his purpose in the'. The check confirms that the target is exactly the input shifted by one (True). Combined with the causal mask, this shift turns one window into many separate questions: at position t, "having seen x[0] to x[t], what is y[t]?".

title: Cross-Entropy Loss for Language Modelling
text: At each position, the model outputs a probability distribution over the 65 characters. The loss at that position is −log(the probability the model gave to the correct next character), and the overall loss is the average over all positions. This is the same cross-entropy loss you have used for classification since Module 1; a language model is simply a 65-way classifier applied at every position. Here is a single position worked by hand, with three possible tokens: Softmax turns the logits [2.0, 1.0, 0.1] into probabilities [0.659, 0.242, 0.099]. The correct token is the first, so the loss is −log(0.659) = 0.417, which matches F.cross_entropy. The table underneath shows how the loss depends on the probability given to the correct token: 0.105 at a probability of 0.9, 0.693 at 0.5, 2.303 at 0.1 and 4.605 at 0.01. The loss punishes confident mistakes severely and rewards confident correct answers. 4.1 Baselines: what does a given loss mean? A loss of, say, 2.0 means nothing on its own. Before training, we compute the validation loss of three very simple predictors, which give us a scale to read our model's loss against: - Uniform: every character equally likely. - Character frequencies (unigram): always predict each character with its overall frequency in the training text, ignoring context entirely. - Previous character only (bigram): predict the next character from the counts of which character follows which in the training text. This uses exactly one character of context. On the validation text, a uniform guess scores 4.174, character frequencies 3.347, and the bigram model 2.482. The bigram model has already learned some real structure: after q, it predicts u with probability 0.898. Our Transformer sees up to 64 characters of context, so to be worth anything it must beat 2.482 clearly. Key terms - Next-token prediction: the task of predicting each token from the tokens before it. - Self-supervised learning: learning from targets created from the data itself, here the next character. - Unigram / bigram model: a predictor using no context / only the previous token. Check yourself. 1. A model gives the correct next character a probability of 0.25. What is its loss at that position? Worked answer −log(0.25) = log(4) ≈ 1.386.

title: Teacher Forcing and Parallel Training
text: During training, the model always predicts each position from the real previous characters, never from its own earlier predictions. If it predicted the wrong character at position 5, position 6 still sees the true character at position 5. This is called teacher forcing: like a teacher correcting a student after every word, the model is always given the right history. Teacher forcing has a huge practical benefit. Because the inputs at every position are known in advance (they are just the real text), the model does not have to wait for its own predictions, so all positions can be computed at once. Together with the causal mask, one forward pass gives a prediction and a loss term at every position in every window. A batch of shape (32, 64) gives 2,048 next-character predictions from a single forward pass. A recurrent network would have to process the 64 positions one after another; a Transformer computes them all together. This parallelism is one of the main reasons Transformers could be trained on far more data than their predecessors. Teacher forcing also has a cost, which we will meet in Section 10: at generation time there is no teacher, and the model must live with its own mistakes. Key terms - Teacher forcing: during training, feeding the model the true previous tokens rather than its own predictions. - Parallel training: computing predictions and losses for all positions in one forward pass.

title: Training Stability: AdamW, Warmup, Schedules and Clipping
text: The training function below brings together four tools you have met in Module 3 and Note 6.4: - AdamW is Adam with decoupled weight decay: a small pull of every weight towards zero, applied separately from the gradient update, which acts as regularisation. It is the standard optimizer for Transformers. - Learning-rate warmup raises the learning rate linearly from almost zero over the first 100 steps, so the first, most chaotic updates are small. In Note 6.4 it was the difference between a post-norm model that collapsed and one that trained. - Cosine decay then lowers the learning rate smoothly from its peak to zero, following half a cosine wave. Large steps early let the model make fast progress; small steps late let it settle into a good solution. - Gradient clipping rescales the gradients whenever their overall size (norm) exceeds a threshold, here 1.0, so that one unusual batch cannot produce a huge, damaging update. clip_grad_norm_ also returns the norm before clipping, which we record as a health check. We also prepare 10 fixed validation batches, so that every validation loss is measured on exactly the same 640 windows. Here is the learning-rate schedule we will use for the main run: a straight climb to the peak over 100 steps, then a smooth cosine descent to zero at step 1,400. The peak learning rate is the most important setting to get right, so we choose it with a short experiment: train for 200 steps at three learning rates, with a constant learning rate and no warmup, and compare the validation loss. We never use the validation data to compute gradients, and we use the same random batches for every run. After 200 steps, a learning rate of 0.001 reaches a validation loss of 2.489, 0.003 reaches 2.330 and 0.01 reaches 2.190. The highest learning rate wins, so we choose 0.01. A caution about short sweeps: they favour higher learning rates, because a larger step size makes faster progress early on, even if it might cause trouble later. That is one reason we pair the chosen rate with warmup and decay, and why we check the full run's curves rather than trusting the sweep blindly. Common mistake: choosing settings by looking at the test set, or at the training loss. Training loss rewards memorisation; the test set must stay untouched until the very end. Choose on validation.

title: Training on Tiny Shakespeare and Reading the Loss Curves
text: Now the main run: 1,400 steps with a peak learning rate of 0.01, 100 warmup steps, cosine decay, AdamW and clipping at 1.0. Every 100 steps, we measure the validation loss. We also keep a copy of the untrained model for comparison. The validation loss falls steadily, from 2.487 after 100 steps to 1.742 at the end. It is still creeping down at the end, but slowly: the last three measurements are 1.752, 1.744 and 1.742, as the cosine schedule brings the learning rate down to zero. The average training loss over the last 100 steps is 1.547. Let's look at the curves, together with the gradient norms. Reading the loss curves (left). Start with the baselines. The model passes the character-frequency baseline (3.347) almost immediately, and the bigram baseline (2.482) at about step 100, where its validation loss is 2.487. From there on it is using more than one character of context. It ends at 1.742, far below the bigram's 2.482. Notice the growing gap between training loss (1.547 at the end) and validation loss (1.742). The model does somewhat better on the plays it trained on than on the held-out ones, but both curves are still falling together, with no sign of the validation loss turning upwards. This is a generalisation gap. There is no observed validation upturn in this run, although that alone cannot rule out all overfitting: in Module 3's terms, "train ↓, validation ↓". Reading the gradient norms (right). The gradient norm starts high in the first few steps, peaking at 0.84 at step 8, then settles around a median of 0.30. It never reaches the clipping threshold of 1.0: clipping was active on 0 of 1,400 steps. In this run, with pre-norm blocks and warmup, clipping turned out to be unnecessary. That is typical of a healthy run: clipping is insurance, which only matters when a bad batch or an unstable setup produces a spike like the 117.6 in Note 6.4's collapsed post-norm run. It costs almost nothing to keep. 7.1 What did the model learn? Let's compare the untrained and trained models' predictions after a few prompts. The untrained model's best guesses are random, around 0.04 to 0.05 each. The trained model is confident and usually right: - After "First Citiz" it predicts 'e' with probability 0.966: it knows the speaker name "First Citizen". - After "KING RICH" it predicts 'A' with 0.986: it knows "KING RICHARD", written in capitals. - After "my good lor" it predicts 'd' with 0.993. But not always. After "What light through yonder windo" its top guesses are 'm' (0.396) and 'n' (0.353), and the correct 'w' gets only 0.069. "Window" is rare in this text, and a small model trained for a couple of minutes has not learned it; "windom" and "window" might be equally plausible to it as spellings. Its knowledge is real but patchy. 7.2 How much context does the model use? The model sees up to 64 characters, but how much does it actually benefit from them? We can measure the validation loss separately at each position in the window: at position 0 the model has seen only one character, at position 63 it has seen 64. At position 0, with just one character to go on, the validation loss is 2.424, close to the bigram model's 2.482. That makes sense: with one character of context, the Transformer can do little more than a bigram model. The loss falls quickly as context grows: 2.196 with 2 characters, 1.952 with 3, 1.794 with 5 and 1.712 with 9. After that, the curve flattens out at roughly 1.7, with some noise from position to position: 1.663 at position 16, 1.770 at 32 and 1.748 at 63. Loss improves rapidly over the first few positions and then levels off in this diagnostic. This is consistent with useful short context, but it does not establish that the model ignores everything beyond ten characters: different positions predict different targets and use different learned position vectors. A controlled context-length test should predict the same held-out target tokens with progressively truncated histories. Longer-range ability depends on the data, training, architecture and task. 7.3 Inside the trained attention In Note 6.3 we built, by hand, a head that attends to the previous token. Did training produce anything similar? Here are the attention weights of the four heads in the first block for the line "KING RICHARD:\nThe king is dead", with numbers summarising, for each head, how much weight goes to each distance back. Two heads have learned sharp positional rules entirely on their own: - Head 1 puts an average weight of 0.97 on the previous character: it is the "previous token" head we designed by hand in Note 6.3, discovered by training. - Head 3 puts 0.91 on the character two positions back. Together, they let the next block see the last three characters directly. Heads 0 and 2 spread their attention more widely over the recent past (no more than 0.24 on any single distance in the first few), gathering broader context. Compare these sharp, purposeful patterns with the noisy weights of the untrained module in Note 6.3. Common mistake: reading too much into a single attention map. Attention shows where information is gathered from, not what is done with it, and later blocks may change everything. Here we backed the pictures with averages over a whole line; for real conclusions, measure over many inputs.

title: Autoregressive Inference
text: Now the second half: generation. A trained model gives us a probability distribution for the next character. To write text, we repeat four steps: 1. Run the model on the text so far (at most the last 64 characters, the context window). 2. Take the logits at the last position only: the model's scores for the next character. 3. Choose a character from them. Section 9 is about how. 4. Append it to the text, and go back to step 1. This is called autoregressive generation: each new token is predicted from the model's own previous outputs. Here is the full function, with the choice step written to support all the strategies of Section 9, followed by 300 characters generated after the prompt "ROMEO:" by sampling from the model's distribution as it is. Compare this with the random characters of the untrained model in Note 6.5. The trained model has learned the form of a play: speaker names in capitals followed by a colon and a line break ("JULIET:", "QUEEN MERSET:", "KINGHAM:"), lines of verse that start with capitals, punctuation in sensible places, and many real words ("I would", "to thee", "that's your", "a man is hither"). It has not learned meaning: the sentences do not make sense, and it invents words ("bleepelies", "excheeksiard") and names ("BUCKINGHRMOP"). For a 162,561-parameter model trained for a couple of minutes on one CPU core, reading one character at a time, that is about what we should expect. Visual walkthrough: Follow the autoregressive loop. Play or step through three character choices. Each chosen character becomes part of the next input; model weights stay fixed. These supplied numbers illustrate the calculation. The web app adds a paused, step-by-step animation of the same example.

title: Greedy Decoding and Sampling
text: At step 3 of the generation loop, the model gives us a probability distribution, and we must turn it into a single choice. This choice, called the decoding strategy, has a big effect on the text. - Greedy decoding always picks the single most likely token. It is deterministic: the same prompt always gives the same text. - Sampling draws the next token at random according to the model's probabilities, so a token with probability 0.3 is chosen about 30% of the time. Sampling is usually modified in one of three ways: - Temperature. Divide the logits by a number T before softmax. T below 1 makes the distribution sharper (more confident); T above 1 makes it flatter (more adventurous); T = 1 leaves it unchanged; and T approaching 0 becomes greedy. - Top-k. Keep only the k most likely tokens and set the rest to zero probability before sampling. - Top-p (nucleus sampling). Keep the smallest set of most likely tokens whose probabilities add up to at least p, and drop the rest. Unlike top-k, the number of candidates adapts to how confident the model is. Let's see temperature's effect on one real distribution: the model's prediction for the character after "...What light through yonder ". At temperature 1.0 the most likely next character is 't' (as in "the" or "thy") with probability 0.12, with an entropy of 3.07. At temperature 0.5 the same distribution becomes much sharper, with 't' at 0.25 and the entropy down to 2.44. At 1.5 it flattens to 0.08 and 3.39. Temperature never changes the order of the candidates, only how strongly the model prefers the top ones. Here, top-p with p = 0.9 keeps 18 candidates, while top-k with k = 5 would keep exactly 5. Now let's measure what each strategy does to the generated text. For each strategy we generate 300 characters after "ROMEO:", three times with different random seeds, and measure two things: - Training-vocabulary words: the share of generated words that appear somewhere in the training text. This measures vocabulary coverage, not factuality, grammaticality or meaning. - Distinct 8-character pieces: the share of all 8-character stretches of the output that are different from each other, a measure of variety. Text that repeats itself scores low. The trade-off is very clear: | Decoding | Real words | Distinct 8-character pieces | |---|---|---| | Greedy | 0.984 | 0.188 | | Temperature 0.5 | 0.919 | 0.992 | | Temperature 1.0 | 0.801 | 0.997 | | Temperature 1.5 | 0.450 | 1.000 | | Top-k, k = 5 | 0.869 | 1.000 | | Top-p, p = 0.9 | 0.830 | 0.997 | Greedy decoding uses almost only real words (0.984), but only 0.188 of its 8-character pieces are distinct: it repeats itself. Raising the temperature trades training-vocabulary word coverage for variety in these samples: at 1.5, fewer than half the words are real (0.450). Top-k and top-p improve on plain sampling at temperature 1.0 (0.869 and 0.830 real words, against 0.801) without losing variety, because they cut off the long tail of unlikely characters, where most invented words come from. Here are some of the samples behind those numbers: The greedy output falls into a loop almost immediately: "the shall the shall the shall..." over and over. Once the model has produced "the shall", the most likely continuation leads straight back to it, and greedy decoding has no way to escape. Temperature 0.5 reads most like English, with plausible phrases such as "serve the contents". Temperature 1.5 dissolves into invented words and stray capitals ("LeWToHat nexhand"). Top-p keeps the variety while producing a more convincing play layout. There is no single best setting: it depends on the use. Lower temperature can make outputs more repeatable; more sampling can increase variety. Neither greedy decoding nor a low temperature guarantees factual accuracy. Our "real words" score only checks membership in the training vocabulary: repeated familiar words can still form meaningless or false sentences. Choose a strategy using evaluations appropriate to the task, including factuality when it matters. Common mistake: concluding that a model is "broken" because greedy decoding produces endless repetition. Repetition loops are a known property of greedy decoding, not necessarily of the model. Try sampling with temperature, top-k or top-p before drawing conclusions. Key terms - Autoregressive generation: producing a sequence one token at a time, each predicted from the tokens generated so far. - Decoding strategy: the rule for choosing a token from the model's distribution. - Greedy decoding: always choosing the most likely token. - Temperature: dividing logits by T before softmax; T 1 flattens. - Top-k / top-p sampling: sampling only from the k most likely tokens / from the smallest set covering probability p. Check yourself. 1. At temperature 0.5, the model's top probability after "...through yonder " rose from 0.12 to 0.25. What would you expect at temperature 0.1? Worked answer Dividing the logits by 0.1 multiplies the differences between them by 10, so the distribution becomes extremely sharp: almost all the probability would go to 't', and the result would be very close to greedy decoding.

title: Training vs. Inference
text: Training and generation use the same model, but they differ in important ways: | | Training | Inference (generation) | |---|---|---| | Input | Real text windows | The prompt plus the model's own output | | Positions predicted | All of them at once (teacher forcing) | One new token per forward pass | | Gradients | Computed (loss.backward()) | Not needed (torch.no_grad()) | | Model mode | model.train() | model.eval() | | Speed bottleneck | Total compute per batch | One forward pass per generated token | Two of these differences show up directly in code: model.train() and model.eval() set the model's training flag (True and False). Our model has no dropout or batch normalisation, so the flag changes nothing here, but in models that have them it changes their behaviour, so the correct mode is a habit worth keeping (Module 2). Inside torch.no_grad(), the loss has requires_grad equal to False: PyTorch does not store anything for backpropagation, which saves memory and time during generation. The last line points to the main cost of generation: 300 new characters need 300 separate forward passes, one after another. Training processes many positions in parallel, but generation is inherently sequential. Production systems speed this up with a KV cache, which stores the keys and values already computed for earlier tokens so that each new step only has to process the newest token. You will meet it again in Module 7. The other important difference is exposure bias: during training the model always saw real text, but during generation it sees its own output, mistakes included. One invented word, such as "BUCKINGHRMOP", becomes part of the context for everything that follows, and the model was never trained to recover from its own errors. Sampling strategies that avoid unlikely tokens reduce this problem; they do not remove it. Key terms - Inference: using a trained model to make predictions, without updating its weights. - KV cache: stored keys and values of earlier tokens, reused so each generation step only processes the new token. - Exposure bias: the mismatch between training on real text and generating from the model's own outputs. Check yourself. 1. Why can training process all 64 positions of a window in one forward pass, while generation needs one forward pass per new character? Worked answer During training, the input at every position is real text that is known in advance, so every position's prediction can be computed at once (with the causal mask keeping each one honest). During generation, the input at the next position is the character the model is about to choose, which does not exist until the current step has finished, so each step must wait for the previous one.

title: The Big Picture: What Is a Pretrained Model?
text: 1.1 A model that works before you train it Let's start with the whole thing working, then take it apart. The cell below downloads a ready-made sentiment model from the Hugging Face Hub, a public website where people share trained models (Note 7.2 tours it properly). The model is called DistilBERT, a compact member of the BERT family of Transformer encoders. The version we load has already been adapted to judge whether a sentence about a film is positive or negative. The pipeline function wraps the whole process, from text in to a label out, in one object. Note the device=device argument: without it, the library may pick a device on its own, and your numbers might not match these notes. Now let's give it four short reviews. I wrote these before running the model, so they weren't chosen to make it look good. Three are right, with a confidence score of 1.000. The fourth, "Two hours of my life I will never get back", is a complaint, but the model calls it positive with a score of 0.745. There's no unhappy word in the sentence; the complaint lives in the idiom. Keep this in mind: a working model is not a perfect one, and Note 7.5 tests this model much harder. We did no training at all. Every weight in that model was set by someone else, on someone else's computer, before we arrived. That is what a pretrained model is: a model whose weights have already been learned, published so that others can use them without training from the start. 1.2 The data we will use throughout Modules 7 and 8 Four sentences prove nothing, so we need a proper test. We'll use the IMDb movie-review dataset: reviews from the Internet Movie Database, each labelled positive or negative, with an official training half and test half. The same split will be used in every note of Modules 7 and 8, so that results from different notes can be compared fairly. The function below builds that split. It does three things, for reasons you met in Module 4: - It removes duplicate reviews before splitting. If a review appears twice, one copy could land in training and the other in evaluation, and the model would be tested on something it has already seen. - It also removes test reviews that appear in the training half. That's the same leak, across the official split. - It carves a validation set out of the training half, with a fixed seed. Settings are chosen on validation and reported once on test. It also cleans one quirk: the reviews contain HTML line-break tags ( ), which we replace with spaces. Finally, fingerprint turns a set of texts into a short code. If two notebooks print the same fingerprint, they are using exactly the same reviews. That gets checked rather than assumed. The first run downloads the dataset into a data/imdb folder next to this notebook. You'll see "Generating train split" progress lines. Each official half has 25,000 reviews, and both contained duplicates: 96 were removed from train and 322 from test. That leaves 22,404 reviews for training, 2,500 for validation and 24,678 for testing, all close to half positive. Running a Transformer over 24,678 reviews on a CPU takes a long time, so most evaluations in these notes use two fixed samples of 1,000 reviews: val_eval (the first 1,000 validation reviews) and test_eval (a seeded sample of the test set). Their fingerprints will appear again in later notes. Common mistake: trusting an official split to be clean. IMDb's halves share some reviews, so a model trained on one half has seen part of the other. Always deduplicate before splitting, and check across any split you are given. 1.3 Same architecture, no pretraining Here is the experiment that shows where the value lies. We'll score the pretrained model on the first 500 validation reviews. Then we build a model with the identical architecture, the same layers and the same number of weights, but with random weights, and score it on the same 500 reviews. The pipeline cuts each review to its first 256 tokens (max_length=256). As you saw in Note 6.2, a Transformer can only look at a limited number of tokens at once, and many reviews are longer than that. Note 7.4 explains truncation in detail. To build the untrained twin, we load only the model's configuration, the description of its architecture without any weights (Section 6 looks inside one), and ask the library to build a fresh model from it. The difference is stark. The pretrained model scores 0.874 on 500 reviews held out from our own training. Its untrained twin scores 0.486, which is chance: it calls almost every review negative (only 8.4% positive) and is right only when the review happens to be negative. Nothing about the code differs. Same architecture, same tokeniser, same pipeline. With architecture and tokeniser held fixed, the trained weights make the difference in this experiment. Figure 7.1.1. The architecture and tokenizer are held fixed. The saved CPU run scores 0.486 with random weights and 0.874 with pretrained/adapted weights on the same 500 validation reviews; this does not audit all upstream exposure. Key terms - Pretrained model: a model whose weights were learned by someone else, usually on a very large dataset, and published for others to use or adapt. - Weights (parameters): the learned numbers inside a model. Training means adjusting them. - Architecture: the structure of a model, meaning which layers it has, their sizes and how they connect. Two models can share an architecture and behave completely differently. - Configuration: a small file that describes an architecture in words and numbers, so the library can rebuild it. - Pipeline: a Hugging Face helper that bundles tokenising, running the model and turning its output into a readable answer. Check yourself. 1. The random-weights model scored 0.486, close to half, even though it knows nothing. Why isn't its accuracy close to zero? Worked answer Because the reviews are balanced. The random model called almost every review negative (only 8.4% positive), and about half the reviews really are negative, so it is right on those almost by default. A model that knows nothing about sentiment lands near the share of the class it guesses, not near zero. That's why chance, not zero, is the baseline to beat. The next section steps back to ask where a model like this comes from. Interpret the evidence carefully. The comparison fixes architecture, preprocessing and tokeniser; it isolates the benefit of trained weights in that setup. These reviews are held out from our own training. Upstream documentation is evidence about earlier training data, not an exhaustive proof that a public checkpoint never encountered related material.

title: The Lifecycle: Data → Pretraining → Downstream Use
text: The sentiment model we loaded did not begin life as a sentiment model. Its story has two stages, and almost every pretrained model you'll meet follows the same pattern. Stage one: pretraining. A large model is trained on a huge collection of general data, such as books and web pages for text. Nobody labels this data. Instead, the model is given a task that the data can grade by itself. In Note 6.6 your Transformer predicted the next character. DistilBERT was pretrained on a close cousin of that task, masked language modelling: words in a sentence are hidden behind a [MASK] token, and the model must guess them from the words on both sides. Guessing hidden words well, across billions of sentences, forces a model to learn a lot about how language works. The result of this stage is a base model: general-purpose, but not yet built for any particular job. Stage two: downstream use. A downstream task is the job you actually care about, such as sentiment, spam detection or question answering. "Downstream" because it comes after pretraining. The base model is adapted to it, usually by adding a small new output layer and training a little more on labelled examples. That extra training is called fine-tuning. Our sentiment model is DistilBERT fine-tuned on SST-2, a dataset of short sentences from film reviews labelled positive or negative. We can watch the base model do its own pretraining task. The fill-mask pipeline hides nothing itself; we write [MASK] where we want a guess. All five guesses are positive adjectives that fit the sentence: "fantastic" with probability 0.110, then "fabulous", "successful" and so on. The base model was never told about sentiment, but filling in blanks taught it that "absolutely" before a blank about a movie is usually followed by strong praise. Now let's compare the two models' parts. In Note 5.1 we split networks into an encoder (often called the body) that builds a representation, and a head that uses it. Hugging Face names the body's weights distilbert.…, so we can count them separately. The bodies are exactly the same size, 66,362,880 parameters each. Only the heads differ. The base model's head (622,650 parameters as counted here) turns each position's vector back into a score for every word in the vocabulary. It doesn't need its own copy of the big word table: the last line shows it reuses the body's word-embedding table, a common trick called weight tying, so the shared table is counted only once, in the body. The SST-2 head (592,130 parameters) turns the whole text into just two scores. The output shapes make the difference concrete: For 1 sentence of 8 tokens, the base model returns 30522 scores at every position: one per vocabulary word, a guess for what could stand there. The SST-2 model returns 2 numbers for the whole sentence, one per class. Same body, different head, different job. Figure 7.1.2. Pretraining produces reusable weights. Inference can use a checkpoint directly; optional adaptation changes selected weights for a downstream objective.
