Key terms - Pretraining: the first, expensive training stage on large, general, usually unlabelled data. - Masked language modelling: a pretraining task in which some words are hidden and the model must predict them from the surrounding words on both sides. - Base model: the result of pretraining, before any task-specific adaptation. - Downstream task: the task you actually want to solve with a pretrained model. - Fine-tuning: further training of a pretrained model on labelled data for a downstream task. - Body and head: the body (encoder) builds representations and is shared across tasks; the head is a small task-specific layer on top. Check yourself. 1. The base and SST-2 models have bodies of identical size. Does that mean the bodies contain identical numbers? How could you check? (Section 7 does exactly this.) Worked answer No. Identical size only means identical architecture; the numbers inside can differ. To check, load both bodies and compare each tensor with the same name, for example with torch.equal or by measuring the size of their difference. Section 7 did this and found that every tensor had changed slightly. So pretraining on blanks produced something useful. The next section asks what, exactly, the model picked up.

title: What a Model Learns During Pretraining
text: 3.1 Probing with blanks Masked-word guessing is a convenient window into a base model, because we can design blanks that only make sense if the model has learned something specific. Here are four probes. Each tests a different kind of knowledge: grammar, a fact about the world, everyday cause and effect, and who typically does what. The results are uneven, and that is the lesson. - Grammar is strong. "She [MASK] to the cinema … yesterday" gets "went" with probability 0.62. The model has learned that "yesterday" calls for a past tense and that "to the cinema" calls for a verb of movement. - Everyday cause and effect is strong. "So boring that I fell [MASK]" gets "asleep" at 0.71. - Facts are shaky. "The capital of France is [MASK]" gets "marseille", "nantes" and "toulouse", all French cities, but not the right one, and with low confidence (0.14 for the top guess). The model learned what kind of word fits, but not the fact. - Typical agents are only partly there. "The [MASK] barked" does get "dog" first, but with only 0.06, barely ahead of "clerk" and "sheriff". Pretraining teaches a model the patterns of its training text: grammar, typical word combinations and common associations. It may also absorb facts, but less reliably, and a small model like DistilBERT holds fewer of them. A pretrained language model is not a database. Treat any fact it produces as a guess to check. 3.2 Representations that depend on context The deeper thing pretraining builds is the representation itself. In Note 5.3 we met static embeddings, where each word gets one fixed vector, and saw their limit: "bank" gets the same vector whether it is a river bank or a savings bank. A Transformer builds contextual representations instead: after each layer, a word's vector has been mixed with information from the words around it. Let's measure that. We take the base model's body, without any head, and feed it six sentences: three use "bank" in the money sense and three in the river sense. For each sentence we collect the vector for "bank" at the input (layer 0) and after each of the six Transformer layers. Each sentence gives 7 vectors of 768 numbers each. Now we compare "bank" with "bank" using cosine similarity (Note 5.3): averaged over all pairs that share a meaning, and over all pairs that don't, at every layer. At layer 0 there is no gap at all. The two groups are equally similar (0.952 and 0.961), because at the input "bank" is mostly just its embedding-table entry plus a position, the same as a static embedding. After the first layer the meanings pull apart, and by the last layer the gap is 0.237: money-sense "bank"s average 0.880 with each other, but only 0.642 with river-sense ones. The plot shows the whole picture. Nobody told the model that "bank" has two meanings. It worked that out because guessing hidden words well requires it: the words around "bank" decide what can fill nearby blanks. This is why pretrained representations are so useful downstream. The hard work of turning text into meaningful vectors has already been done. These are six hand-written sentences, so treat the exact values as an illustration. The pattern of a gap that is absent at the input and opens up inside the network is the general behaviour of contextual models. Key terms - Probing: testing what a model has learned by giving it inputs designed to need a specific piece of knowledge. - Contextual representation (contextual embedding): a vector for a word that depends on the sentence around it; the same word gets different vectors in different contexts. - Hidden states: the vectors a Transformer produces after each layer; hidden_states[0] is the input embedding, and the last is the final output of the body. Common mistake: asking a pretrained language model for facts and trusting the answer. Its training rewards text that sounds right, so a fluent wrong answer, like a French city that isn't the capital, is a normal outcome rather than a rare glitch. Check yourself. 1. At layer 0, "bank" in a river sentence was just as similar to "bank" in a money sentence as two money-sense "bank"s were. Why does the input layer behave like a static embedding? Worked answer Layer 0 is the input to the Transformer: each token's vector is its row from the embedding table plus a position vector. No attention has happened yet, so no information from the other words has been mixed in. "Bank" therefore looks almost the same in every sentence, exactly like a static embedding. Context only enters through the attention layers. Because these representations are general, one pretrained body can serve many tasks. The next section shows that directly.

title: Foundation Models and Their Capabilities
text: A model pretrained on broad data and then adapted to many different tasks is often called a foundation model. The name says what it is for: you build on it. Large language models used in chat assistants, image–text models like CLIP (which you met in Note 5.5 and will use for real in Note 7.5) and the encoder we are using here all play that role, at very different scales. We can show the idea in miniature. The library has a different model class for each kind of head. Let's load the same base checkpoint four times, each time asking for a different head. The library printed a LOAD REPORT for each model. This is not an error, and you will see these tables often, so it's worth reading one carefully: - UNEXPECTED lists weights that are in the downloaded file but not needed by the model you asked for. Here they are the masked-word head (vocab_transform, vocab_projector and so on), which none of the other three tasks use, so they are skipped. - MISSING lists weights the model needs but the file doesn't contain. Here they are the new heads (classifier, qa_outputs). The library creates them with random values, and the note tells you to train them on your task. Now let's check what the four models have in common: All four start from the same pretrained body, down to the last number (we compared one weight matrix exactly with torch.equal). Only the small heads differ: the masked-word head we've already met, a two-layer pre_classifier + classifier for whole-text classification, a qa_outputs layer that marks where an answer starts and ends in a passage, and a classifier that labels each token separately (for example, as a person's name, a place, or neither). The heads on three of them are random, so those models can't do their tasks yet. That's the point: the expensive part, the body, is shared, and only a small head has to be trained for each new task. Module 8 does that training. Figure 7.1.3. A pretrained body can support different output interfaces. Newly initialised heads require training, and task adaptation can update the body as well as the head. Key terms - Foundation model: a model pretrained on broad data and designed to be adapted to many downstream tasks. - Transfer learning: reusing what a model learned on one task or dataset to help with another. - LOAD REPORT: the table Hugging Face prints when a checkpoint's weights don't exactly match the model class requested. UNEXPECTED weights are skipped; MISSING weights are created at random. Check yourself. 1. You load a base model with AutoModelForTokenClassification and the LOAD REPORT lists classifier.weight as MISSING. If you ran this model on a sentence right away, what would its labels be like, and why? Worked answer Essentially random. The MISSING note means the classifier layer was created with random weights, so even though the body produces good contextual vectors, the head turns them into labels by an untrained rule. The model must be fine-tuned on labelled examples of the tagging task before its labels mean anything. A shared body is the promise. The next section tests how much it is actually worth, by comparing it with the alternatives.

title: Pretraining vs. Training from Scratch vs. Traditional ML
text: Suppose you need a sentiment classifier for film reviews. You have three broad options: - Traditional machine learning: turn each review into word counts and fit a linear model. The classic version is TF-IDF + logistic regression. TF-IDF scores each word by how often it appears in a review, down-weighted if it appears in almost every review (like "the"). - Training a neural network from scratch: start from random weights and learn everything from your own labelled data. We'll use the small bag-of-embeddings network from Note 5.3. A full Transformer trained from scratch would need far more data and computing than we have. - Using a pretrained model: here, the SST-2 model off the shelf, with no IMDb training at all. The fair way to compare them is to vary how many labelled IMDb reviews the first two get: 100, 1,000, or all 22,404. Small samples are noisy, so for 100 and 1,000 we repeat each experiment on five different random draws of training reviews and report the spread. Everything is scored on the same 500 validation reviews as in Section 1. One more detail keeps the comparison honest. The neural network needs a setting chosen: how many epochs to train. We choose it on a different slice of validation (reviews 1,000 to 2,000), never on the 500 we report. The small network is the one from Note 5.3, redefined here so this notebook stands alone. Its vocabulary is built only from the reviews it is given. Now we run all of the combinations. The 100-label and 1,000-label rows each train five models, one per draw. Read the table from top to bottom: - With 100 labels, both methods are weak and unstable. TF-IDF averages 0.627 but ranges from 0.508 to 0.748 depending on which 100 reviews it got. The network from scratch is barely above chance (0.541). - With 1,000 labels, both improve a lot (0.826 and 0.798) but are still below the pretrained model. - With all 22,404 labels, both beat the off-the-shelf pretrained model: TF-IDF reaches 0.918 and the network 0.890, against 0.874. That last result deserves a check, because 500 reviews is not a large test. The sign test (Note 5.6) looks only at reviews where exactly one of two models is right, and asks whether the split between them could plausibly be a coin flip. With 500 reviews, one review is worth 0.2% of accuracy. TF-IDF was right on 43 reviews where the pretrained model was wrong, and wrong on only 21 where it was right; a split that lopsided would happen by chance with probability 0.008. So TF-IDF with all the labels really is better here. The from-scratch network's edge (40 against 32, p = 0.410) could easily be luck. The picture shows the real trade-off. The dashed green line is what you get for free: no labels, no training, 0.874. The other two methods have to climb towards it with labelled data, and they need several thousand labels to reach it. So why didn't the pretrained model win outright? Because it was adapted to a different dataset: SST-2's short single sentences, not IMDb's long reviews, which we also cut to 256 tokens. With enough labels of exactly the right kind, even a simple method can beat a powerful model that was tuned for something slightly different. That points to the natural next step, which Module 8 takes: start from the pretrained model and adapt it to your data. You then get its head start and the benefit of your labels. Common mistake: assuming the biggest or most famous model will win. A pretrained model is only as good as its match to your task. Always compare it against a simple baseline on your own data. Here, a TF-IDF model that trains in seconds beat a Transformer with tens of millions of parameters once it had enough labels. Key terms - TF-IDF (term frequency–inverse document frequency): a way of turning a text into numbers that counts each word, giving less weight to words that appear in most documents. - Training from scratch: training a model starting from random weights, using only your own data. - Baseline: a simple reference method that a more complex one must beat to justify its cost. Check yourself. 1. Your team has 300 labelled examples of customer emails and needs a sentiment classifier next week. Based on this section's results, which approach would you try first, and why? Worked answer The pretrained model, measured against a simple baseline. With a few hundred labels, the results here showed TF-IDF and a network trained from scratch to be weak and unstable (TF-IDF averaged 0.627 with 100 labels, and the from-scratch network managed 0.798 even with 1,000), while the pretrained model scored 0.874 with none. Use the 300 labels to evaluate the pretrained model (and, as Module 8 shows, possibly to adapt it). Emails are not film reviews, so measure before trusting it. We've treated the pretrained model as a black box that comes with weights. Now let's open the box and look at what you actually download.

title: Weights, Architecture and Configuration
text: When you download a model from the Hub, you mainly get two kinds of file: a configuration that describes the architecture, and a weights file that holds the learned numbers. The code that turns them into a working network lives in the Transformers library on your computer. (A third group of files, for the tokeniser, comes alongside; Note 7.2 lists them all.) 6.1 The configuration The configuration is a small JSON file, readable as plain text. It was downloaded with the model and is already in the local cache. Most of these lines describe the architecture in Module 6's terms: - dim: 768 is the width of every token's vector (called d_model in Module 6); - n_layers: 6 and n_heads: 12 are the number of Transformer blocks and the number of attention heads in each; - hidden_dim: 3072 is the width inside each feed-forward network; - vocab_size: 30522 and max_position_embeddings: 512 set the size of the word table and the longest input the model can take; - dropout values are used only during training. Two lines belong to the task, not the architecture: id2label maps output 0 to NEGATIVE and output 1 to POSITIVE, which is how the pipeline knew which word to print, and finetuning_task records that it was adapted on SST-2. This is the file we used in Section 1.3 to build the untrained twin. 6.2 Where the parameters are Let's count the parameters in each part of the model. The model has 66,955,010 parameters. More than a third of them, 35.6%, are in the embedding tables, before any Transformer layer is reached. The six Transformer layers hold 63.5%, and the sentiment head only 0.9%. We can check the embedding count by hand from the configuration: The word table alone is 30,522 rows of 768 numbers, which is 23,440,896 parameters, and the position table adds 393,216. Together with two small LayerNorm vectors, that makes the 23,835,648 above. This split matters in practice: a large vocabulary is expensive, and Note 7.6 will see it again when we shrink models. 6.3 From parameters to file size Each parameter is stored as a 32-bit floating-point number, which takes 4 bytes. So the weights file should be about four times the parameter count: It is: 66,955,010 parameters × 4 bytes is 267.8 MB, exactly the size of the file. The .safetensors format stores raw numbers with a short index and nothing else. Unlike Python's general-purpose pickle format, loading it cannot run hidden code, which makes it the safe choice for files downloaded from strangers. Note 7.6 builds on this rule, parameters × bytes per parameter, to estimate memory. The weights themselves are stored as a state dict: a dictionary from each weight's name to its tensor, exactly as in your own PyTorch models. There are 104 named tensors. The names spell out where each one lives (distilbert.embeddings.word_embeddings.weight has shape (30522, 768), one row per vocabulary word), and the last four are the head: a 768 × 768 layer followed by a 2 × 768 layer that produces the two class scores. Figure 7.1.4. Configuration describes the architecture, weights supply learned numbers, and the matching tokenizer defines the text interface. These schematic file objects are not a screenshot. Key terms - State dict: a dictionary mapping each weight's name to its tensor; this is what gets saved and loaded. - Safetensors: a file format for storing weights as plain numbers, safe to load because it cannot contain executable code. - Weight tying: reusing one weight matrix in two places, such as the word-embedding table and the output layer that predicts words. Check yourself. 1. A model has 110 million parameters stored as 32-bit numbers. Roughly how large is its weights file? How large would it be if each number were stored in 16 bits instead? Worked answer About 110 million × 4 bytes = 440 MB. At 16 bits (2 bytes) per number it would be about 220 MB. Note 7.6 explores what is lost and gained by storing numbers with fewer bits. A weights file is a snapshot of a model at one moment. The last section looks at those snapshots, and at how models change over time.

title: Checkpoints and Model Versions
text: 7.1 Checkpoints A checkpoint is a saved set of weights (together with its configuration) from a particular moment in a model's training. In Note 5.3 you kept a copy of the weights from the best epoch; that copy was a checkpoint. On the Hub, each published model is a checkpoint, and models are often built from one another: the SST-2 model is a checkpoint made by fine-tuning the base checkpoint. How much did that fine-tuning change? We can measure it directly. Below we load the base model's body and compare every tensor with the SST-2 body, using the relative change: the size of the difference divided by the size of the original. All 100 tensors in the body changed (none is identical), but only a little: on average by 1.85% in the embeddings and between 2.14% and 2.41% in the Transformer layers. Fine-tuning didn't rebuild the model. It nudged every weight slightly, and that was enough to turn a word-guesser into a sentiment classifier. Module 8 makes those nudges itself. 7.2 Versions Models on the Hub are stored in repositories that track their history, like code on GitHub. Each change is a commit with its own ID, and a model's files can be updated after you first use them. When the library downloads a model, it stores the files in a cache folder named after the exact commit. The folder our files came from is named 714eb0fa89d2…, the same ID as the latest of the repository's 26 commits. The three latest commit titles describe changes to the documentation and an extra file format, but a commit could just as easily replace the weights. If your application has to give the same answers next month, ask for an exact version with revision=: Pinning a revision is the model equivalent of fixing a library version in requirements.txt. Note 7.6 returns to this when we look at reproducibility in deployed systems. Key terms - Checkpoint: a saved snapshot of a model's weights and configuration at a particular point in training. - Repository (repo): a Hub storage space for one model, with its files and their full history. - Commit and revision: a commit is one recorded change to a repository, identified by a long ID; a revision is the version you ask for, which can be a commit ID or a branch name such as main. Common mistake: loading a model by name only in a system that must stay reproducible. from_pretrained(name) gives you whatever the latest version is on the day you download it. Pin the commit with revision= and record it next to your results. Check yourself. 1. A colleague reruns your evaluation a year from now and gets a different accuracy, with the same code and the same data. Name two things that could have changed, and how pinning would help with one of them. Worked answer The model could have changed (someone pushed new weights or a new tokeniser to the repository), or the software could have changed (a new library version that processes text or computes results slightly differently). Pinning the model with revision= and its commit ID removes the first risk; pinning library versions in requirements.txt handles the second.

title: The Big Picture: Where Hugging Face Fits in AI Engineering
text: Let's begin with the whole workflow in three short cells. First, we ask for a model by its repository name, an owner and a model name separated by a slash, just like a GitHub project. Two lines, two libraries. AutoTokenizer gives us the tokeniser; its fast text-splitting engine comes from the Tokenizers library. AutoModelForSequenceClassification comes from Transformers, and so does the code that builds the network. Both looked up the name on the Hub, downloaded what they needed, and stored it. Now we use them: The model is sure this one is positive: 1.0 against 0.0, rounded. Where did the downloaded files go? Every download is stored in a local cache, a folder that by default is ~/.cache/huggingface/hub in your home directory. (You can move it by setting the HF_HOME environment variable, which is what was done when these notes were built.) The second time you load the same model, nothing is downloaded: the library finds the files in the cache. That is the whole ecosystem in one picture: - the Hub stores and publishes models and datasets, with their documentation; - the libraries (Transformers, Datasets and Tokenizers, with a helper library called huggingface_hub underneath) fetch them and turn them into working Python objects; - the cache keeps local copies so you download each file only once; - your code sits on top and decides what to do with the model. Figure 7.2.1. The Hub and local cache supply compatible artifacts. Tokenizers, Datasets and Transformers serve different stages of the application; cards supply evidence to inspect. Key terms - Hugging Face Hub: a website hosting openly shared models, datasets and demos, each in its own repository. - Repository name: the owner/name identifier of a Hub repository, such as distilbert/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english. - Local cache: the folder where downloaded files are kept so they are not downloaded again. - Transformers, Datasets, Tokenizers: Hugging Face's main libraries, for models, data and text splitting respectively. The next section looks at the top layer: what is actually stored in a repository.

title: The Hub, Model Repositories and Model Cards
text: 2.1 What is in a repository? A model repository is a folder of files with a history, much like a code repository on GitHub. The huggingface_hub library can list a repository's files and their sizes without downloading anything. The repository has 17 files, and they fall into four groups. - The configuration: config.json, the architecture blueprint you read in Note 7.1. - The weights, five times over: model.safetensors, pytorch_model.bin, tf_model.h5, rust_model.ot and onnx/model.onnx are each about 268 MB (267.833 MB, 267.844 MB, 267.950 MB, 267.846 MB and 267.956 MB). They hold the same learned numbers, saved in formats for different software: the safe format we used in 7.1, the older PyTorch format, TensorFlow's format, a Rust library's format, and ONNX, a format for running models outside Python. The onnx/ folder also has its own copy of the tokeniser files, so that version works without the rest of the repository. - The tokeniser: vocab.txt lists the vocabulary, one token per line, and tokenizer_config.json holds tokeniser settings. - Documentation: README.md is the model card, and map.jpeg is a picture the card displays. .gitattributes is a bookkeeping file for the version-control system. Transformers does not download all of this. It picks only the files it needs for PyTorch, and prefers .safetensors when a repository offers it. We'll check exactly what landed on our disk at the end of this section. 2.2 The model card The model card is the repository's README.md: a document describing what the model is, how it was trained, what it is for and where it fails. The top of the file holds machine-readable metadata, and the rest is written for people. The metadata says the model was trained on sst2 (the dataset is also part of a benchmark collection called glue), works on English (en), and is released under the apache-2.0 licence (Section 4). The headings show a well-organised card: details, how to use it, intended uses and misuses, risks, and how it was trained. Cards can also declare evaluation results in a structured block called model-index. Here are its accuracy entries: Two numbers, and only one of them is useful. On the glue validation split, a set of SST-2 sentences the model did not train on, the card reports an accuracy of 0.9106. It also reports 0.9886 on its own sst2 training split. A model's score on the data it was trained on says almost nothing about new data, as you saw when diagnosing overfitting in Module 3, so ignore that number. Note too that both numbers are on SST-2's short sentences, not on reviews like IMDb's. Note 7.3 measures what that means in practice. The most valuable part of a good card is often its honest list of problems: The authors report that the model treats sentences about different countries very differently: 0.89 probability of positive for "This film was filmed in France", but 0.08 for Afghanistan. Nothing in such a sentence says anything good or bad about the film. We will test this claim ourselves in Section 4. 2.3 What landed on your computer Now let's look in the cache for this repository and see which of the 17 files we actually have. We have 5 of the 17 files: the configuration, the safetensors weights, the two tokeniser files and the card (fetched just now, when we read it). That's 268.1 MB rather than more than a gigabyte for all five weight formats. The path shows how the cache is organised: one folder per repository (models--owner--name), then a snapshots folder with one subfolder per commit (the 714eb0fa… ID we pinned in Note 7.1), then the files. Figure 7.2.2. A repository can contain documentation, configuration, weights and tokenizer artifacts in several formats. Download only the compatible files required by your framework. Key terms - Model repository: a Hub folder holding a model's configuration, weights, tokeniser files and documentation, with version history. - Model card: the repository's README.md, describing the model, its training, intended uses, limitations and evaluation. - Card metadata: the machine-readable header of a model card, with fields such as license, language, datasets and model-index. - ONNX: a file format for running models outside the framework that trained them. Common mistake: quoting a model card's benchmark number as if it applied to your data. A card's numbers describe its evaluation data; this card's are for short SST-2 sentences. Measure on your own data before relying on them. Check yourself. 1. The repository holds five copies of the weights, but loading the model downloaded only one. Why is that a good design, and which file would it have chosen if model.safetensors were missing? Worked answer Downloading all five would waste over a gigabyte of disk and bandwidth on formats your framework can't use; each format exists so that users of different software can get exactly one. Transformers prefers model.safetensors because it is safe to load. Without it, a PyTorch user would get pytorch_model.bin, the older PyTorch format, which works but, like any pickle file, could in principle run code when loaded, so it should only come from sources you trust. Check yourself. 1. The card reports an accuracy of 0.9886 on sst2 train and 0.9106 on glue validation. Which would you put in a report to your manager, and why? Worked answer The validation figure, 0.9106. The training figure, 0.9886, measures the model on sentences it learned from, so it mostly shows how well it memorised them. Even the validation figure should come with a caveat: it is for short SST-2 sentences, and your data may behave differently. Best of all is a figure measured on your own data. With the Hub covered, the next section turns to the libraries that use it.

title: The Core Libraries: Transformers, Datasets, Tokenizers
text: 3.1 Transformers: one interface for many architectures The Transformers library contains code for hundreds of model architectures. The Auto classes (AutoConfig, AutoTokenizer, AutoModel…) save you from knowing which class each repository needs: they read the repository's config.json, look at its model_type, and build the matching class. Downloading only the configuration (a few kilobytes) is enough to see this: Four repositories, four different architectures: DistilBERT, GPT-2, BERT and CLIP. Yet the same line of code, AutoConfig.from_pretrained(name), handled all of them. The architectures field records which class the weights were saved from: a sequence classifier, a language model with a word-prediction head (GPT2LMHeadModel), a bare BERT body, and a combined image–text model. The rest of Module 7 loads all four. Note 7.4 covers the Auto classes for loading models in detail. 3.2 Datasets: data that doesn't fill your memory The Datasets library does for data what Transformers does for models: it downloads datasets from the Hub by name, and gives them a common interface. We'll load IMDb's official train and test files, as in Note 7.1. The result is a DatasetDict: a dictionary of splits, each a Dataset with named columns (features) and a number of rows. Each split has 25000 reviews. Let's look inside the training split: The label column is a ClassLabel with names neg and pos, stored as 0 and 1, and the split is exactly balanced: 12500 of each. Indexing a row gives a plain Python dictionary. (This first review shows the official files' quirks: no cleaning, and the IMDb split from Note 7.1, with duplicates removed, is built on top of this raw version.) How does a library handle datasets far larger than memory? It doesn't load them into memory at all: The table is a MemoryMappedTable, backed by a 33.4 MB file on disk in the Apache Arrow format, a column-based layout designed for fast reading. Memory mapping means the operating system reads parts of the file only when they are needed, so a dataset bigger than your RAM still opens instantly. This is also why the library writes cache files: every operation produces a new Arrow table on disk. Datasets works best through a few operations that each produce a new dataset. filter keeps the rows that pass a test: Only 49 of the 25000 training reviews are under 30 words. You'll see "Filter" progress bars as these operations run. map applies a function to every row, or with batched=True, to batches of rows at a time, which is much faster. The most common use is tokenising. Here we count how many DistilBERT tokens each review needs, without cutting any off. Expect one warning, "Token indices sequence length is longer than the specified maximum sequence length…": it is the tokeniser pointing out that some reviews are longer than the model can accept. That's true, and exactly what we want to measure. The median review is 233 tokens long, the longest is 3127, and 44.3% of reviews are over 256 tokens, with 14.8% over 512, the most DistilBERT can read at once. (These are raw reviews; the tags still in them add a few tokens each.) The histogram shows the long tail: Most reviews are a few hundred tokens long, but a long tail stretches far past the 512-token limit. Every model in this module has to decide what to do with that tail: cut it off, which is called truncation, or split the review into pieces. Note 7.4 covers the choice; the 256-token setting used in Note 7.1 cuts off a large share of reviews. To prepare data for a model, we tokenise with truncation and remove the raw text column. We'll use the first 1,000 reviews to keep this quick: Each row now holds input_ids (the token IDs), an attention_mask (Note 7.4) and a token_type_ids column we'll explain in a moment. Finally, set_format("torch") makes rows come out as PyTorch tensors, and a DataLoader batches them, just as in your own training loops. Because reviews have different lengths, the batches need padding: a data collator is a function that assembles a batch, and DataCollatorWithPadding pads each batch to its longest member. A batch of 8 reviews, each padded to 256 tokens (the length of the longest review in the batch, which hit the truncation limit), plus 8 labels. The collator also renamed label to labels, the name Transformers models expect when they compute a loss. This dataset is ready for training, which is exactly where Module 8 picks it up. Figure 7.2.3. Inspect examples, transform them under a declared policy, then dynamically pad and mask each batch. Learned preprocessing must be fitted on training data only. Key terms - Dataset / DatasetDict: a table of examples with named columns / a dictionary of such tables, one per split. - Features: the named, typed columns of a dataset, such as text (a string) and label (a class label). - Apache Arrow: a column-based file format for fast reading of large tables. - Memory mapping: reading a file on disk as if it were in memory, fetching only the parts that are used. - map and filter: Datasets operations that transform every row, or keep only some rows, producing a new dataset. - Data collator: a function that combines individual examples into a batch, for example by padding them to equal length. Check yourself. 1. A colleague tries to load a 200 GB text dataset on a laptop with 16 GB of RAM using Datasets, and expects it to crash. Why might it not? Worked answer Datasets stores data as memory-mapped Arrow files. The operating system reads only the parts being used into memory, so opening and iterating over a dataset much larger than RAM works, a batch at a time. It would still need 200 GB of disk space, and operations like map write new files to disk. 3.3 Tokenizers: fast, and specific to each model Which tokeniser did AutoTokenizer give us? The answer is a small surprise. We asked for DistilBERT's tokeniser and got a BertTokenizer. Recall from Section 2.1 that this repository's tokenizer_config.json is tiny: it doesn't name a tokeniser class, so the library fell back to the general BERT tokeniser, which works because DistilBERT uses BERT's vocabulary. The BERT tokeniser also produces token_type_ids, which BERT uses to tell two sentences in one input apart. DistilBERT doesn't use them, and the check above shows its outputs are identical with or without them. Repositories are not all equally tidy, and knowing what each file does helps you spot why a tokeniser behaves unexpectedly. The Tokenizers library does the actual splitting, in fast compiled code written in Rust. Its most important lesson is one you met in Note 6.2: a model and its tokeniser are a pair. Let's tokenise the same sentence with the tokenisers of two different models. The same 42-character sentence becomes 17 IDs for DistilBERT and 9 for distilgpt2, and the IDs share nothing. DistilBERT's vocabulary has 30,522 entries and distilgpt2's 50,257. The splits differ too: - DistilBERT lowercases everything (GOOD became good), marks the start and end with [CLS] and [SEP], and marks word-continuation pieces with ##: "unbelievably" became five pieces, un ##bel ##ie ##va ##bly. - distilgpt2 keeps capitals, adds no special tokens, and marks a piece that starts with a space with Ġ. "unbelievably" is a single token in its larger vocabulary. The last line makes the point directly: ID 2204 is good to DistilBERT but a completely different piece of text to distilgpt2. Feeding one model's IDs to the other may not raise any error. It silently produces nonsense. The difference in algorithm shows when we look inside: Both are "fast" tokenisers, backed by the Tokenizers library. DistilBERT uses WordPiece and distilgpt2 uses BPE (byte-pair encoding, which you built a version of in Note 6.2). Before splitting, DistilBERT's tokeniser runs a normaliser that lowercases and strips accents: "Café FÊTE" becomes 'cafe fete'. This is what "uncased" means in the model's name. One more feature of fast tokenisers is invaluable when you build applications: offset mapping, which records which characters of the original text each token came from. Each token knows its source characters, even after lowercasing: the token good maps back to characters 37–41, which read 'GOOD' in the original. Special tokens like [CLS] map to nothing (0–0). Offsets let you highlight words in the original text, for example to show a user which part of a review a model reacted to. Key terms - Auto classes: Transformers classes (AutoConfig, AutoTokenizer, AutoModel…) that read a repository's configuration and build the matching class. - Fast tokeniser: a tokeniser backed by the compiled Tokenizers library. - WordPiece and BPE: two subword algorithms; WordPiece marks continuation pieces with ##, GPT-2's BPE marks pieces that begin with a space with Ġ. - Normaliser: the step before splitting that cleans text, for example by lowercasing and removing accents. - Offset mapping: for each token, the start and end positions of the characters it came from. Common mistake: loading a tokeniser from one repository and a model from another. The shapes may match, so nothing crashes, but the IDs mean different things to each, and the predictions are meaningless. Load both from the same repository name. Check yourself. 1. You tokenise a review with distilgpt2's tokeniser and pass the IDs to the SST-2 DistilBERT model. Will you get an error? If not, what will the predictions be worth? Worked answer It depends on the IDs. DistilBERT's embedding table has 30,522 rows, so any ID of 30,522 or more causes an index error. Our sample sentence's distilgpt2 IDs include 30642 and 48943, so it would crash, which is at least a warning. If every ID happens to be smaller, there is no error at all: the model looks the IDs up, but each one means a different token to DistilBERT than it did to distilgpt2. The model sees a meaningless jumble and its predictions are worthless, with nothing to tell you so. Knowing how to load a model is half the job. The other half is knowing whether you're allowed to, and whether you should.

title: Licences, Usage Restrictions and Responsible Selection
text: 4.1 Licences Every model is someone's work, released under some terms. A licence states what you may do with it: use it commercially, change it, redistribute it, and under what conditions. On the Hub, the licence is usually declared in the card's metadata, so we can check it in code. Three different situations appear in this table. - A standard open licence. Four models use apache-2.0, a widely used permissive licence: you may use, change and redistribute the model, including commercially, as long as you keep the licence and copyright notices. - A custom licence with gated access. meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B and google/gemma-2-2b declare their own licences, llama3.2 and gemma. These are custom terms written by the model's publisher, with their own conditions, for example on how the model may be used. Both are gated (manual): you must sign in, read and accept the terms on the Hub page, and wait for approval before downloading. - No declared licence. openai/clip-vit-base-patch32 shows None. Let's see what access looks like for a gated model without an account: The Hub refuses: a GatedRepoError with HTTP status 401, "not authorised". The metadata was public (we read the licence above), but the files are not until you accept the terms. To use such a model, you would log in with an access token (hf auth login) after accepting its terms on the website. Nothing in Modules 7 and 8 needs one. What about CLIP's missing licence? The card's metadata contains only a tag and a demo-widget setting, and no line of the card mentions a licence at all. That doesn't mean the model is free to use. In most countries, work published without a licence gives you no automatic right to reuse it. The card does say a lot about intended use: its headings include "Primary intended uses" and "Out-of-Scope Use Cases". What to do in practice is to look for the licence where the model was originally published (the authors' own code repository), use the model only for the purposes its creators describe, and get advice before building a product on it. Note 7.7 makes this part of a model-selection checklist. In these notes we use CLIP for learning, which is within its stated research purpose. 4.2 Responsible selection: test the card's warnings A licence tells you what you may do; the card's limitations tell you what you should worry about. Section 2.2's card warned that sentences about different countries get very different sentiment. Let's test that claim with six countries, chosen before running the cell. The missing Hub metadata field is not proof that the original project has no licence. The original CLIP repository includes an MIT licence; verify the terms and provenance applicable to the exact weights and distribution you intend to use. Licence terms and intended-use recommendations are different questions. The warning holds on today's model. "This film was filmed in Afghanistan." gets a positive probability of 0.165, against 0.965 for France and 0.963 for the United States. Nigeria gets 0.736. The exact values differ from the card's (0.89 and 0.08), which is a good reason to measure rather than copy, but the pattern is the same: the model's judgement of a neutral sentence depends on the country named in it. If this model screened reviews written about films from around the world, some would be judged more harshly purely because of where they were made. Responsible selection means doing this kind of check as a matter of routine: 1. read the licence and any usage restrictions; 2. read the card's intended uses, out-of-scope uses and limitations; 3. test the warnings that matter for your application, on inputs like your users' inputs; 4. record what you found, and decide whether the model is acceptable for the use you have in mind. Key terms - Licence: the legal terms under which a model may be used, changed and shared. - Permissive licence: a licence such as Apache 2.0 that allows broad use, including commercial use, with few conditions. - Custom licence: terms written by a model's publisher for that model, often with specific use restrictions. - Gated model: a model whose files can be downloaded only after you sign in and accept its terms. - Intended use / out-of-scope use: what a model's creators designed it for, and uses they advise against. Common mistake: treating "downloadable" as "allowed". A model can be public on the Hub and still carry a licence that forbids your use, or carry no licence at all. Check the terms before you build on a model, not after. Check yourself. 1. You find a model on the Hub that scores well on your data, but its card has no licence. Your product is commercial. What do you do? Worked answer Don't build on it yet. Look for a licence where the model was originally published, such as the authors' paper or code repository, or contact the authors. If none can be found, treat the model as not licensed for your use, get legal advice, or choose a model with a clear licence. Note 7.7 includes this step in its selection checklist. Check yourself. 1. You plan to use the SST-2 model to flag negative product reviews from customers in many countries. Based on Section 4.2, describe one test you would run before deploying it. Worked answer For example: write a set of neutral and mildly positive review sentences that differ only in the country, city or nationality mentioned (or in names typical of different regions), run them through the model, and compare the positive probabilities. Large differences for otherwise identical sentences, like the 0.965 and 0.165 measured here, would mean customers from some places get systematically harsher judgements. You'd then decide whether to mitigate it, monitor it, or choose a different model.

title: The Big Picture: Matching Models to Problems
text: A common way to pick a model is to search for something popular and try it. Sometimes it works. More often it wastes an afternoon on a model that was never right for the job. A better habit is to describe the problem first, in a few concrete questions, and let the answers filter the search: 1. What is the task? What goes in and what must come out: a label for a whole text, a label for each word, a span copied from a passage, new text, a vector, a label for an image? This decides the kind of model (Section 2). 2. What do the inputs look like? Language, domain (tweets, legal contracts, film reviews), and above all length. A model that reads 512 tokens can't read a 20-page document in one go (Section 3). 3. What hardware will run it, and how fast must it answer? This sets an upper limit on model size (Section 3). 4. How good must it be, measured how? And on whose data? A benchmark number is evidence, not a guarantee (Section 4). 5. Where will it run, and what are you allowed to do with it? On your own machine or through someone else's service (Section 5), and under what licence (Note 7.2). Only after these questions does it make sense to look at specific models. The questions turn "find a good model" into "find a model that does this task, on inputs like these, within this budget, this well, under these terms", which is far easier to answer. Figure 7.3.1. Requirements narrow a shortlist; documentation and representative evaluation determine whether a candidate actually fits. Popularity and parameter count alone do not decide. The first filter is the task itself, so that is where we start.

title: A Map of Common Tasks
text: Every model on the Hub is tagged with the task it was built for, its pipeline tag, and the Hub's search can filter by it. Here are seven well-known models, one per common task, with the tag the Hub gives each: These tags are the vocabulary of model search. What each means in practice: | Task (pipeline tag) | Input → output | Typical use | |---|---|---| | text-classification | text → one label for the whole text | sentiment, spam, topic, intent | | question-answering | question + passage → the span of the passage that answers it | searching manuals, FAQs, documents | | summarization | long text → shorter text | news digests, meeting notes | | text-generation | prompt → continuation | drafting, chat, code completion | | sentence-similarity (also feature-extraction) | text → a vector of numbers | semantic search, clustering, duplicate detection | | image-classification | image → one label from a fixed set | product photos, medical scans | | zero-shot-image-classification | image + candidate labels in words → the best label | classifying into categories chosen at run time | Notice how the same architecture serves different tasks. The first two models are both DistilBERT, one fine-tuned for classification and one for question answering. What makes them different is the head and the fine-tuning (Note 7.1, Section 4). Let's run three of these tasks with small models. Question answering and summarisation stay on the map only, to keep downloads down, and the image tasks get their turn in Note 7.5. Text classification, which you already know: Text generation with distilgpt2, a small version of GPT-2. With do_sample=False, the pipeline always picks the most likely next token: greedy decoding, from Note 6.6. The model continues the prompt fluently but falls into a loop: "It's a very good movie" twice in 20 tokens. Greedy decoding often repeats like this, exactly as you saw with your own model in Note 6.6. Note 7.5 tries the sampling strategies that fix it. Embeddings with all-MiniLM-L6-v2, a small model trained so that sentences with similar meanings get similar vectors. The pipeline returns one vector per token; averaging them gives one vector per sentence. Each sentence becomes a vector of 384 numbers. The two film sentences share almost no words ("thrilling, beautifully acted film" against "exciting movie with superb performances"), yet their cosine similarity is 0.734, while each scores about zero against the sentence about a parcel (−0.007 and 0.008). The model compares meanings, not words, which is what makes semantic search possible. Note 7.5 builds a search engine on it. Key terms - Pipeline tag (task tag): the Hub's label for the task a model was built for, such as text-classification; it is also the name you pass to pipeline(...). - Greedy decoding: generating text by always choosing the single most likely next token. - Sentence embedding: one vector representing a whole sentence, built so that similar meanings give nearby vectors. Check yourself. 1. A support team wants to find past tickets that describe the same problem as a new ticket, even when worded differently. Which task tag would you search for, and why not text-classification? Worked answer sentence-similarity (or feature-extraction): embed every past ticket once, embed the new ticket, and return the past tickets whose vectors are closest. Text classification needs a fixed set of labels decided in advance, but "the same problem as this ticket" isn't a fixed label: there could be thousands of distinct problems, and new ones appear all the time. Knowing the task narrows the search to a few kinds of model. Within a kind, the next filter is whether a model fits your hardware and your inputs.

title: Model Size, Context Length and Compute Requirements
text: 3.1 Size and memory, before you download You can find out how big a model is without downloading it. A .safetensors file begins with a short header that lists every tensor's name, shape and number type, and huggingface_hub can read just that header. Combined with each model's configuration (a few kilobytes), it tells us how many numbers a model stores and how long an input it accepts. That's a size ladder spanning several hundred times, from 22,713,728 stored numbers (MiniLM) to 7,615,616,512 (Qwen2.5-7B, a general-purpose language model). Three things to read from this table: - "Stored as" matters. The BERT models store 32-bit floats (F32, 4 bytes each). The Qwen models store BF16 (bfloat16), a 16-bit format, 2 bytes each. So Qwen2.5-0.5B, with more numbers than BERT-large, takes less disk: 0.99 GB against 1.34 GB. MiniLM also stores a few integers (I64), which are position indexes rather than learned weights. (The header counts everything stored, so its total can differ slightly from the number of trainable parameters.) - Context length varies enormously. All four BERT-style encoders accept at most 512 tokens. The Qwen models accept 32,768 and 131,072. For long documents, that alone can decide the choice. - Disk size predicts memory. To run a model you must at least hold its weights in memory, so the file size is a lower bound on the memory you need. Running it needs more: activations, and for generation, the cache of past keys and values (Note 7.6). Using the rule from Note 7.1, parameters × bytes per parameter, we can estimate the weight memory in different number formats: Qwen2.5-7B needs 30.46 GB just for its weights in float32, or 15.23 GB in a 16-bit format. On a laptop with 16 GB of RAM, even the 16-bit version leaves almost nothing for the operating system and for the computation itself. The small models on this ladder take well under a gigabyte. This kind of arithmetic takes seconds and saves you from downloading 15.23 GB only to watch your machine run out of memory. Note 7.6 covers ways to shrink these numbers, such as quantisation. 3.2 Input length and compute How does input length affect cost? In Note 6.3 you saw that attention compares every token with every other token, so its cost grows with the square of the length. But a Transformer layer also contains linear layers, the Q, K, V and output projections and the feed-forward network, whose cost grows only in proportion to the length. Which part dominates depends on the length. We can count the multiplications per token in one DistilBERT layer: - the linear parts need about 4·d² + 2·d·d_ff, with d = 768 and d_ff = 3072, the same for every token; - attention needs about 2·L·d per token: one dot product with each of the L positions to get the scores, and one weighted sum over L value vectors. At 128 tokens, attention is only 2.7% of the work; at 512 tokens, the most DistilBERT accepts, it's 10.0%. The two parts become equal only at 4608 tokens, and attention dominates beyond that (64.0% at 8192). So for short-context models like DistilBERT, cost grows roughly in proportion to length. For long-context models like the Qwen family, which accept inputs of tens of thousands of tokens, the quadratic part takes over. That is why very long inputs are so expensive, and why so much engineering goes into making attention cheaper. Let's check the prediction by timing the SST-2 model on the same long text, truncated to different lengths, in batches of 16: Interpret the evidence carefully. The 4,608-token crossover is from this simplified multiplication count for DistilBERT's width and feed-forward expansion. It is not a universal Transformer boundary or a measured runtime crossover. Configured position limits also do not guarantee equal quality at every length. The measured time per review rises in a near-straight line with length: each doubling of the token count roughly doubles the time. That's what the multiplication count predicted for this range, where the linear parts dominate. (Your timings will differ from the ones printed here, since they depend on your processor, but the shape of the curve should be the same.) Two practical consequences follow. Truncating reviews to 256 tokens instead of 512 roughly halves inference cost. And if your inputs are long, context length and compute have to be judged together: a model that can read 32,768 tokens will also charge you for reading them. Key terms - Context length (context window): the maximum number of tokens a model can take as input at once. - bfloat16 (BF16): a 16-bit number format, 2 bytes per number, widely used for storing and running large models. - Weight memory: the memory needed just to hold a model's parameters: parameters × bytes per parameter. - Truncation: cutting an input down to a maximum number of tokens. Common mistake: choosing a model by parameter count alone. Two models with similar parameter counts can differ in storage format (float32 or bfloat16), context length and speed. Check the file sizes, the number types and the context length too. Check yourself. 1. A model has 3 billion parameters stored in bfloat16. Estimate its weight memory. Would you expect it to run on a laptop with 8 GB of RAM? Worked answer 3 billion × 2 bytes = about 6 GB for the weights alone. On an 8 GB laptop that leaves very little room for the operating system, other programs and the computation itself, so it would probably fail or be extremely slow. A smaller model, or a more compressed format (Note 7.6), would be needed. Check yourself. 1. Attention's cost grows with the square of the input length. Why, then, did doubling the length from 256 to 512 tokens only roughly double DistilBERT's time per review? Worked answer Because at these lengths most of the work is in the linear layers, whose cost grows only in proportion to length. At 512 tokens, attention is just 10.0% of DistilBERT's multiplications. Doubling the length doubles the linear work and quadruples the small attention part, so the total roughly doubles. The quadratic part dominates only for much longer inputs, beyond about 4608 tokens for this layer size. A model that fits your task and your hardware still has to be good enough. That is what model cards and benchmarks claim to tell you.

title: Reading Model Cards, Benchmarks and Limitations Critically
text: 4.1 Check the claim on its own terms A benchmark is a fixed, public dataset with an agreed way of scoring, so that different models can be compared on equal terms. SST-2 is one such benchmark, and it is part of a larger collection called GLUE. Our SST-2 model's card makes its claim in two places: The card's text says "an accuracy of 91.3 on the dev set" (dev set is another name for validation set). Its metadata says 0.9106 on the GLUE validation split. These don't quite agree: 91.3 in the text against 0.9106 in the metadata. Small inconsistencies like this are common, because card text and metadata are often written at different times or from different runs. They are a first hint to verify rather than copy. Let's verify it ourselves. The SST-2 validation set is small and public: The validation set has 872 sentences. Look at the first one: it is lowercase, and there are spaces before the punctuation (it 's, journey .). Benchmark text has often been preprocessed, and may look quite different from what your users will type. Now we run the model on all 872: We get 0.9106, exactly the figure in the card's metadata. So the claim is honest, for SST-2. That's the first step of critical reading: confirm that a claim can be reproduced on its own terms. The next step is to ask whether it holds on yours. 4.2 Check it on your data Our data is IMDb, with the fixed split from Note 7.1. The function is copied here so this notebook stands alone, and the fingerprints confirm it gives exactly the same reviews. The fingerprints match Note 7.1's. Now the same model on the 1,000 val_eval reviews, truncated to 256 tokens: Accuracy drops from 0.9106 on SST-2 to 0.8820 on IMDb validation. Same task (positive or negative), same domain (films), a few points lower. Why? The obvious difference is length: The median SST-2 sentence is 24 tokens long; the median IMDb review is 214. The model was fine-tuned on single sentences and is now reading whole reviews, often with mixed opinions: a reviewer may praise the acting and still hate the film. On the 601 reviews that fit within 256 tokens, accuracy is 0.9068, close to the card's figure. On the 399 that were cut off, it is 0.8446. Be careful about what this does and doesn't show. It's tempting to say "truncation costs about six points", but the two groups differ in more than truncation: long reviews may also be more nuanced, more sarcastic or simply harder. This comparison shows that the model does worse on long reviews; it doesn't separate why. Note 7.7 measures the effect of the truncation length directly, by running the same reviews at different lengths. 4.3 What the model has seen: contamination There's one more question to ask of any benchmark number: could the model have seen the test data during training? If so, its score measures memory, not ability. This is called contamination, and it can happen at either training stage. DistilBERT was pretrained on bookcorpus (a collection of books) and wikipedia, so IMDb reviews are unlikely to be in its pretraining data, and it was fine-tuned on SST-2's training split, not on its validation split. For this model, both our measurements are clean. But the question needs asking every time: - Models pretrained on large web crawls may have read IMDb pages, and popular benchmarks themselves often end up in crawled data. A suspiciously high score on a famous dataset is a warning sign. - Models fine-tuned on a dataset will score well on any split they were trained on. If you carve your validation set from IMDb's training half, as we did, a model fine-tuned on IMDb's training half has seen it. Note 7.7 meets exactly this case. Read the card's training-data section, and if it doesn't say what the model was trained on, treat its benchmark scores with suspicion. Figure 7.3.2. The card text, structured metadata, and reproduced SST-2 score refer to a different evaluation context from the IMDb run. All displayed numbers come from the source reference results. Key terms - Benchmark: a fixed public dataset and scoring rule used to compare models. - GLUE: a widely used collection of English language-understanding benchmarks, including SST-2. - Dev set: another name for a validation set. - Domain shift (distribution shift): a difference between the data a model was trained or evaluated on and the data it meets in use. - Contamination: test or benchmark data appearing in a model's training data, which inflates its scores. Common mistake: treating a lower score on your data as a sign that you made a mistake. A drop from a card's benchmark to your data is normal; it measures the distance between the two datasets. Verify your pipeline on the benchmark itself, as we did, and then believe your own number. Check yourself. 1. The card's text says 91.3 and its metadata says 0.9106. You measured 0.9106 on SST-2 and 0.8820 on IMDb. Which number belongs in a report about using this model for IMDb reviews, and why? Worked answer 0.8820, the number measured on IMDb validation, because it is measured on the kind of data the model will actually see. The SST-2 figures describe a different dataset. The 0.9106 we reproduced is still useful: it shows our pipeline runs the model correctly. (Report the final figure on the test set, once settings have been chosen on validation.) Check yourself. 1. Reviews cut off at 256 tokens scored 0.8446, against 0.9068 for reviews that fit. A colleague concludes that using 512 tokens would raise the cut-off group's accuracy to about 0.9068. What's wrong with that reasoning? Worked answer The two groups differ in more than truncation. Long reviews may be harder in their own right: more mixed opinions, more plot summary, more sarcasm. Giving the model 512 tokens might help, but there's no reason to expect it to reach the short-review accuracy, and some reviews are longer than 512 anyway. The way to find out is an experiment that changes only the truncation length on the same reviews, which Note 7.7 does. So far every model has run on our own computer. The last filter is where the model should run at all.

title: Hosted APIs vs. Local Models
text: There are two ways to use a pretrained model: - Locally: you download the weights and run them on hardware you control, a laptop, a server or a cloud machine you rent. Everything in this module so far has been local. - Through a hosted API: someone else runs the model on their servers. Your code sends the input over the internet and receives the output. Hugging Face, the major AI labs and cloud providers all offer this. An API (application programming interface) is simply a defined way for one program to ask another for something. A hosted call looks like this. The listing is shown but not run, because it needs an account and an access token, a secret key that identifies you: Which models are available this way, from which providers and at what price changes often, so check the provider's current documentation. The trade-offs, though, are stable: | Question | Local model | Hosted API | |---|---|---| | Setup | Download weights, install libraries, provide hardware | An account, a token and a few lines of code | | Which models | Any model whose weights you can download | Whatever the provider offers, including models too big to run yourself | | Cost | Hardware and electricity, roughly fixed | Pay per request or per token, growing with use | | Speed | No network delay; limited by your hardware | Network round trip on every call; powerful hardware behind it | | Privacy | Data never leaves your machine | Data is sent to the provider; check their terms | | Versioning | You pin the exact weights (Note 7.1, Section 7) | The provider may update or retire a model | | Availability | Works offline; you handle failures | Depends on the provider's uptime and rate limits | Neither is better in general. A prototype, or a feature that needs a model far bigger than your hardware, often starts on a hosted API. A product with steady high volume, strict privacy rules or a need for exactly reproducible behaviour often ends up local. Many teams use both: a hosted model to explore, and a local model once they know what they need. Note 7.6 returns to this choice with measured costs. Key terms - Hosted API: a service that runs a model on the provider's servers and returns results to your code over the internet. - Access token: a secret key that identifies you to a service; keep it out of notebooks and code you share. - Rate limit: a cap on how many requests a service accepts from you in a given time. Common mistake: pasting an access token directly into a notebook and then sharing the notebook. Anyone who reads it can use your account. Store tokens in an environment variable, or log in once with hf auth login, and keep them out of your code. Check yourself. 1. A hospital wants to classify doctors' notes by urgency. A hosted API offers a model that scores slightly better than the best local one. List two questions you would need answered before choosing the hosted option. Worked answer For example: Can patient data legally be sent to this provider at all, and what do their terms say about storing or using it? Is the provider's model version pinned, or could it change without warning? What does it cost at the hospital's volume, and is the network delay acceptable for urgent cases? What happens to the service if the provider has an outage or reaches a rate limit?

title: The Big Picture: From Repository to Working Code
text: Every use of a pretrained text model follows the same five steps, whether a pipeline does them for you or you write them yourself: 1. Load the tokeniser and the model from the same repository (Note 7.2). 2. Preprocess: turn texts into token IDs, cut long ones to a maximum length, pad short ones so a batch forms a rectangle, and build an attention mask that marks which positions are real. 3. Run the model in inference mode, on the right device. 4. Decode the outputs: raw scores (logits) → probabilities → labels. 5. Save the model and tokeniser if your application needs its own copy. Figure 7.4.1. Tokenization, model computation, logits, probabilities and label mapping are separate steps. Weights stay fixed during this inference flow. We'll use the fixed IMDb split from Note 7.1 (its function is copied here so the notebook stands alone; the fingerprints confirm the reviews are the same) and work with the first 32 validation reviews.

title: The Pipeline API
text: A pipeline bundles a tokeniser, a model and the decoding step for one task. We create one by naming the task and the model. Always pass device. If you don't, the library picks a device itself, and on some machines (for example a Mac with an Apple GPU) it will choose the GPU even though the rest of your code runs on the CPU. Your results could then differ slightly from someone else's for no obvious reason. Inside are the two objects we'll load ourselves in Section 3: a BertTokenizer (Note 7.2 explained why a DistilBERT model gets a BERT tokeniser) and a DistilBertForSequenceClassification model. By default, a text-classification pipeline returns only the best label and its probability. top_k=None returns every class: The model is sure this mixed sentence is positive: 0.9997346997261047 for POSITIVE and 0.0002653122355695814 for NEGATIVE, which add up to 1. Give a pipeline a list and it returns a list. For real reviews you should always set the truncation length, and for many texts a batch_size, so they are processed several at a time (Section 6 measures why). The first review comes out NEGATIVE with probability 0.9940033555030823, and the model gets 0.906 of these 32 reviews right. We keep each review's probability of POSITIVE (for a NEGATIVE result, that is 1 minus the score) to compare against our own code in the next section. Key terms - Pipeline: a Hugging Face object that bundles a tokeniser, a model and output decoding for one task. - top_k: how many of the highest-scoring labels a classification pipeline returns; None means all of them. - batch_size: how many inputs are processed together in one forward pass. Common mistake: creating a pipeline without device=. The library's automatic choice can differ between machines, so the same notebook can run on different hardware for different people, with slightly different numbers. State the device explicitly.

title: Loading Tokenizers and Models Explicitly
text: The explicit route uses the two Auto classes from Note 7.2. For a classification model we use AutoModelForSequenceClassification, which builds the body and the classification head. Two more steps follow loading: .to(device) moves the weights to the chosen device, and .eval() switches the model to inference behaviour (Section 5 shows why). The configuration's id2label tells us that output 0 means NEGATIVE and output 1 means POSITIVE. We need it to decode the outputs. Now we process the same 32 reviews ourselves, in batches of 8, and compare the probabilities with the pipeline's. Each step is one line: tokenise with truncation and padding, run the model, and apply softmax to the logits. The largest difference between our probabilities and the pipeline's is 5.96e-08, a rounding-level difference in the last digits of 32-bit arithmetic, and all 32 labels agree. Our explicit code does exactly what the pipeline does. The rest of this note looks at each of its steps in turn. Key terms - AutoModelForSequenceClassification: the Auto class that builds a model with a whole-text classification head. - id2label: the configuration's map from output position to label name. Check yourself. 1. Our explicit code and the pipeline agree to within 5.96e-08. Name two settings that, if you changed them in only one of the two, would make them disagree by much more. Worked answer For example: a different max_length (the model would see different amounts of each long review), leaving out the attention mask in one of them (padded reviews would change), running one in train mode (dropout would add noise), or pairing the model with a different tokeniser. Any of these changes the model's input or behaviour, not just the arithmetic.

title: Preprocessing and Decoding Outputs
text: 4.1 Padding and attention masks A model processes a batch as one tensor, and a tensor must be a rectangle: every row the same length. Texts are not. Padding fixes this by adding a filler token to the end of each shorter text until all match the longest. Let's tokenise two texts of different lengths. The tokeniser returns three tensors. Look at input_ids: both rows start with 101 ([CLS]) and the real text ends with 102 ([SEP]), as in Note 7.2. The first text needs only 6 tokens, so it is padded with six zeros: the padding token [PAD] has ID 0, added on the right. (token_type_ids is the extra BERT output from Note 7.2, which DistilBERT ignores.) The attention mask has a 1 for every real token and a 0 for every padding position. The model uses it inside attention: positions with a 0 are blocked, so no real token can attend to padding. It is the same idea as the causal mask in Note 6.3, which blocked future positions. Without it, the meaningless [PAD] vectors would be mixed into the real tokens' representations. 4.2 Truncation The opposite problem is a text that is too long. DistilBERT can read at most 512 tokens, because it has only 512 learned position embeddings (Note 7.1, Section 6). Truncation cuts a text down to a maximum length. Here is the longest of the 1,000 val_eval reviews, tokenised with and without it: Without truncation, the review is 1602 tokens long, and the tokeniser prints a warning that this is longer than the model's limit of 512. With max_length=256 it becomes exactly 256 tokens, and it still ends with a proper [SEP] token: truncation cuts off the end of the text, but keeps the special tokens. Everything after the cut is simply never seen by the model. What happens if we ignore the warning and pass the full review to the model? The model fails: a RuntimeError complaining that a tensor of size 1602 doesn't match one of size 512, the position-embedding table. (With some library versions, the error is an IndexError instead.) That warning from the tokeniser was worth reading. Always set truncation=True and a max_length for real-world text. 4.3 Why the attention mask matters Padding should change nothing about a review's prediction: a review should get the same answer whether it is processed alone or in a batch next to a longer one. Let's test that on our 32 reviews. We process them as one padded batch, once with the attention mask and once without it, and compare each against processing the review alone, where it needs no padding at all. In this batch, 15 of the 32 reviews needed padding, and 18.4% of all positions are padding. With the mask, every review's probability matches the one-at-a-time result to within 2.21e-06, rounding noise. Without the mask, probabilities move by as much as 0.764, and 2 reviews flip to the wrong side of 0.5. Same model, same reviews; the only difference is whether the model was told which positions were real. Passing the whole tokeniser output with model(enc) includes the mask automatically. The danger is code that passes only input_ids. 4.4 From logits to probabilities to labels The model's raw output is a pair of logits, unnormalised scores, one per class. To turn them into probabilities we apply softmax, as in Module 2: exponentiate each logit, then divide by the sum so they add up to 1. Here it is by hand for the first review: The logits are 2.772 for NEGATIVE and −2.338 for POSITIVE. Exponentiating gives 15.9923 and 0.0965, which sum to 16.0887. Dividing each by the sum gives probabilities 0.994 and 0.006. The larger one wins, and id2label turns position 0 into the word NEGATIVE. That's exactly the pipeline's answer (NEGATIVE, 0.9940033555030823), and it matches the true label. Two practical points. First, only the difference between logits matters: adding the same number to both leaves the softmax unchanged. Second, a probability of 0.994 is the model's confidence, not a guarantee. Note 7.1 showed this model confidently wrong about an idiom, and Note 7.5 looks at how far to trust these scores. Figure 7.4.2. Padding adds positions, an attention mask restricts access to padded positions, and truncation discards input. This illustration is not a causal future-token mask. Key terms - Padding: adding filler tokens ([PAD], ID 0 here) so all texts in a batch have the same length. - Attention mask: a tensor of 1s (real tokens) and 0s (padding) that stops attention from using padding positions. - Truncation: cutting a text down to a maximum number of tokens; truncation=True, max_length=…. - Logits: a model's raw, unnormalised output scores, one per class. - Softmax: the function that turns logits into probabilities: exponentiate, then divide by the sum. Common mistake: calling the model with input_ids only, for example model(enc["input_ids"]), on a padded batch. Nothing fails, but padded reviews get different, wrong predictions. Pass the whole encoding with model(enc) so the attention mask goes in too. Check yourself. 1. A batch has two reviews, of 40 and 300 tokens, and you tokenise with truncation=True, max_length=256, padding=True. What is the shape of input_ids, and how many 0s are in the first row of the attention mask? Worked answer The longer review is cut to 256 tokens, so the batch is padded to 256: input_ids has shape (2, 256). The first review has 40 real tokens (including [CLS] and [SEP]), so its mask row has 40 ones and 256 − 40 = 216 zeros. Check yourself. 1. Logits of [2.772, −2.338] give probabilities [0.994, 0.006]. What probabilities would logits of [12.772, 7.662] give, and why? Worked answer The same, [0.994, 0.006]. Both logits were increased by 10, and softmax depends only on the differences between logits: adding 10 multiplies every exponential by the same factor, which cancels when dividing by the sum. The difference is 5.11 in both cases. Visual walkthrough: Follow padding and attention masking. 1. Tokenize two inputs. A: [101, 42, 102] · B: [101, 17, 25, 102]. IDs are arbitrary vocabulary indices in this toy example; 101/102 mark boundaries and 0 is padding. 2. Pad this batch. A: [101, 42, 102, 0] · B unchanged. The longest example has four tokens, so the shorter example receives one padding position. 3. Construct masks. A: [1, 1, 1, 0] · B: [1, 1, 1, 1]. The mask allows attention to real tokens and prevents attending to the padded key. This is not a causal future-token mask. 4. Run fixed weights. IDs + masks → logits → label. Padding creates a batch shape; it does not restore content discarded by truncation. Inference changes no weights. The app adds a paused animation of this same supplied example.

title: Running Inference: Eval Mode, Inference Mode, Device Placement
text: 5.1 Eval mode In Module 3 you met dropout, which randomly switches off a share of the network's units during training to reduce overfitting. That randomness is useful while learning but harmful when you want a stable answer. PyTorch models have two modes: model.train() turns dropout on and model.eval() turns it off. from_pretrained already returns a model in eval mode, but it is good practice to call .eval() explicitly, because any code that calls .train() (for example a fine-tuning loop in Module 8) switches dropout back on. Here is the same review, run three times in each mode: In train mode, the POSITIVE logit for one and the same review comes out as -2.3716, -2.78 and -2.0684: dropout makes every run different. In eval mode it is -2.3384 every time. A model left in train mode gives answers that change on every call, and slightly worse ones on average. 5.2 Inference mode During training, PyTorch records every operation so that it can compute gradients later (Module 2's autograd). At inference time there is nothing to learn, and that recording only wastes memory and time. Two context managers switch it off: A plain call produces logits that require gradients and carry a grad_fn (here AddmmBackward0), the record PyTorch keeps for backpropagation, along with every intermediate tensor it needs. Under torch.no_grad() nothing is recorded. torch.inference_mode() goes slightly further: its outputs are marked as inference tensors, which lets PyTorch skip some extra bookkeeping. For pure prediction, inference_mode is the best choice. Use no_grad if you need to use the outputs later in code that records gradients. 5.3 Device placement A model's weights and its inputs must be on the same device. If the model is on a GPU and the inputs are on the CPU, PyTorch stops with an error saying they are on different devices. The pattern is always the same: move the model once with model.to(device), and move every batch with enc.to(device), as all our cells have done. In this notebook both are on the CPU. On a machine with an NVIDIA GPU, the setup cell would choose cuda, and the same code would place both on the GPU. Note 7.6 compares the two.
