Key terms - Eval mode / train mode: model.eval() disables dropout (and other training-only behaviour); model.train() enables it. - torch.no_grad() / torch.inference_mode(): context managers that stop PyTorch recording operations for gradients; inference_mode is the faster, stricter one. - Device placement: putting the model's weights and its input tensors on the same device (CPU or GPU). Common mistake: forgetting .eval() after training or fine-tuning. The model keeps dropout on, so evaluation scores are noisy and slightly too low, and the same input gives different answers each time. Check yourself. 1. A colleague's evaluation script gives a slightly different accuracy every time it runs on the same data with the same model. Name the most likely cause, and how you would check for it. Worked answer The model is probably in train mode, so dropout makes every run slightly different. Check with model.training (it should be False), or run the same input twice and compare the outputs. If they differ, call model.eval() before evaluating.

title: Batching Inputs and Managing Memory
text: 6.1 Padding waste Batching lets the model process several texts in one forward pass, which uses the hardware more efficiently. But a padded batch is as long as its longest member, so every shorter review pays for tokens it doesn't have. How much waste depends on which reviews end up together. Here are the first 256 validation reviews in batches of 32, in the order given and sorted by length. The 256 reviews contain 50,878 real tokens. Batched in the order given, the model processes 65,536 positions, so 22.4% of its work is spent on padding. Sorted by length, similar lengths share a batch, and the total drops to 53,984, with only 5.8% padding. Same reviews, same model, a fifth less work. (Every batch in the given order was padded to the full 256 tokens, because each batch of 32 happened to contain at least one long review.) If you sort, remember to put the results back in the original order afterwards. 6.2 Timing batch sizes Let's time it. We run the 256 reviews with batch sizes 1, 8 and 32, then batch size 32 sorted by length. The timings are printed with units; yours will differ, since they depend on your processor. On this CPU, larger batches are somewhat faster per review than one review at a time, and sorting by length gives a further saving on top, roughly in line with the padding it removes. The gain from batching on a CPU is modest. A GPU can process many more inputs in parallel, so there the gain from batching is usually much larger (Note 7.6). 6.3 Memory Batching has a cost: memory. While a batch passes through the model, every layer holds the vectors of every token, and attention computes a score for every pair of tokens in every head. We can estimate both for DistilBERT from its configuration (768 numbers per token, 12 heads, 4 bytes per number): One review of 256 tokens needs about 0.8 MB of token vectors per layer, and 3.1 MB if the attention scores are stored in full. A batch of 32 multiplies both by 32 (25.2 MB and 100.7 MB). Doubling the length to 512 doubles the token vectors but quadruples the attention scores, to 402.7 MB, because scores grow with length squared (Note 6.3). A batch of 256 reviews at 512 tokens would need 3221.2 MB just for one layer's scores. Libraries often avoid storing the full score matrix, but the lesson holds: memory grows with batch size × length, and faster still with length when attention is computed in full. If a large batch runs out of memory, reduce the batch size or the maximum length. Key terms - Batching: processing several inputs in one forward pass. - Padding waste: computation spent on padding positions in a batch. - Sorting by length (length bucketing): grouping inputs of similar length into the same batch to reduce padding. Check yourself. 1. You need to classify one million short product reviews overnight on a CPU. Describe two changes from Section 6 that would make it faster, and one thing you must be careful about if you sort the reviews. Worked answer Batch the reviews (for example 32 at a time) instead of processing them one by one, and sort them by length so each batch has little padding. Truncating to a sensible max_length also helps. If you sort, you must keep track of each review's original position and put the predictions back in the original order; otherwise predictions get attached to the wrong reviews.

title: Saving and Reloading Models and Tokenizers
text: An application that downloads its model from the Hub every time it starts depends on the Hub being available, and on the model not having changed (Note 7.1, Section 7). Often you want your own copy. save_pretrained writes a model or tokeniser to a folder in the same format as a Hub repository, and from_pretrained accepts a folder path as well as a repository name. In Module 8 this is how you'll save your fine-tuned models. The folder holds the configuration, the weights (267.833 MB, the same size as on the Hub) and the tokeniser. The library saved it as one tokenizer.json file, the Tokenizers library's complete description of the tokeniser, rather than the vocab.txt file the Hub repository had. "Writing model shards" refers to the weights file: very large models are split into several files, called shards. This one fits in one. Now let's reload from the folder and check that nothing changed: The reloaded tokeniser produces the same token IDs, and the reloaded model produces outputs identical to the original, bit for bit. We then delete the copy, because it takes as much disk as the original model. In a real project you would keep it, and record which repository and commit it came from. Key terms - save_pretrained: saves a model or tokeniser to a folder in Hub format. - from_pretrained(path): loads from a local folder as well as from a Hub repository name. - Shard: one of several files that together hold a large model's weights. Common mistake: saving the model but not the tokeniser. The folder then can't be used on its own, and someone may pair the model with a different tokeniser. Save both into the same folder. Check yourself. 1. You fine-tune a model, save it with model.save_pretrained("my-model"), and send the folder to a colleague. Their AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("my-model") fails. What did you forget, and why does it matter which tokeniser they use? Worked answer You saved the model but not the tokeniser: also run tokenizer.save_pretrained("my-model"). It matters because the model only understands token IDs from its own tokeniser. If your colleague loads a tokeniser from somewhere else, the IDs may mean different tokens (or come from a different vocabulary), and the model's predictions would be wrong, possibly without any error.

title: The Big Picture: Turning Model Capabilities into Features
text: Every application in this note has the same structure. A pretrained model supplies one capability, a function from an input to an output. The application wraps it with everything a user needs: - Input handling: what counts as a valid input, and what happens to one that isn't (empty text, the wrong type, a 100-page document). - Fit checks: is this input the kind of thing the model was built for? A film-review classifier will happily score a password-reset request; the application should notice. - Decision rules: when to answer, and when to hold back, for example by passing uncertain cases to a person. - Evaluation: measured on the whole system, with the numbers a product owner cares about: how often it answers, and how often it's right when it does. Figure 7.5.1. An application adds input validation, decision rules, error handling and measured quality to a pretrained capability. The OOD check is a heuristic to validate, not a guarantee. All the IMDb work uses the fixed split from Note 7.1. The function is copied here, and the fingerprints confirm the same reviews.

title: Practice: IMDb Sentiment Classification
text: 2.1 The aggregate We start from the sentiment model and measure it on the 1,000 val_eval reviews. The helper positive_prob returns each text's probability of being positive. It sorts texts by length before batching, to cut padding (Note 7.4, Section 6), and puts the results back in the original order. The model scores 0.882 on the validation reviews. That's the aggregate. An application meets individual inputs, so let's look at those. 2.2 Individual inputs We test five groups of inputs, written before running the model: clearly positive, clearly negative, ambiguous (mixed or lukewarm), the four negation sentences from Note 5.3, and inputs that are not film reviews at all. Read the groups one at a time. - Clear inputs get confident, correct answers (1.000 and 0.000). - Negation, which defeated Note 5.3's model, is handled correctly. There, a bag-of-embeddings model averaged word vectors, so "not good" still looked positive. Here, "the movie was not good" gets 0.000 and "the movie was not bad" gets 0.999. A Transformer reads words in context, so "not" changes the meaning of the word after it. - Ambiguous inputs get confident answers too, and that's a problem. "The acting was superb, but the story made no sense" gets 0.001: the model reads the "but" clause as decisive, which is defensible. But "It was fine, I guess." gets 1.000 positive, and "Not as bad as the critics said, but not good either" gets 0.003. A human would call these lukewarm. The model, fine-tuned on sentences labelled only positive or negative, has no way to say "in between", and pushes them to an extreme with near-total confidence. - Out-of-distribution inputs get answers anyway. The gibberish "asdkjh qwe zzz" is called negative with P(positive) = 0.004, a confidence of 0.996. "Please reset my password." gets 0.011. Only "The parcel arrived on Tuesday." gets an uncertain-looking 0.586. (The French review gets 0.928, positive, which happens to be correct. The model was trained on English, so don't count on that: it may simply be reacting to words like "film" that look the same in both languages.) The lesson for the application is the most important point in this note: a high confidence score does not mean the input made sense. The model's probabilities describe how strongly an input resembles one class compared with the other, not whether it belongs to the model's world at all. Section 6 builds a separate check for that. Key terms - Capability: what a model can compute from an input, such as a probability of positive sentiment. - Out-of-distribution (OOD) input: an input unlike the data a model was trained on. - Confidence: the probability a classifier gives to its chosen class; here, the larger of P(positive) and 1 − P(positive). Check yourself. 1. The model gave "asdkjh qwe zzz" a confidence of 0.996. Why can't a two-class softmax ever say "this isn't a review"? Worked answer A two-class softmax always splits a probability of 1 between "positive" and "negative"; there's no third option for "neither". The output only compares the two classes with each other, so any input, even gibberish, is pushed towards whichever class its features resemble slightly more, and the softmax can make that look very confident. Detecting that an input doesn't belong needs a separate signal, such as the review-likeness check in Section 6.

title: Practice: Text Generation with a Small Pretrained Model
text: In Note 6.6 you generated Shakespeare-like text with your own small Transformer and compared decoding strategies. Here we do the same with distilgpt2, a pretrained language model trained on web text. Generating text is a loop: predict a probability for every possible next token, choose one, append it, repeat. The interesting choice is how to choose. 3.1 Temperature reshapes the distribution First, let's look at the model's probabilities for the token after "The movie was", and how temperature changes them. Logits are divided by the temperature T before the softmax: T below 1 sharpens the distribution towards the top choices, T above 1 flattens it. At T = 1.0, the model's own distribution, the top choice " a" has probability 0.067, and the top five tokens together hold only 0.267. Most of the probability is spread over thousands of other tokens. At T = 0.7, the same five tokens hold 0.540; at T = 1.5, only 0.074. The order never changes, only how sharply the probability is concentrated. 3.2 Four ways to choose We compare four strategies from Note 6.6, each continuing "The movie was" for 40 tokens: - greedy: always take the most likely token; - temperature 0.7: sample from the sharpened distribution; - top-k 40: sample from the 40 most likely tokens only; - top-p 0.9: sample from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to 0.9 (also called nucleus sampling). Sampling is random, so we fix the seed before each call. That way you get the same text as these notes. Greedy decoding produces one fluent clause ("a hit in the United States and was a hit in the United Kingdom", already repeating itself), then gets stuck emitting blank lines (\n) until it runs out of tokens. Once a blank line is the most likely next token, it stays the most likely next token. The sampled versions are more varied and readable, though not exactly sensible: distilgpt2 invents a "gritty pilot" and a quote from someone called Laffer. The model has learned what film writing sounds like, not what is true (the same lesson as Note 7.1, Section 3). One sample per strategy proves little, so let's measure repetition over several prompts and seeds. We count the share of 3-word sequences that repeat earlier ones in the same text: 0 means no repetition. Greedy decoding repeats itself in its texts (a mean of 0.18, up to 0.30), while none of the 9 sampled texts for any sampling strategy repeats a 3-word sequence. (Our measure counts words, so greedy's runs of blank lines aren't even included; its real repetition is worse.) For open-ended writing, sampling with a moderate temperature, top-k or top-p is the usual choice. For tasks with one right answer, such as extracting a date, greedy is often better, because variety is not wanted. Key terms - Temperature: a number that divides the logits before softmax; below 1 sharpens the distribution, above 1 flattens it. - Top-k sampling: sampling only from the k most likely tokens. - Top-p (nucleus) sampling: sampling only from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities sum to at least p. - Degenerate repetition: a generator getting stuck repeating the same words or tokens. Common mistake: comparing decoding strategies on a single sample each. Sampling is random: one lucky or unlucky sample says little. Fix the seeds and compare several prompts and samples. Check yourself. 1. Why does greedy decoding get stuck in loops, while sampling usually escapes them? Worked answer Greedy decoding is deterministic: the same context always gives the same next token. Once the text enters a pattern where the pattern itself makes the next repeat most likely (as with the blank lines), greedy has no way out. Sampling sometimes picks a less likely token, which changes the context and lets the text move on.

title: Practice: Pretrained Embeddings for Semantic Similarity
text: 4.1 What the embeddings capture A sentence-embedding model turns a whole text into one vector, so that texts with similar meanings get nearby vectors. We use all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Note 7.3), with the pooling it was trained for: the average of its token vectors, ignoring padding. Each vector is then scaled to length 1, so a dot product between two vectors equals their cosine similarity. In Note 5.3 we found that embeddings learn what their objective rewards: vectors trained to predict sentiment grouped words by sentiment, while vectors trained to predict neighbouring words grouped them by topic. Let's ask what MiniLM's vectors reward. We compare one sentence with four others: The paraphrase scores 0.734, as expected. But "A dull, badly acted film" scores 0.737, as high or higher, even though it says the opposite. Meanwhile "A delicious, beautifully cooked meal", which shares the positive sentiment and even the word "beautifully", scores only 0.344. MiniLM was trained to bring together texts about the same thing, such as a question and its answer, or two descriptions of the same event. So its vectors capture topic far more than opinion. That's exactly what search needs, but it means these embeddings, used as they are, are a poor way to measure sentiment. 4.2 Semantic search Search is the classic use: embed a collection of documents once, embed each query, and return the documents whose vectors are closest. We embed the first 1,000 training reviews and try three queries written before running. The results match the meaning of the queries, not their exact words. The best match for "terrible special effects and wooden acting" says the special effects "should be named special defects" without using the word "terrible". For "a heartwarming story about a family", all three are moving, positive reviews. As in Section 4.1, the search finds topics, not opinions: the horror query returns one review that loved its film and two that hated theirs, and one of the "terrible special effects" results is a positive review that mentions bad acting at the start. Key terms - Sentence-embedding model: a model that maps a text to one vector, placing similar meanings close together. - Mean pooling: averaging a text's token vectors (ignoring padding) to get one vector for the whole text. - Semantic search: retrieving documents by similarity of meaning, using embeddings, rather than by matching words. Check yourself. 1. A colleague wants to use MiniLM similarity to find reviews that "agree" with a given review. Based on Section 4.1, what would go wrong? Worked answer MiniLM similarity mostly measures topic. Reviews of the same film, or of similar films, would score as similar whether they agree or disagree. Section 4.1's opposite-sentiment sentence scored 0.737, as high as a true paraphrase. To find reviews that agree, you'd need to combine similarity with a sentiment signal, or use a model trained to compare stances.

title: Practice: CLIP for Zero-Shot Image Classification and Text-to-Image Retrieval
text: 5.1 From the toy to the real thing In Note 5.5 you built a toy version of CLIP: an image encoder and a text encoder trained so that matching image–caption pairs had similar vectors. It worked, but it could only recognise what its small training set described. Trained without sneakers, it matched sneaker images to "sandal" and "ankle boot". The real CLIP was trained the same way on an enormous collection of images and captions from the web. That lets it do zero-shot classification: we write each class as a sentence ("a photo of a sneaker."), embed the sentences, and give each image the class whose sentence is most similar. No training on our classes at all. We use the Fashion-MNIST test file from Module 5. Fashion-MNIST images are tiny (28 × 28), greyscale and drawn light-on-dark, very unlike CLIP's web photos, so two settings may matter: whether to invert the images to dark-on-white, and how to word the class template. To choose them fairly, we use two separate sets of images: the first 300 to choose settings, and 1,000 others to report the result. Both changes help: inverting the images to dark-on-white, like a product photo, and describing them as black-and-white photos. The best combination scores 0.750 on the choosing images, against 0.633 for the plain setup. Now we use that combination, once, on the 1,000 reporting images: CLIP classifies 0.733 of the 1,000 new images correctly, against 0.100 by chance, with no training on Fashion-MNIST at all. The result on the reporting images is close to the 0.750 seen on the choosing images, as it should be when settings are chosen fairly. The per-class results tell the real story: - Sneakers, the class Note 5.5's toy could not recognise, are recognised 0.79 of the time. CLIP learned what a sneaker is from the web, not from our data. - Trousers and bags are almost perfect (0.98). They have distinctive shapes. - Shirts nearly always fail (0.15), most often called pullovers, and dresses manage only 0.48. At 28 × 28 pixels in greyscale, a shirt, a T-shirt, a pullover and a coat really are hard to tell apart. Their differences (buttons, collars, fabric) are mostly lost at this size. 5.3 Text-to-image search Because images and text share one space, we can also search images with words: embed a query sentence and return the closest images. For "sneaker", "bag" and "dress", 4 of the top 5 images are right. The mistakes are understandable: a sandal for "sneaker", a T-shirt for "dress", and a plaid shirt for "bag". For "shirt", only 2 of the top 5 are shirts and the other three are T-shirts, the same confusion the per-class numbers showed. In the dataset's labels a T-shirt and a shirt are different classes, but in everyday English the word "shirt" covers both, and CLIP learned its idea of a "shirt" from everyday English. Key terms - Zero-shot classification: classifying into classes the model was never trained on, by describing each class in words. - Prompt template: the sentence pattern used to describe each class, such as "a photo of a {}.". - Text-to-image retrieval: finding the images whose embeddings are closest to a text query's embedding. Common mistake: choosing a template or preprocessing step on the same images you report. Trying several settings and reporting the best one on the same data overstates accuracy. Choose on one set, report on another, as we did with the 300 and the 1,000. Check yourself. 1. Our zero-shot CLIP reached 0.733 on Fashion-MNIST; a small CNN trained on Fashion-MNIST in Module 5 did better. When would you still choose CLIP? Worked answer When you have no labelled data for your classes, or the classes change often. CLIP needs only a sentence per class, so a new category ("a photo of a raincoat") can be added instantly, without collecting and labelling images or retraining. It's also useful for searching images with free-text queries. If you have plenty of labelled images for a fixed set of classes, a trained model will usually be more accurate (Module 8 shows ways to adapt pretrained models).

title: Designing a Reusable Inference Pipeline That Handles Errors and Invalid Inputs
text: 6.1 Two thresholds, chosen on validation Section 2 showed two weaknesses an application must handle: the model answers inputs that aren't film reviews, and it is sometimes unsure. We'll handle each with a rule, and set each rule's threshold on validation data before looking at the test set. - Review-likeness check. For any input, we compute its MiniLM embedding's similarity to the closest of our 1,000 known training reviews (Section 4). Genuine reviews resemble other reviews; a password-reset request doesn't. We set the threshold so that 99% of 500 unused validation reviews pass. An input scoring below that is flagged as out of domain. - Abstention. The model's confidence on the val_eval reviews from Section 2 tells us how sure it usually is. We set the threshold at the 10th percentile, so the service holds back on its least confident tenth of reviews and leaves them for a person. Genuine reviews almost all score above 0.364 in review-likeness, and the confidence threshold is 0.948. Both were set without touching the test set. 6.2 The service The class below wraps everything. It returns one result per input, as a dictionary with a status: ok (with a label), abstain (unsure), out_of_domain (not a film review), rejected (invalid input, with the reason) or error (the model failed). The design choices worth copying: - Check inputs before the model sees them. Wrong types, empty or whitespace-only text, and absurdly long text are rejected with a reason, instead of crashing or wasting computation. - Never let one bad input break a batch. Invalid items are set aside, the rest are processed together, and a model failure is caught and reported as a status rather than raised. - Return reasons, not just answers. A caller can show "low confidence" or "not a film review" to a user, or route the item to a person. - Keep the thresholds as settings, so they can be re-tuned without changing code. Every input gets a sensible outcome. The two clear reviews and "the movie was not bad" are answered. The gibberish, the parcel and the password request are all flagged out_of_domain, with review-likeness scores of 0.238, 0.16 and 0.141, below the 0.364 threshold. The sentiment model alone had been 0.996 and 0.989 sure about two of them. Empty and whitespace-only text, None, a number and a 25,000-character string are rejected with clear reasons, and none of them crashed anything. Notice one remaining weakness: "The acting was superb, but the story made no sense." is answered NEGATIVE with confidence 0.999. Abstention only catches uncertainty the model admits; it can't catch confident mistakes on genuinely mixed reviews. Key terms - Inference service: code that wraps a model with input checks, decision rules and error handling, and returns structured results. - Abstention: declining to answer an input, typically when confidence is low, so that a person or another system can handle it. - Out-of-domain detection: checking whether an input resembles the data a model was built for. - Threshold: the cut-off value in a decision rule; set it on validation data. Check yourself. 1. Why did we set the review-likeness threshold using genuine reviews only, rather than a mix of reviews and non-reviews? Worked answer Because the goal is to keep genuine reviews flowing: the threshold controls how many real reviews are wrongly flagged (here about 1%), and we can only measure that on genuine reviews. We didn't have a representative collection of the non-reviews users might send, and any such set we invented would bias the threshold towards the examples we happened to think of. The cost is that we don't know exactly how many non-reviews would slip through, so that is worth monitoring once the service is live. Interpret the evidence carefully. Review-likeness is a heuristic demonstrated on these inputs, not a guarantee of robust out-of-domain detection. Validate false accepts and false rejects on representative in-domain and out-of-domain examples before deploying it. Visual walkthrough: Trace three service decisions. 1. Validate the input. Empty input → reject. Validation happens before model inference. A model score cannot repair an invalid request. 2. Check the declared domain. Flagged out of domain → hold back. This course uses a review-likeness heuristic, which can falsely accept or reject inputs. 3. Apply a confidence threshold. Illustration: 0.88 ≥ 0.80 → answer. These are invented decision-rule values, not a measurement of model calibration. 4. Abstain when required. Illustration: 0.63 < 0.80 → abstain. The source run answers 909, abstains on confidence for 79, and flags 12 as out of domain. All 91 non-answered cases form the held-back group. The app adds a paused animation of this same supplied example.

title: Evaluating Application-Level Performance
text: 7.1 What the service does on unseen reviews Now the test set, used once. We run the service on the 1,000 test_eval reviews. With 1,000 reviews, each review is worth 0.1 percentage points of accuracy. The service answered 909 reviews, abstained on 79 and flagged 12 genuine reviews as out of domain: about 1%, matching the rate we designed on validation. Three numbers describe the application: - Accuracy if we answered everything: 0.875. This is the model's raw accuracy. - Coverage: 0.909 of reviews were answered. - Accuracy on the answered reviews: 0.899. The held-back reviews really were the hard ones: the model would have got only 0.637 of them right. Abstention bought a higher accuracy on what we do answer at the cost of answering fewer reviews, and that is a product decision, not a technical one. 7.2 Which way the errors go Accuracy hides which mistakes a model makes. A confusion matrix counts each combination of true and predicted label: Of 485 negative reviews (434 + 51), 434 were recognised; of 515 positive reviews (74 + 441), 441 were. The model misses positive reviews more often than negative ones: a recall of 0.856 for positive against 0.895 for negative. If the feature exists to surface unhappy customers, missing 51 negative reviews matters more than the positive mistakes. If it exists to quote praise on a poster, the 74 missed positives matter more. The same model can be good enough for one feature and not the other. 7.3 The coverage–accuracy trade-off Our threshold is one point on a continuum. If we rank the test reviews from most to least confident and answer only the top share, we get a curve: The curve falls steadily as we answer more. Answering only the most confident half gives 0.984 accuracy; 80% gives 0.932; our service's point, about 90%, gives 0.899; answering everything gives 0.875. (The curve is jagged at the far left, where only a few reviews are answered.) This is the tool for a product conversation: "If people can review one review in ten, the model is right 0.899 of the time on the rest; if they can review half, 0.984." 7.4 Speed per request Finally, how long does one request take? A request runs two models, the classifier and the review-likeness embedding. Each request takes tens of milliseconds on this CPU (the printed time will differ on your machine). Note 7.6 looks at how latency, batching and hardware trade off in deployment. Figure 7.5.2. Of 1,000 source test reviews, 909 were answered, 79 received a confidence abstention and 12 were flagged out of domain. Held-back accuracy 0.637 applies to all 91 non-answered reviews. Key terms - Coverage: the share of inputs for which the system gives an answer. - Selective accuracy: accuracy measured only on the inputs the system answers. - Confusion matrix: a table counting each combination of true and predicted label. - Recall (per class): the share of a class's real examples that the model labels correctly. Common mistake: reporting only the model's accuracy for an application with abstention or filtering. Always report coverage alongside accuracy on answered inputs. A system that answers only its easiest 10% can show near-perfect accuracy and still be useless. Check yourself. 1. A manager asks for "at least 0.95 accuracy". Using the coverage–accuracy numbers, what would you tell them, and what decision do they need to make? Worked answer Answering everything gives 0.875, below the target. On the coverage–accuracy curve, accuracy reaches 0.932 at 80% coverage and 0.984 at 50%, so 0.95 requires answering somewhere between half and four-fifths of reviews. The manager has to decide whether it's acceptable for people to handle the rest, and how many people that needs. Alternatively, the model must be improved, for example by fine-tuning it on IMDb data (Module 8).

title: The Big Picture: From Notebook to AI Feature
text: A deployed model is judged on more than accuracy. Here are the constraints that come up in almost every project, and the questions behind them: | Constraint | The question | Measured in | |---|---|---| | Latency | How long does one user wait? | milliseconds per request | | Throughput | How many requests can one machine handle? | requests (examples) per second | | Memory | Does the model fit on the machine? | megabytes or gigabytes | | Cost | What does each request cost? | money per request or per hour | | Reproducibility | Will it give the same answers next month? | pinned versions and records | They pull against each other. A bigger model may be more accurate but slower and hungrier; batching raises throughput but makes each request wait for its batch; quantising saves memory but may cost accuracy. Engineering a feature means choosing a point among these trade-offs, and that needs measurements, which is what this note provides. Figure 7.6.1. Deployment choices trade quality, latency, throughput and memory. The directions shown are engineering considerations to test on the target workload, not measured universal laws. We'll use the fixed IMDb split from Note 7.1 (the function is copied here; the fingerprints confirm the reviews are the same).

title: Latency and Throughput
text: Latency is the time from receiving one request to returning its answer: what a single user experiences. Throughput is how many requests the system completes per second: what the operator pays for. They're related but not the same, and improving one can hurt the other. We load the sentiment model explicitly, as in Note 7.4, with a small helper that runs a list of texts and returns their logits. Now we send 100 validation reviews, one request at a time, and time each one. We report the median, the 95th percentile (p95: 95% of requests were faster than this) and the slowest. Latency is not a single number. Some requests take noticeably longer than the median, and in a real service the slow ones are what users complain about. That is why services set targets on high percentiles ("p95 under 50 ms") rather than on the average. Here the main cause of the spread is easy to see: Latency rises in a nearly straight line with the number of tokens in the request, as Note 7.3 predicted for a model of this size. The cluster on the right is the 40 of 100 reviews that hit the 256-token limit: truncation also caps the worst-case latency. Lowering max_length is therefore a direct latency lever, paid for in accuracy on long reviews (Note 7.3, Section 4). 2.2 Throughput and batching Serving requests one at a time is simple, but it leaves the hardware under-used. If many requests arrive together, we can batch them (Note 7.4): Batching 32 reviews at a time, sorted by length, processes more reviews per second than handling them one by one. That's the throughput side. The latency side is the catch: in a live service, a request that arrives first has to wait for the batch to fill before it is processed. Real servers use dynamic batching: collect whatever requests arrive within a short window (a few milliseconds), run them together, and return each result. A larger window gives bigger batches and more throughput, at the price of a little extra latency for everyone. Key terms - Latency: the time to serve one request. - Throughput: the number of requests served per second. - Percentile (p95): the value below which 95% of measurements fall; used to describe the slow end of latency. - Dynamic batching: grouping requests that arrive close together in time into one batch. Common mistake: reporting only average latency. A service whose average is fine but whose slowest 5% of requests take ten times longer will still frustrate users. Report percentiles, and look at what makes the slow requests slow. Check yourself. 1. Your service must answer each request within 100 ms, and requests arrive one at a time, a few per minute. Would you use dynamic batching? Why or why not? Worked answer No. With requests arriving a few per minute, a batching window would almost never collect more than one request, so there's no throughput to gain, and every request would wait for the window to close, adding latency for nothing. Dynamic batching pays off when many requests arrive close together.

title: CPU vs. GPU Inference
text: A GPU (graphics processing unit) has thousands of simple arithmetic units that work in parallel, and a Transformer is mostly large matrix multiplications, which parallelise very well. So GPUs usually run Transformers much faster than CPUs, if they are given enough work at once. That last condition is why batching matters more on a GPU: a single short request leaves most of a GPU idle, while a batch of 32 or 64 keeps it busy. On a CPU, as we just measured, batching gives a smaller gain. The cell below compares the two if your machine has an NVIDIA GPU; otherwise it says so and skips the timing. These notes were run on a CPU, so the comparison was skipped. If your machine has an NVIDIA GPU, you'll see both numbers, and you'll typically find the GPU many times faster on the batch. A few practical points either way: - A GPU has its own memory. The model and every batch must fit in GPU memory, which is often smaller than the computer's main memory. Section 4 shows how to estimate that. - Moving data costs time. Inputs travel from main memory to the GPU and results travel back, which is why to(device) sits around every batch, and why tiny requests gain little. - Cost and availability differ. GPUs are expensive to buy or rent, and a small model like ours may serve its traffic perfectly well from cheap CPU machines. Measure before assuming you need one. - Other accelerators exist. Apple computers have their own GPU, which PyTorch calls mps. That's why Note 7.4 asked you to pass device= explicitly, so the same code doesn't silently run on different hardware for different people. Key terms - GPU: a processor with many parallel arithmetic units, well suited to the matrix multiplications in neural networks. - GPU memory: the GPU's own memory, which must hold the model and each batch. Check yourself. 1. A colleague benchmarks a model on a GPU with batch size 1 and concludes "the GPU is barely faster than the CPU, so it isn't worth it". What would you ask them to try? Worked answer Try larger batch sizes, such as 32 or 64. A single request leaves most of a GPU's parallel units idle, and the time to move data to and from the GPU dominates. With a full batch, the GPU's advantage usually shows clearly. They should also make sure they synchronise before stopping the timer, since GPU work runs in the background.

title: Memory Requirements and Model Size
text: 4.1 Parameters × bytes, checked Since Note 7.1 we have estimated model size as parameters × bytes per parameter. Let's check that rule against the model's actual tensors in three number formats. The rule is exact: 66,955,010 parameters take 267.8 MB in float32 (4 bytes each) and 133.9 MB in either 16-bit format (2 bytes each). Halving the bytes halves the memory. Remember that this is the weights only: running the model also needs memory for activations, which grows with batch size and length (Note 7.4, Section 6), and generation adds the KV cache (Section 6 below). 4.2 What fewer bits cost Fewer bits means each number is stored less exactly, or within a smaller range. The two 16-bit formats make different trade-offs: The first three lines show each format's limits: - float32 can represent numbers up to about 3.4e+38 with a relative precision of about 1.2e-07, roughly seven significant digits. - float16 keeps reasonable precision (9.8e-04, about three digits) but its range stops at 6.55e+04. A larger number becomes inf, infinity: 70000 is stored as inf. - bfloat16 keeps float32's full range (70000 is stored as 70144.0, slightly off but not infinite) but has less precision (7.8e-03, about two digits): adding 0.001 to 1 changes nothing, giving 1.000000. For neural networks, range is often the bigger danger, since an overflow to infinity breaks a computation completely. So bfloat16 has become the common choice for training and running large models on hardware that supports it, such as the Qwen models in Note 7.3, which are stored in BF16. Weights themselves cope well with reduced precision, which is what makes the next section possible. Key terms - float32, float16, bfloat16: 32- and 16-bit floating-point formats; bfloat16 keeps float32's range with less precision, while float16 keeps more precision with a much smaller range. - Precision (relative precision): the smallest relative difference a format can represent between two nearby numbers. - Range: the largest (and smallest) magnitudes a format can store before overflowing to infinity. - Overflow: a value too large for the format, stored as infinity. Check yourself. 1. A model has 1.5 billion parameters. Estimate its weight memory in float32 and in bfloat16. Would you expect it to fit in a GPU with 4 GB of memory? Worked answer 1.5 billion × 4 bytes = 6 GB in float32, and × 2 bytes = 3 GB in bfloat16. In bfloat16 the weights alone would take most of a 4 GB GPU, leaving little room for activations (and a KV cache, for generation), so it would be very tight. Int8 quantisation (about 1.5 GB of weights) would make it fit comfortably.

title: Quantisation: The Core Idea
text: 5.1 Rounding weights to whole numbers 16-bit formats halve memory. Quantisation goes further by storing weights as small integers, usually 8-bit integers (int8), whole numbers from −127 to 127, which take 1 byte each. The trick is a scale: we choose a number s so that the largest weight maps to 127, divide every weight by s, round to the nearest whole number, and store the integers plus s. To use the weights, multiply back by s. Here it is on four example weights: The largest magnitude is 1.27, so the scale is 1.27 / 127 = 0.01. Dividing by it gives 80, −30, 5 and −127, all whole numbers that fit in one byte, and multiplying back gives exactly the original weights. (The long decimals in the first line are float32's own rounding of 0.8, 0.3 and so on, from Section 4.2.) Real weights won't divide so neatly, so rounding loses a little. Let's do the same to a real layer, the first feed-forward layer of DistilBERT's first Transformer block, with one scale per output row (per-channel scales), since rows can have very different ranges: The layer's 3072 × 768 weights shrink from 9.44 MB to 2.36 MB, plus 12.3 kB of scales. The price is rounding error: on average 2.84e-04, which is 0.87% of a typical weight's size. That's small, but errors in thousands of weights add up through six layers, so the real test is the model's output. 5.2 The whole model The function below applies the same rounding to every nn.Linear layer in a copy of the model: the attention projections, the feed-forward layers and the classifier. To keep the code simple, it puts the rounded-and-rescaled values back as float32 (so the model runs as before), and it counts what int8 storage would take. Rounding the Linear layers to int8 takes the model from 267.8 MB to 138.8 MB, about half, not a quarter. The reason is in the second line: the embedding tables (23,834,112 numbers, 95.3 MB) aren't Linear layers and stay in float32. This is Note 7.1's observation that a third of DistilBERT is embeddings, showing up again in practice. Size is only good news if the answers survive. We compare the int8 model with the original on the first 300 validation reviews: The original scores 0.873 on these 300 reviews, and the int8 version 0.877. They agree on 0.997 of the labels, which is all but one review, and no probability moved by more than 0.0804. With 300 reviews, one review is worth about a third of a percentage point, so the tiny accuracy difference is one review changing sides, not a real improvement. Quantisation cost us essentially nothing here. 5.3 The library route In practice you don't write quantisation by hand. torchao, PyTorch's quantisation library, does the same int8 weight-only quantisation in one line, replacing each Linear layer's weights with real int8 tensors: torchao's model saves to 138.9 MB, matching our hand-built estimate, with the same accuracy (0.877) and the same agreement (0.997) with the original. Our by-hand version was the core idea; the library adds efficient storage and computation. 5.4 Smaller is not automatically faster Does a smaller model run faster? Let's time the original, a bfloat16 copy and the torchao int8 model on the same 16 reviews: On this CPU, neither smaller version is faster. The bfloat16 copy is several times slower than float32, and the int8 model is somewhat slower too. Speed depends on whether the hardware and software have fast routines (kernels) for the number format. This processor and this PyTorch build are heavily optimised for float32 matrix multiplication. Many GPUs and some server CPUs have dedicated fast paths for 16-bit and int8 arithmetic, and there these formats are typically faster as well as smaller. So the reliable benefit of quantisation is memory, while the speed benefit depends on the hardware. Measure on the machine you will deploy to. Figure 7.6.2. Illustrative symmetric rounding with scale 0.01. The exact reconstruction arithmetic is computed in the figure script; it is separate from the notebook's measured model experiment. Key terms - Quantisation: storing numbers with fewer bits, here as 8-bit integers plus a scale. - int8: 8-bit integers, 1 byte each; we use −127 to 127. - Scale: the number that converts between the original values and the integers. - Per-channel quantisation: using a separate scale for each row (output channel) of a weight matrix. - Weight-only quantisation: quantising the stored weights while computing with higher-precision activations. - Kernel: a low-level routine that performs an operation, such as matrix multiplication, for a particular hardware and number format. Common mistake: assuming quantisation always makes a model faster. It always reduces memory, but speed depends on whether your hardware has fast int8 or 16-bit kernels. On this CPU, both smaller formats were slower than float32. Check yourself. 1. Why did int8 quantisation of the Linear layers bring DistilBERT only from 267.8 MB to 138.8 MB, rather than to a quarter of its size? What would you have to quantise to get closer to a quarter? Worked answer Because only the Linear layers were quantised. The embedding tables, 95.3 MB of the original 267.8 MB, stayed in float32 at 4 bytes per number. To get closer to a quarter, you would also have to quantise the embeddings (and any other large float32 tensors); libraries offer this, with the usual need to check accuracy afterwards. Visual walkthrough: Round, reconstruct, measure error. 1. Choose an illustrative scale. w = 0.806 · scale = 0.01. This scalar example illustrates uniform rounding. The notebook separately measures an actual quantized model. 2. Round to an integer. q = round(0.806 / 0.01) = 81. 81 is inside signed int8 range. A full quantizer must define clipping and how scales are selected. 3. Reconstruct the value. ŵ = 81 × 0.01 = 0.810. The integer and scale together approximate the original value. 4. Measure reconstruction error. ŵ − w = 0.004. Smaller weight error need not imply an equal change in application quality. Measure quality, latency and peak memory on the intended workload. The app adds a paused animation of this same supplied example.

title: Batching, Caching and Resource Utilisation
text: The cheapest computation is the one you don't do. Sections 2 and 3 covered batching, which does the same work more efficiently. This section covers two kinds of caching, which avoid repeating work at all. 6.1 Caching responses In many applications the same inputs come up again and again: popular products, common questions, a viral review. A response cache stores each answer the first time it is computed and returns it directly for later identical requests. We simulate 1,000 requests drawn from 200 reviews, where, as in real traffic, a few reviews are requested far more often than others: Only 163 distinct reviews were requested among the 1,000 requests, so with a cache the model runs 163 times and the other 83.7% of requests are answered instantly from memory. How well a cache works depends entirely on how repetitive your traffic is, so measure that on real request logs before building one. Notice the cache key: it contains the model name and the max_length setting as well as the text. If you update the model or change a setting, old cached answers must not be served as if they came from the new configuration. Forgetting this is a classic source of confusing bugs. 6.2 The KV cache in text generation Generation has its own, internal cache. In Note 6.6 we saw that a decoder generates one token at a time, and that each new token attends to all the previous ones. Without a cache, every step reruns the model over the whole text so far, recomputing keys and values for tokens that haven't changed. The KV cache stores each token's keys and values once and reuses them, so each step only processes the one new token. Let's time distilgpt2 generating 100 tokens both ways: With the cache, generation is several times faster, and the text is identical: the cache changes how much work is done, not the result. Counting the token positions the model processes shows why: For a 10-token prompt and 100 new tokens, generating without the cache processes 5,950 token positions, because every step re-reads everything before it. With the cache it processes 109: the prompt once, then one new position per step. The timing gap was smaller than this count suggests, because each cached step also has to attend over all the stored keys and values, and each step has fixed overheads. The longer the text, the bigger the saving. The KV cache does cost memory, though: it holds keys and values for every layer and every past token, and for long conversations with large models it can rival the weights themselves in size. 6.3 Resource utilisation Put together, a well-run inference service keeps the hardware busy with useful work. It batches requests so the processor is fully used, sorts or buckets by length so little of that work is padding (Note 7.4), caches repeated responses, uses the KV cache for generation, and sizes the model and its number format to the machine's memory. Each lever trades something away (batching adds waiting time, caching uses memory and risks stale answers, quantisation may cost accuracy), so the right mix depends on your traffic and your latency target. Key terms - Response cache: stored answers to previous requests, returned directly when the same request repeats. - Cache key: the information that identifies a cached answer; it must include everything that affects the answer (input, model version, settings). - Cache hit rate: the share of requests answered from the cache. - KV cache: stored attention keys and values for past tokens, reused at each generation step. Check yourself. 1. You upgrade your service to a newer model but forget to change the cache key, which contains only the input text. What will users experience, and for how long? Worked answer Users will receive the old model's answers for every input that was cached before the upgrade, while new inputs get the new model's answers. The service will behave as a confusing mix of two models, until each cached entry expires or the cache is cleared, which may be never if the cache has no expiry. The fix is to include the model version in the key, so a new model starts with a fresh cache.

title: Hosted vs. Local Inference
text: Note 7.3 compared hosted APIs and local models in general terms. With the measurements from this note, we can be more concrete about what "running it yourself" involves. Running locally means you own every constraint in this note: you measure latency and throughput, choose the hardware (CPU or GPU) and the number format, decide batching and caching, size the machines for peak traffic, and keep them running. In return you get control: the exact model version, data that never leaves your systems, and costs that are mostly fixed regardless of how many requests you serve. Using a hosted service means the provider owns most of them: they choose hardware, batching and quantisation, and you pay per request or per token. You give up control over versions and data location, and you add a network round trip to every request's latency. | | Local (self-hosted) | Hosted API | |---|---|---| | Latency | Model time only; you control it | Model time plus network round trip | | Throughput | Limited by the machines you run | Scales with the provider, within rate limits | | Memory and hardware | Your problem: size the model to the machine | The provider's problem | | Cost | Mostly fixed (machines), cheaper at high steady volume | Grows with use, cheaper at low or bursty volume | | Versions | Pinned by you (Section 8) | The provider may change or retire a model | | Data | Stays on your systems | Sent to the provider | A useful way to decide is a break-even estimate: work out what a hosted service would charge for your expected monthly requests, and compare it with the monthly cost of machines that can serve the same traffic, using throughput measured as in Section 2. Below the break-even volume, hosted is usually cheaper and simpler; above it, local usually wins, if you have the skills to run it. Key terms - Self-hosting: running a model on machines you control. - Break-even volume: the request volume at which self-hosting and a hosted service cost the same. Check yourself. 1. A startup expects a few hundred requests a day at first, possibly growing a hundredfold within a year. Which option would you suggest at launch, and what would you measure to decide whether to switch later? Worked answer At launch, a hosted service: a few hundred requests a day cost little, and you avoid running machines. Measure the monthly request volume and its growth, the hosted cost per request, and the throughput a local machine achieves for your model, as in Section 2. When the projected hosted bill exceeds the cost of machines that could serve the traffic (plus the effort of running them), it's time to consider self-hosting. Privacy or version-control needs may also force the switch earlier.

title: Model Versioning and Reproducibility
text: A deployed model must give the same answer to the same input, both from one request to the next and from one month to the next, unless you decide to change it. Three things make that possible. Record exactly what you ran. A short manifest written next to your results lists the model and its exact commit, the settings, the evaluation data's fingerprint, the result, and the software versions: Everything needed to reproduce the 0.8733 accuracy is here: the repository and the commit 714eb0fa… (Note 7.1, Section 7), max_length 256, which reviews were used (with a fingerprint, 52b8a6ed1ef8, to check they're the same), and the Python, PyTorch and Transformers versions. Saved as a JSON file next to a deployed model, a manifest like this answers "which model produced this?" months later. Check that inference is deterministic. In eval mode, the same input should give exactly the same output (Note 7.4): The same review gives bit-identical logits twice in a row. Processed inside a padded batch of 8, its logits differ by at most 1.91e-06, the tiny floating-point differences that come from doing arithmetic in a different order. That level is harmless for a label, but it means "identical" comparisons in tests should use a tolerance, and it explains why a score can wobble in its last digits between a batched and an unbatched service. Pin the software too. Library updates can change tokenisation, defaults or numerical details. A requirements.txt with exact versions, like the one that comes with these notes, together with the pinned model commit, is what makes a result reproducible by someone else. Key terms - Manifest: a small file recording the model, its exact version, settings, evaluation data and software versions behind a result. - Deterministic inference: getting exactly the same output for the same input every time. - Tolerance: the small difference allowed when comparing floating-point results. Common mistake: recording only the model's name. A name like distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english can point to different weights over time; the commit ID, the settings and the library versions are what pin a result down.

title: Define a Requirement and Select Candidate Models
text: 1.1 The requirement A vague goal ("a good sentiment model") can't be checked. A requirement turns it into criteria that a measurement can pass or fail. Writing it down before looking at any results also protects you from choosing whichever model happens to look best and then inventing reasons afterwards. Here is ours: Each line comes from a real constraint: - Accuracy at least 0.85 on our validation reviews: the product team's minimum for the feature to be worth having. - p95 latency within 100 ms for one review on a laptop CPU, because users wait for the answer (Note 7.6). - At most 600 MB of float32 weights, so the model fits beside the rest of the application. - An allowed licence: Apache 2.0, MIT or CC-BY 4.0, all of which permit commercial use (CC-BY requires credit to the authors). - Documented training data that doesn't include our evaluation reviews, so that our measurements mean something (Note 7.3, Section 4.3). The decision rule, also fixed in advance, is: among candidates that pass every check, choose the one with the highest validation accuracy; then tune its settings on validation, and confirm once on test. 1.2 The data We evaluate on the fixed IMDb split from Note 7.1 (the function is copied here; the fingerprints confirm the same reviews). Searching the Hub for text-classification models about sentiment (Notes 7.2 and 7.3) turns up thousands. Three kinds are worth testing, and we take one of each: - a general sentiment model: the SST-2 DistilBERT we've used throughout this module; - a model fine-tuned on exactly our task: a DistilBERT trained on IMDb by the TextAttack project; - a widely used model from another domain: a RoBERTa model for sentiment in tweets, from Cardiff University. All three are tagged text-classification. The two DistilBERTs have weight files of 267.8 MB; the RoBERTa model's is 501.0 MB. Two of them only offer the older pytorch_model.bin format, not safetensors (Note 7.2), which is acceptable for well-known publishers but worth noticing. Key terms - Requirement: a set of concrete, checkable criteria a model must meet, written before any measurement. - Decision rule: the procedure, fixed in advance, for choosing among candidates that meet the requirement. - Candidate: a model shortlisted for testing.

title: Inspect Documentation and Licence
text: The three cards differ sharply: - SST-2 DistilBERT: licence apache-2.0, training data declared (sst2, glue), a 3990-character card, and named labels (NEGATIVE, POSITIVE). - TextAttack IMDb DistilBERT: no licence (None), no declared datasets, a 615-character card, and unnamed labels (LABEL_0, LABEL_1), so we don't even know which output means positive. - Twitter RoBERTa: licence cc-by-4.0, trained on tweet_eval, and three labels: negative, neutral and positive. The TextAttack card is short enough to read in full: It says the model was fine-tuned on "the imdb dataset" for 5 epochs with a maximum sequence length of 128, and that its best "eval set accuracy" was 0.88. But which parts of IMDb? This repository also contains the training script's settings, train_args.json, and reading it answers the question: This settles it. The model was trained on IMDb's train split, all of it, and its dev_split, the data used to choose its best epoch, was IMDb's test split. That has two consequences for us: - Our validation set is inside its training data. We carved validation from IMDb's training half (Note 7.1), so this model has seen every one of our validation reviews, with their labels. Its validation score will measure memory, not skill. - Even the test split is not perfectly clean for it. Choosing the best of 5 epochs by test accuracy is a mild form of tuning on test, which nudges its test score upwards. This is the contamination problem from Note 7.3, found in the model's own records. Without train_args.json we'd have had to guess. Many repositories don't include such records, which is itself a reason for caution. Finally, the Twitter model's card, on its data and labels: It was pretrained on about 124 million tweets and fine-tuned on the TweetEval benchmark, with labels 0 negative, 1 neutral and 2 positive. Tweets are short, informal and full of usernames and links, which is a different domain from long film reviews. And our task has no "neutral" class, so we must decide how to use its three outputs (Section 3). Key terms - Label scheme: the set of output classes and what each output position means. - Training records: files that document how a model was trained, such as arguments, logs and data splits. - Evaluation leakage: evaluation data that a model saw during training or model selection, which inflates its score. Common mistake: assuming a model with unnamed labels (LABEL_0, LABEL_1) uses the order you expect. The mapping is whatever its trainer used. Check it with inputs whose answer is obvious before trusting any accuracy number. Check yourself. 1. The TextAttack model chose its best epoch using IMDb's test split. Why does that make its reported 0.88 slightly optimistic, even though it never trained on test? Worked answer Choosing among several checkpoints by their test accuracy means the chosen one is partly the luckiest on that test set. Its test score includes some of that luck, so a fresh test set would probably give a slightly lower number. The effect is small with only 5 checkpoints to choose from, but it is the same mistake as tuning settings on test, and it means no part of IMDb's official data gives a perfectly clean estimate for this model.

title: Implement and Test on Representative Inputs
text: 3.1 Loading the candidates We load all three with the Auto classes from Note 7.4. RoBERTa prints a LOAD REPORT with two UNEXPECTED weights, roberta.pooler.dense.: a pooling layer the checkpoint contains but this classification class doesn't use. As in Note 7.1, Section 4, that is harmless. The two DistilBERTs have 66,955,010 parameters each; the RoBERTa model has 124,647,939. 3.2 Making the outputs comparable Each candidate speaks a different label language, so we need one function that turns any of them into P(positive). First, the TextAttack model's unnamed labels. Two reviews with obvious answers tell us the mapping: LABEL_1 gets 0.998 for the glowing review and LABEL_0 gets 0.998 for the scathing one, so LABEL_1 is positive. For the Twitter model, we decide before measuring to compare only its positive and negative outputs and ignore neutral: P(positive) = P(pos) / (P(pos) + P(neg)). Our task forces a choice between two answers, so the honest comparison is between those two outputs. One function now serves all three models: Aggregate accuracy comes later. First, we run the inputs that matter for the feature: clear cases, the negation and lukewarm cases from Note 7.5, two inputs that aren't reviews, and the start of a real validation review. All three get the clear cases right, and all three call "the movie was not bad" positive. The differences are in how they handle uncertainty: - SST-2 DistilBERT is extreme everywhere: 1.000 for "It was fine, I guess." and 0.004 for gibberish, as we saw in Note 7.5. - TextAttack IMDb DistilBERT is far more moderate on unclear inputs: 0.787 for "It was fine, I guess.", 0.351 for the "not bad, not good" sentence, and 0.401 and 0.641 for the two non-reviews. Its scores are closer to "unsure" where a person would be unsure, which is a useful property. - Twitter RoBERTa sits in between, and with its neutral option ignored it is also confident on the lukewarm sentence (0.971). On the real review (a negative one), all three are right. Representative inputs don't choose the model on their own, but they show which behaviours to watch for, and they would catch a broken label mapping immediately. Check yourself. 1. Why did we decide how to treat the Twitter model's neutral output before measuring its accuracy? Worked answer Because if we chose the treatment of "neutral" after seeing the accuracies, we could pick whichever option made the model look best, which is tuning on our evaluation data. Deciding in advance, based on what the task needs (a positive-or-negative answer), keeps the measurement honest.

title: Measure Quality, Latency and Resource Use
text: 4.1 Quality on validation All three candidates are measured on the same 500 validation reviews, truncated to the same 256 tokens. The SST-2 model scores 0.874 and the Twitter model 0.834. The TextAttack model scores 0.982, far ahead, and we know why: it was trained on these very reviews (Section 2). Its number is real, but it measures the wrong thing. Without having read train_args.json, this is exactly the result that would have won the decision. 4.2 Latency and memory Next, p95 latency for single reviews on this CPU (Note 7.6), and weight memory from parameters × 4 bytes: All three are well inside the 100 ms limit on this machine, and the two DistilBERTs are about equally fast, as expected, since they share an architecture. The larger RoBERTa model is noticeably slower and needs 498.6 MB of weights, against 267.8 MB for the DistilBERTs. All fit under 600 MB. 4.3 Applying the requirement Now we apply every criterion from Section 1 to every candidate: Only the SST-2 model passes every check. The TextAttack model fails twice, on the licence and on training data that overlaps our evaluation. Either failure alone rules it out, whatever its accuracy. The Twitter model has an acceptable licence and clean data, but its 0.834 falls short of 0.85: tweets are not film reviews. 4.4 Tuning a setting on validation The chosen model has one important setting, max_length, the truncation length. Notes 7.3 and 7.4 showed that 256 tokens cuts off many reviews. Note 7.3 couldn't separate the effect of truncation from the fact that long reviews are harder, because it compared different reviews. Here we run the same 300 validation reviews at three lengths, and use the sign test to see whether the difference is real: Interpret the evidence carefully. The documentation check rejects a known contaminated candidate. For other candidates, “no documented overlap found” is more accurate than a guarantee of clean upstream training. An absent licence field is missing evidence; inspect original publisher terms before concluding that no licence exists. Accuracy rises with the amount of review the model can read: 0.843 at 128 tokens, 0.873 at 256 and 0.903 at 512. Comparing 512 with 256 on the same reviews, 12 reviews are right only at 512 and 3 only at 256. That split would arise by chance with probability 0.04, so the gain from reading more is real, not noise. More tokens cost more time (Note 7.3), so we check that 512 tokens still meets the latency requirement: It does, with room to spare on this machine. So the validation evidence chooses max_length=512. 4.5 One look at the test set The model and its setting are now fixed, so we use the test set once to confirm the result. For comparison, we also run the rejected TextAttack model on the same test reviews. Its test score is the closest we can get to a fair measure of what IMDb fine-tuning achieves. The chosen setup scores 0.888 on 500 test reviews, a little below its 0.903 on validation. That is normal: some of a validation score's height comes from having chosen the best setting on it. The TextAttack model falls from 0.982 on validation to 0.916 on test. Most of its apparent lead was leakage. On the same test reviews it was right on 36 that our model got wrong, and wrong on 22 that ours got right; a split like that would occur by chance with probability 0.087. So on these 500 reviews we can't be confident it's better at all, and its test score is itself a little optimistic, since it picked its best epoch on IMDb test. If it is better, the most likely reason is clear: it was fine-tuned on IMDb itself. That's the idea Module 8 takes up, adapting a model to your data yourself, with a licence and records you control. Figure 7.7.1. Source validation and CPU measurements under declared requirements. The IMDb-trained candidate has known evaluation exposure and missing licence evidence; other candidates are screened by documented information. Key terms - Screening: eliminating candidates on non-negotiable criteria (licence, data, size) before comparing performance. - Setting (hyperparameter) tuning: choosing values such as max_length by their validation results. - Confirmatory test: a single use of the test set after all choices are made, to estimate real-world performance. Common mistake: letting a spectacular number override the rules. The TextAttack model's 0.982 was the most impressive result in this note, and it was the least trustworthy. A number that looks too good is a signal to check what the model was trained on, not a reason to skip the checks. Check yourself. 1. The chosen model scored 0.903 on validation and 0.888 on test. Why is it normal for the test score to be a little lower, and would it have been a problem if it had been much lower? Worked answer The setting (max_length 512) was chosen because it did best on validation, and part of that advantage is luck specific to those 300 reviews. On new reviews, that luck doesn't repeat, so a slightly lower score is expected. A much lower test score would be a warning: it could mean the validation set is unrepresentative, that something leaked, or that the setting was overfitted to validation, and you'd investigate before deploying.

title: Document Limitations and Failure Cases
text: 5.1 Looking at failures A decision isn't complete without knowing how the chosen model fails. Here are the first three validation reviews (in validation order, not chosen by outcome) that it gets wrong at the chosen setting: The model gets 29 of 300 validation reviews wrong. The first three show recognisable patterns: - A positive review that reads like a complaint. "Low budget Brit pop melodrama … cannot hide the fact that we have all been here before" is labelled positive, but most of its first sentences criticise the film. The model gives it 0.011. - A negative review that opens with neutral plot summary. The "Romulus, My Father" review spends its opening describing the story; the model, unsure, leans positive at 0.613. - A review with mixed feelings. "I really liked this movie … Great story with great actors but with a terrible end" is labelled positive, but the model fixes on the "terrible end" and gives it 0.003. None of these is a bug. They are the hard cases of sentiment: mixed opinions, sarcasm and summary. Knowing them tells a product team what to expect, for example that mixed reviews are where human review adds most. 5.2 The decision record Finally, we write the decision down, with its evidence, in a form the next person can check. It builds on the manifest from Note 7.6, extended with what was rejected and why, and with known limitations. The record pins the model to commit 714eb0fa…, states the setting (max_length 512), gives the validation and test results with the fingerprints of exactly which reviews they came from, records the latency on this machine, explains why each other candidate was rejected, and lists known limitations. Those limitations come from this note and earlier ones: confidence on lukewarm reviews and on non-reviews (Note 7.5), truncation after 512 tokens (Section 4.4), and the country bias reported in the model's card (Note 7.2). If the feature misbehaves in six months, this record says where to look first, and it makes the decision easy to revisit when a better candidate appears. Key terms - Failure analysis: examining the inputs a model gets wrong to find patterns. - Decision record: a document stating what was chosen, why, on what evidence, and with which known limitations. Common mistake: recording only the winning accuracy. Without the settings, the exact data, the model commit and the reasons other candidates were rejected, nobody, including you in six months, can check or revisit the decision. Check yourself. 1. Six months after deployment, a new sentiment model appears on the Hub with an Apache 2.0 licence, declared training data and a claimed accuracy of 0.95 on IMDb. Using this note's process, what would you do before replacing the current model? Worked answer Run it through the same process. Add it as a candidate, read its card and any training records (especially: does its training data include IMDb, and which splits?), check the licence and label mapping, test it on the same representative inputs, measure it on the same validation reviews (same fingerprint) with the same latency and memory checks, and only if it passes and wins, confirm once on the test set and update the decision record. A claimed 0.95 on IMDb is exactly the kind of number that should trigger a contamination check.

title: The Big Picture: From General-Purpose to Task-Specific
text: A pretrained model is a generalist. DistilBERT knows English well, from guessing hidden words in books and Wikipedia (Note 7.1). A small chat model knows how to follow instructions. Neither knows what our product team means by a negative review, which reviews matter, or how our users write. Adaptation closes that gap, and the main ways to do it form a spectrum, ordered by how much of the model they change: | Approach | What changes | Labelled data needed | Compute needed | |---|---|---|---| | Prompting | nothing: we only change the input, by describing the task in words | none (or a few examples in the prompt) | inference only | | Feature extraction | a small new model trained on the frozen model's outputs | some | one pass over the data, plus a quick fit | | Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) | a small set of new or selected weights inside the model | some to many | training, but with few weights to update | | Full fine-tuning | every weight in the model | many | training of the whole model | Moving down the table, adaptation becomes more powerful, but also costs more data and compute, and risks damaging what the model already knew. The rest of this note tries each approach on the same task and data, so the trade-offs are measured, not just described. Figure 8.1.1. Prompting changes the input; a frozen encoder supports a trained head; LoRA changes selected adapters; full fine-tuning makes the selected base parameters trainable. More complexity need not improve quality. The data Everything in Module 8 uses the fixed IMDb split from Note 7.1. The function is copied here, and the fingerprints confirm the same reviews. Many reviews are longer than the 128 tokens we'll feed DistilBERT in this module. Rather than keeping only the start of each review, the helper below keeps the beginning and the end, where reviewers often give their verdict. Note 8.2 explains this choice and measures how much it helps.

title: The Adaptation Spectrum: Prompting, Feature Extraction, PEFT, Full Fine-Tuning
text: We'll compare the approaches on the first 100 validation reviews, where every review is worth one percentage point of accuracy. 2.1 Prompting: describe the task in words The cheapest adaptation changes no weights at all. With an instruction-following model, you write the task as a question, and the model answers. We use SmolLM2-360M-Instruct, a small open chat model with about 360 million parameters, loaded in float32 because its stored bfloat16 format is very slow on most CPUs (Note 7.6). Its chat template (Note 8.6 looks inside) wraps our question in the special markers the model was trained with: The template added a system message we didn't write ("You are a helpful AI assistant named SmolLM…"). That's this model's default. Then comes our question, and finally the start of the assistant's turn, where the model should write its answer. Let's ask it about a real review: It answers "Negative", correctly. To score 100 reviews quickly and fairly, we don't generate free text. Instead we compare the model's scores for the two possible answer words at the first position of its reply, and take whichever is higher. This avoids having to parse answers like "Negative." or "It is negative". With no training and no labels at all, prompting gets 0.84 of the 100 reviews right, and it says "positive" for 0.49 of them, about the right balance. That's a strong start for zero effort. The costs are elsewhere: every prediction runs a 360-million-parameter model over a long prompt, and the only way to improve it is to rephrase the prompt, which is fragile. 2.2 Feature extraction: train a small model on frozen features Feature extraction keeps a pretrained model completely frozen, meaning its weights are never changed, and uses it only to turn each review into a vector of numbers, its features. A small, fast model, here logistic regression, then learns to map those vectors to labels. This is the encoder-plus-linear-probe idea from Note 5.1, with a pretrained encoder. We use DistilBERT's body, average its token vectors (mean pooling, Note 7.5), and train on 1,000 labelled reviews. With 1,000 labels, feature extraction reaches 0.844 on 500 validation reviews, and 0.86 on the first 100, the same reviews prompting saw. On those 100 reviews the two approaches are within two reviews of each other. Neither one changed a single weight of a pretrained model. 2.3 PEFT and full fine-tuning: change the model itself The last two approaches do change the pretrained model, by training it further on labelled examples. That's fine-tuning (Note 7.1, Section 2). - Full fine-tuning updates every weight. It's the most flexible, but it needs the most memory and compute, and every task gets its own complete copy of the model. Note 8.4 runs it properly. - Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) freezes the pretrained weights and trains a small number of extra ones. The most popular method, LoRA, adds small "correction" matrices beside some of the layers. Often around 1% of the parameters are trained, which makes training cheaper, keeps the original model intact, and lets one base model serve many tasks. Note 8.5 builds it. We'll see full fine-tuning at small scale in Section 4. Key terms - Adaptation: making a general pretrained model better at a specific task. - Prompting: adapting a model only by describing the task in its input; no weights change. - Chat template: the format of special markers an instruction-tuned model expects around system, user and assistant messages. - Feature extraction: using a frozen pretrained model to produce features, and training a separate small model on them. - Frozen: describes weights that are not updated during training. - Fine-tuning: further training of a pretrained model's own weights on labelled task data. - PEFT (parameter-efficient fine-tuning): fine-tuning that trains only a small number of new or selected weights while the rest stay frozen. - LoRA (low-rank adaptation): a PEFT method that adds small trainable matrices to some layers (Note 8.5). Check yourself. 1. Prompting scored 0.84 on 100 reviews without any labels. Give two reasons a team might still prefer to train a small classifier, even if it scored about the same. Worked answer For example: cost and speed (the small classifier runs the much smaller DistilBERT encoder once per review, while prompting runs a 360-million-parameter model over a long prompt); stability (a trained classifier's behaviour is fixed, while prompt behaviour can change with small wording changes or a model update); calibrated probabilities and easy thresholds (Note 7.5); and the ability to improve steadily by adding labelled data, which prompting can't use directly.

title: When to Fine-Tune, and When Not To
text: Fine-tuning is powerful, but it's often not the first thing to try. Before you start, it helps to ask these questions in order, from cheapest to most expensive: 1. Does a ready-made model already do the task? In Note 7.7, a downloadable sentiment model met our requirement without any training. If one exists with a suitable licence, measure it first (Note 8.3 makes it a baseline). 2. Can prompting do it? For a capable instruction model, a clear prompt, perhaps with a few examples in it, may be enough, as Section 2.1 suggests. 3. Is a simple model on frozen features enough? Feature extraction is cheap to train and easy to retrain when labels change. 4. Only then: fine-tune.
