It is worth it when you have enough good labelled data, when the task or its data differ from anything the model saw (special vocabulary, formats or labels), or when you need a small, fast model to do well what only a large, slow one can do by prompting. Fine-tuning is the wrong tool when: - you have very few labels. A few dozen examples can't adjust millions of weights reliably. Section 5 shows how quickly a small training set leads to overfitting. - the task changes often. Each change means new data and a new training run. A prompt or a retrained simple classifier adapts faster. - what's missing is knowledge, not behaviour. Fine-tuning shapes how a model responds, but it is a poor way to teach it new or changing facts, which it may then recall wrongly (Note 7.1, Section 3). Feeding the relevant documents into the prompt usually works better. - a simple baseline already meets the requirement. If TF-IDF or an off-the-shelf model is good enough, the extra cost and risk of fine-tuning buy nothing. Common mistake: jumping straight to fine-tuning because it feels like the "real" machine-learning solution. Start from the cheapest approach that could work, measure it, and move along the spectrum only when the measurements say you must. Check yourself. 1. A legal team wants a model to answer questions about contracts signed this week. Is fine-tuning a good way to give the model that knowledge? What would you do instead? Worked answer No. Fine-tuning shapes how a model behaves, but it's a poor and slow way to store new facts: the model may recall them wrongly, and this week's contracts would need retraining every week. A better approach is to find the relevant contract text and put it into the prompt, so the model answers from the document in front of it. (That approach is called retrieval-augmented generation.)

title: Full Fine-Tuning: What Changes During Training
text: Let's watch full fine-tuning happen at small scale. We take DistilBERT's pretrained body, add a new, randomly initialised classification head (Note 7.1, Section 4, hence the LOAD REPORT), and train everything on a deliberately small set of 160 reviews for three passes (epochs). After each epoch we check accuracy on the training reviews themselves and on 200 validation reviews. The loop is the familiar one from Module 2: forward pass, loss, backward pass, optimiser step. Note 8.4 takes it apart. Three things happen. - Epoch 1 learns almost nothing useful. The training loss barely moves (0.697), and the model calls every validation review positive (1.00), which scores 0.525, the share of positive reviews among them. The new head starts random, and 10 small steps are not enough. - Epoch 2 is where it learns the task. Accuracy jumps to 0.925 on the training reviews and 0.850 on validation, from only 160 labelled examples. The pretrained body already understands language; training mostly has to connect that understanding to the new head. - Epoch 3 keeps improving on the training reviews (0.969) while validation drops to 0.800, with the model now leaning positive (0.69). Section 5 returns to this. How much did the pretrained weights move? We compare the body after training with the body we started from, layer by layer, using the relative change from Note 7.1, Section 7: Every one of the 66,955,010 parameters was trainable, including 592,130 in the new head, and every part of the body moved, but only slightly: between 0.395% and 0.624% on average. The last Transformer layer, nearest the new head, changed most. Full fine-tuning is gentle nudging of a model that already works, not rebuilding it. Even so, those small nudges have consequences, which we measure next. Key terms - Epoch: one pass through all the training examples. - Classification head: the new layer(s) on top of a pretrained body that map its features to the task's labels; it starts random. - Relative change: the size of the change in a weight tensor divided by the size of the original. Check yourself. 1. In epoch 1, the model predicted "positive" for every validation review. Why might a freshly initialised head do that, and why did accuracy still come out at 0.525? Worked answer A random head produces arbitrary scores; with a slight bias towards one output, every review falls on the same side. Ten small updates in epoch 1 weren't enough to fix that. Predicting one class for everything scores the share of that class in the data, and 0.525 of these 200 validation reviews happen to be positive. That's chance level for this set, not real skill.

title: Catastrophic Forgetting and Overfitting
text: Two things can go wrong when you fine-tune, and they're easy to confuse: the model can fit its small training set too closely, and it can lose abilities it had before. 5.1 Overfitting You met overfitting in Module 3: a model learns the quirks of its training examples instead of the general pattern, so it keeps improving on them while getting worse on new data. Here are the numbers from Section 4 as a picture: Through epoch 2, both curves rise together. In epoch 3 the training loss falls sharply and training accuracy keeps climbing, but validation accuracy drops from 0.850 to 0.800, and the gap between the two widens. With only 160 examples, the model has started to memorise them. One caution: the drop is 10 of 200 validation reviews in a single training run, so treat it as a warning sign rather than proof. But it is exactly the pattern to watch for, and it's why the fine-tuning notes choose their checkpoint on validation (Note 8.4). 5.2 Catastrophic forgetting Overfitting is about the task we're training on. Catastrophic forgetting is about everything else: when a model's weights are adjusted for a new task, it can lose some of what it could do before. DistilBERT was pretrained to guess hidden words. Does our fine-tuned body still do that as well? To find out, we hide 15% of the words in 200 validation reviews used nowhere else, and measure how well the original word-guessing head does. First on top of the pretrained body, then with the fine-tuned body swapped in. The loss is the cross-entropy of its guesses; lower is better. With the pretrained body, the word-guessing loss on the 3557 hidden words is 3.381. With the fine-tuned body, it rises to 3.920. Bodies that moved by less than 1% on average have measurably lost some of their original skill, after training on just 160 reviews. That's catastrophic forgetting in miniature. It matters when you want the adapted model to keep doing other things too, and it's one reason PEFT methods, which leave the original weights untouched, are attractive. Note 8.5 measures how much less LoRA forgets. Figure 8.1.2. Source small-run measurements illustrate an overfitting warning and degraded masked-word retention. The retention experiment uses a tied output projection and is not a complete capability audit. Key terms - Overfitting: improving on the training examples while getting worse on new data. - Catastrophic forgetting: losing previously learned abilities when a model is trained on a new task. - Masked-word (word-guessing) loss: the cross-entropy of a masked language model's guesses for hidden words; used here as a measure of the pretrained skill. Common mistake: checking only the new task after fine-tuning. A model can score well on the task you trained it for and still have lost abilities your application relies on. If other behaviours matter, measure them before and after. Check yourself. 1. A colleague says "our fine-tuned model's validation accuracy is excellent, so it can't have forgotten anything". What's wrong with that argument? Worked answer Validation accuracy measures only the task the model was fine-tuned for. Forgetting is about other abilities, such as the pretrained word-guessing skill measured in Section 5.2, which got worse even while the new task improved. To know whether anything was forgotten, you have to test those other abilities directly. Interpret the evidence carefully. This is one masked-word retention probe on 200 IMDb reviews, not a complete test of general knowledge. DistilBERT ties its vocabulary projection to its input embeddings: loading a changed body also changes those shared output weights. The other masked-word head layers remain original. This setup measures the resulting combined system; it is not a strictly fixed-decoder experiment.

title: Data, Compute and Quality Trade-offs: Choosing a Strategy
text: Putting the measurements together gives a practical way to choose. Three resources trade against each other: - Data. Prompting needs no labels. Feature extraction got 0.844 from 1,000. Full fine-tuning learned the task from 160 examples but immediately began to overfit. More good labels make the heavier methods safer and stronger. Note 8.2 is about making those labels good. - Compute. Prompting costs nothing to set up but runs a large model on every request. Feature extraction costs one pass to compute features and a quick fit. Fine-tuning costs real training time and memory. Full fine-tuning needs memory for every weight's gradient and optimiser state (Note 8.5 counts them), PEFT far less. - Quality and risk. The heavier methods can fit a task most closely, but they risk overfitting on small data and forgetting old skills, and each fully fine-tuned task needs its own complete copy of the model. A reasonable default path, which the rest of Module 8 follows: 1. establish baselines: a simple model, an off-the-shelf model and frozen features (Note 8.3); 2. try PEFT (Note 8.5) and full fine-tuning (Note 8.4) on the same data, with checkpoints chosen on validation; 3. evaluate everything on the same test reviews, including forgetting, and keep an adapted model only if it beats the baselines by enough to justify its costs (Note 8.7). Check yourself. 1. You have 50,000 labelled support tickets, a GPU, and a requirement for a small model that answers in milliseconds. Which end of the spectrum would you start from, and why? Worked answer The fine-tuning end. With 50,000 labelled examples there's plenty of data to fine-tune safely, a GPU makes training practical, and a requirement for a small, fast model rules out prompting a large one. You'd still set baselines first (Note 8.3), then try PEFT and full fine-tuning of a small model, and keep the one that meets the requirement on validation and test.

title: The Big Picture: From Raw Data to a Training-Ready Dataset
text: Data preparation is a pipeline, and each stage answers a question: 1. Task: what goes in, what comes out, and what does each label mean? 2. Quality: is the data what we think it is? Empty texts, markup, oddities? 3. Cleaning and deduplication: remove noise, and make sure each example appears once. 4. Formatting: shape each example the way the model expects it, whether text plus label for a classifier or a conversation for a chat model. 5. Splits: separate training, validation and test data, reproducibly. 6. Leakage: make sure no evaluation example, or anything derived from it, reaches training. 7. Balance: check how the labels are distributed, and choose metrics that suit it. 8. Length: fit each example into the model's token limit without losing what matters. 9. Packaging: tokenise and store the result in a form training code can stream. The order matters. Several of the worst mistakes, such as splitting before deduplicating, come from doing the right steps in the wrong order. Figure 8.2.1. Group duplicate examples before splitting; keep validation and test out of training updates. Fit learned preprocessing on train, then apply the declared policy to held-out data.

title: Defining the Task and Expected Output
text: Before touching the data, be precise about the task: one IMDb review in, one label out, positive or negative. The labels are the model's expected output, so we need to know exactly what they mean. The first place to look is the dataset card (Note 7.2): The card tells us the task (binary sentiment classification), the size (25,000 training and 25,000 test reviews) and one crucial detail: the reviews are highly polar. The dataset's authors kept strongly positive and strongly negative reviews, judged from the reviewers' own star ratings, and left out the lukewarm middle. So a model trained on IMDb has never seen a genuinely mixed review labelled as such, which helps explain the lukewarm-review behaviour we saw in Note 7.5. The card is also a warning about documentation. Its licence is other, and 16 places in it say "More Information Needed", including languages and how the labels were made. Many dataset cards are incomplete; when one is, find the original source (here the authors' website and paper) before relying on the data. Now the data itself: Two columns: text and label, with label names neg (0) and pos (1). That is our expected output: an integer class, 0 or 1. Key terms - Expected output (target): what the model should produce for each input; here, a label 0 or 1. - Labelling rule: how the labels were decided; for IMDb, from the reviewers' star ratings, keeping only clearly positive or negative reviews. - Highly polar: strongly one-sided; IMDb excludes mixed or neutral reviews.

title: Data Collection and Quality
text: Over all 50000 reviews: - Lengths vary enormously, from 4 words to 2470, with a median of 173. Length is the subject of Section 9. - No review is empty. - 58.4% contain HTML tags. Almost all are line breaks (201935 of them), plus a handful of italics tags. These are left over from the web pages the reviews were collected from, and they mean nothing to a sentiment model. - 119 reviews contain a web address. The shortest reviews are worth a look, because extremes often reveal problems: They are short but genuine. "Read the book, forget the movie!" is a perfectly clear negative review. The third shows something else: "More suspenseful, more subtle, much, much more disturbing...." is labelled negative, yet on its own it reads as praise. It's probably comparing the film unfavourably with something else. Some labels can only be understood with context the text doesn't contain, so a perfect score is not a realistic target. Common mistake: skipping a manual look at the data. Summary statistics can't tell you that the shortest "reviews" are real, or that a label needs context. Reading a few examples, chosen by a rule such as the shortest or the first ones, takes minutes and often changes your plan.

title: Cleaning and Deduplication
text: Cleaning removes content that carries no signal for the task. For IMDb that means the tags, which we replace with spaces (the italics tags are too rare to matter). We'll keep the web addresses: they're rare, and a reviewer linking to something is part of what they wrote. Deduplication matters more. A review that appears twice is weighted twice in training, and if its copies end up on both sides of a split, the model is tested on something it has already seen. We look for exact copies, and for near-copies that differ only in capitalisation, punctuation or spacing: Each official half contains exact duplicates: 96 extra rows in train and 199 in test. Normalising text adds only 3 more near-copies in each half (99 and 202), so IMDb's duplicates are mostly exact. Most importantly, 123 reviews appear in both official halves, so evaluating on the official test set without deduplication would test the model on 123 reviews it trained on. Do duplicates at least agree on their labels? Yes: no duplicated text carries conflicting labels, so there's no label noise to resolve here. If copies of a text disagreed, we'd have to decide which label is right, or drop them. The most repeated training review appears 3 times. It reads like a description of a TV show, a reminder that "movie reviews" scraped from the web aren't always about movies. Key terms - Cleaning: removing content that carries no signal for the task, such as leftover HTML markup. - Exact duplicate: an example identical to another, character for character. - Near-duplicate: an example that differs from another only trivially (here: case, punctuation, spacing). - Normalisation: transforming text into a standard form so that trivially different texts compare as equal. Check yourself. 1. Normalising case and punctuation found only 3 more duplicates per half. Name another kind of near-duplicate that our normalisation would miss, and how you might find it. Worked answer For example: the same review with a few words changed or a sentence added, or the same text posted with a different ending. Normalisation only removes trivial formatting differences. To catch these you'd compare overlapping word sequences (for example with a technique called MinHash), or compare sentence embeddings (Note 7.5) and flag pairs with very high similarity for review. Visual walkthrough: Keep duplicate groups in one split. 1. Find identical examples. A: “good film” · B: “bad film” · C: “good film”. This exact-match toy policy groups A and C; real preprocessing and near-duplicate policies must be declared. 2. Group before splitting. Group 1: {A, C} · Group 2: {B}. Splitting rows first could place the same text in train and test and inflate evaluation. 3. Assign whole groups. Train: {A, C} · Test: {B}. This two-group example explains the boundary; it is far too small for a useful model evaluation. 4. Fit only on train. Learn preprocessing from train → apply to test. Test data never supplies gradients or fitted vocabulary/statistics under this protocol. Validation is a separate group-held-out split. The app adds a paused animation of this same supplied example.

title: Labelling and Instruction Formatting
text: The same data can be shaped for different kinds of model. For a classifier, as in Notes 8.3–8.5, an example is just the text and an integer label. For an instruction-tuned chat model, as in Note 8.6, the same example becomes a short conversation: an instruction containing the review, and the answer written out as words, wrapped in the model's chat template (Note 8.1): The classification example is {'text': ..., 'label': 0}. The instruction example is the same review and label, rewritten as a user turn ("Is this movie review positive or negative?") and an assistant turn ("negative"), inside the special markers SmolLM2 was trained with. Only the tokeniser was downloaded for this, a few megabytes. Instruction formatting turns any labelled dataset into training data for a chat model. The choices you make (the wording of the instruction, the exact answer words, the system message) become part of what the model learns, so keep them consistent across every example. Note 8.6 shows how such examples are trained on, including the important detail of which tokens the loss is computed on. Key terms - Instruction formatting: rewriting a labelled example as an instruction and a response for a chat model. - User / assistant turn: the parts of a conversation written by the user and by the model. Check yourself. 1. Half your instruction examples end with the answer "negative" and half with "Negative." (capitalised, with a full stop). What problem might this cause after fine-tuning? Worked answer The model learns two answer forms, so at prediction time it may produce either, and code that looks for exactly "negative" will miss "Negative.". The examples also teach the model that the answer's form varies for no reason, which wastes some of what it learns. Choose one format and apply it to every example.

title: Training, Validation and Test Splits
text: Module 4 introduced the three splits. Training data fits the weights, validation data chooses settings and checkpoints, and test data is used once at the end to estimate real-world performance. Here is the function that builds the split used throughout Modules 7 and 8, with the steps in the right order: deduplicate each half, drop test reviews that also appear in train, clean, then carve validation out of the training half with a fixed seed. The result has 22,404 training reviews, 2,500 validation reviews and 24,678 test reviews, each close to half positive. val_eval and test_eval are the fixed 1,000-review samples used for most evaluations. The fingerprints are the split's identity card: any notebook that prints the same fingerprints is evaluating on exactly the same reviews, so results can be compared fairly. Why fix the seed? Change it, and you get a different split: With seed 1, the validation set's fingerprint changes, and only 226 of its 2,500 reviews were in seed 0's validation set, about what chance predicts. Results measured on the two splits are not directly comparable. Fixing the seed, and printing a fingerprint to prove it, is what lets Notes 8.3–8.7 compare their numbers. Key terms - Training / validation / test split: data for fitting weights / for choosing settings / for one final estimate. - Fingerprint: a short hash of a split's contents that proves which examples it contains. - Reproducible split: a split that comes out the same every time, by fixing the random seed.

title: Leakage and Contamination, Including Pretraining Contamination
text: Leakage is any way information from evaluation data reaches training. It makes scores optimistic, sometimes wildly so. The most common cause is doing steps in the wrong order. Here's what would have happened if we had split IMDb's training half before removing duplicates: Splitting first leaves 16 validation reviews with an identical copy in the training part. The model would be "validated" partly on reviews it had memorised. Deduplicating first, as our function does, leaves none, and no test review appears in training either. Leakage takes other forms too: - Leakage through preprocessing. Anything fitted on data, such as a vocabulary, a scaler or a choice of settings, must be fitted on training data only. Choosing a setting by its test score is leakage too. - Leakage through groups. Several reviews by the same person, or about the same film, can share phrasing. If one goes to training and another to test, the test is easier than real use. When groups matter, split by group. - Contamination of a pretrained model. In Note 7.7 we found a model fine-tuned on IMDb's training half, which contains our validation set, and that had chosen its checkpoint on IMDb's test half. Its validation score measured memory. Pretraining can contaminate too: a model pretrained on a large web crawl may have read IMDb reviews, or even the benchmark itself. DistilBERT was pretrained on books and Wikipedia (Note 7.3), which makes this unlikely for our model, but for models trained on web crawls you often can't rule it out. The safest defence is evaluation data the model can't have seen, such as data collected after its training. Common mistake: splitting first and cleaning later. Deduplication, filtering and any fitted preprocessing must happen before the split (for deduplication) or on the training split only (for anything learned from data). Otherwise evaluation data leaks into training. Check yourself. 1. A team picks the epoch with the best test accuracy and reports that accuracy. Which kind of leakage is this, and why does it make the number optimistic? Worked answer It's leakage through model selection: the test set has been used to make a choice. Among several epochs, the one with the best test score is partly the luckiest on that test set, so its reported score includes that luck and overstates performance on new data. Choose the epoch on validation, then report test once.

title: Class Imbalance and Data Distribution
text: IMDb is exactly balanced (the official halves each have 12,500 reviews of each class), and our splits stay close to half positive. Real data often isn't balanced: complaints might be 5% of support tickets, fraud far less of transactions. Let's see what imbalance does to evaluation. We need a real classifier's predictions, so we load the SST-2 model from Module 7 and run it on 500 validation reviews. The encode function fits each review into 128 tokens in one of three ways, which Section 9 explains and compares. For now we use the version labelled head+tail. Now we build an imbalanced evaluation set by a fixed rule: the first 225 negative and the first 25 positive reviews from those 500, so 90% negative. We compare the SST-2 model with a "model" that always says negative: The do-nothing classifier wins on accuracy, 0.900 against 0.848, because it is right about every negative review, and negatives are 90% of the set. It's also useless: its recall on positive reviews is 0.000 and its F1 score for the positive class is 0.000. The real model finds 0.800 of the positive reviews and 0.853 of the negative ones. On imbalanced data, accuracy rewards ignoring the rare class, so report per-class recall, the F1 score for the class you care about, and the confusion matrix (Note 7.5), and always compare with the majority-class baseline. Imbalance in training data causes a related problem: a model can learn to favour the common class. Common remedies are to resample (show the rare class more often), to weight the loss towards the rare class, or to move the decision threshold, each chosen on validation. IMDb needs none of these, but your data might. Key terms - Class imbalance: some labels being much more common than others. - Majority-class baseline: always predicting the most common label; any useful model must beat it on the metrics that matter. - Recall: the share of a class's real examples that the model identifies. - F1 score: a single score combining precision (how many predicted positives are right) and recall; useful when one class is rare. Check yourself. 1. A fraud model reports 0.995 accuracy on data where 0.5% of transactions are fraud. What's the first number you'd ask for, and why? Worked answer The recall on fraud (and the precision, or the F1 score for the fraud class). A model that labels every transaction "not fraud" already scores 0.995 accuracy, so accuracy says nothing about whether the model catches any fraud at all. Compare with that majority-class baseline too.

title: Tokenisation and Sequence-Length Management
text: Our model reads at most 512 tokens, and in Module 8 we'll train with only 128 to keep training affordable on a CPU. How much of a typical review fits? The median validation review is 214 tokens, and one in ten is longer than 608. At 128 tokens, 85.6% of reviews don't fit; even at 512, 13.9% don't. So which 128 tokens we keep is a real decision. There are three simple strategies: - head: keep the beginning, the usual default (Note 7.4); - tail: keep the end; - head+tail: keep the first quarter of the budget and the last three quarters, skipping the middle. Here's what each keeps of one 215-token review: Head keeps the opening and stops mid-review. Tail and head+tail both keep the final verdict ("it just has to be seen."). Head+tail also keeps the opening. Which matters more is a question for measurement. Here are all three strategies with the SST-2 model at 128 tokens, on the same 500 validation reviews, with sign tests on paired predictions: Keeping the end of the review matters a great deal. Head scores 0.842; tail 0.888 and head+tail 0.880. Both beat head-only clearly (sign tests p = 0.014 and 0.042). Reviewers often summarise their verdict at the end, and the head-only cut throws it away. Between tail and head+tail, though, there's no meaningful difference: 19 reviews favour tail, 15 favour head+tail, p = 0.61. We'll use head+tail for the rest of Module 8. It is statistically not significantly different in this paired comparison from tail on validation, and it keeps the opening as well, which helps reviews that state their verdict first. Either would be a defensible choice. Head-only would not. Key terms - Token budget: the maximum number of tokens an example may use; here 128. - Head, tail and head+tail truncation: keeping the beginning, the end, or both ends of a text that exceeds the budget. Common mistake: accepting the default truncation without checking it. Keeping only the beginning is the default almost everywhere, and for IMDb at 128 tokens it cost about four points of accuracy against keeping the end. Measure the options on validation. Check yourself. 1. For a dataset of customer emails, where the request usually comes in the first lines and the rest is a long signature and quoted history, which truncation would you try first, and how would you confirm it? Worked answer Head truncation, because the request comes first and the tail is signature and quoted history. Confirm it as in Section 9: run the options (head, tail, head+tail) on the same validation emails, compare accuracy with a sign test, and choose on validation, not on intuition alone.

title: Practice: Building the Dataset with Hugging Face Datasets
text: Finally, we package everything for training. We take the 1,000 training reviews that Notes 8.3–8.5 train on, the 1,000 val_eval reviews and the 1,000 test_eval reviews, apply head+tail truncation to 128 tokens, and store token IDs and labels in a DatasetDict (Note 7.2). We don't pad here: a data collator pads each batch to its own longest member when training (Note 7.4). Three splits of 1,000 examples, each with input_ids and labels, and no example longer than 128 tokens. A data collator turns any 8 examples into a padded batch, adding the attention mask: The batch has the shapes training code expects: input_ids and attention_mask of shape (8, 128), and 8 labels. Saved with save_to_disk, the whole prepared dataset takes 1.5 MB, in Arrow format. Notes 8.3–8.5 rebuild exactly the same data with the same functions, so that each notebook stands alone; the fingerprints confirm they match. Key terms - DatasetDict: a dictionary of named Dataset splits (Note 7.2). - Data collator: a function that combines examples into a padded batch. - save_to_disk: saves a dataset in Arrow format for fast reloading.

title: The Big Picture: Why the Baseline Comes First
text: A baseline does three jobs: - It sets the bar. An adapted model is only worth its training cost, memory and complexity if it clearly beats the best simpler option. - It catches mistakes. If a sophisticated model scores below a simple baseline, something is often wrong: a bug, leakage, a bad setting. - It tells you where the gains come from. Comparing rungs that differ in one thing at a time (more labels, a pretrained encoder, adapting the encoder) shows which ingredient matters. Our ladder has three rungs below fine-tuning, plus a do-nothing floor: | Rung | Method | Labelled IMDb reviews used | What it tests | |---|---|---|---| | floor | always predict the most common label | (counts only) | is anything learned at all? | | 1 | TF-IDF + logistic regression | 1,000, and all 22,404 for reference | how far simple word counts go | | 2 | a pretrained sentiment model, off the shelf | 0 | what someone else's adaptation gives for free | | 3 | frozen DistilBERT + logistic regression | 1,000 | what pretrained features give without changing the model | Fine-tuning in Notes 8.4 and 8.5 uses the same 1,000 labelled reviews as rungs 1 and 3, the same validation reviews for every choice, and the same test reviews for the final number. That shared setup is what makes the comparison fair. Figure 8.3.1. Baselines share a declared evaluation protocol. Off-the-shelf, frozen-feature and trained alternatives use different upstream training and sometimes different input information; disclose those differences. The data and the protocol All rungs use the fixed split (Note 7.1), with fingerprints, and the same subsets: 1,000 training reviews (the first 1,000 of the training split), the 1,000 val_eval reviews for every choice of setting, and the 1,000 test_eval reviews, used once per rung. We also fingerprint the 1,000 training reviews, so Notes 8.4 and 8.5 can prove they train on the same ones. We report four numbers for every rung: accuracy, recall for each class, and F1 for the positive class (Note 8.2). We start with the floor: always predict the most common label in the 1,000 training reviews. The training subset has slightly more negative reviews, so the floor always says negative. It scores 0.505 on validation, chance level, with a recall of 1.0 for negatives and 0.0 for positives. Every rung must clear this comfortably.

title: Rung 1: TF-IDF + Logistic Regression
text: TF-IDF turns each review into a long vector of word weights (Note 7.1). Here we use single words and word pairs (ngram_range=(1, 2)), keep only terms that appear in at least two reviews, and dampen very frequent words (sublinear_tf). Logistic regression then learns one weight per term. The vectoriser is fitted on the training reviews only, never on validation or test (Note 8.2, Section 7). One setting needs choosing: C, which controls regularisation, how strongly large weights are discouraged. Smaller C means stronger regularisation. We try four values and choose by validation accuracy, then evaluate the chosen model once on test. We do this twice: with the 1,000 labelled reviews, and with all 22,404 as a reference for what plenty of labels can do. With 1,000 labels, the best setting is C=3, with validation accuracy 0.866 and test accuracy 0.828. Note the gap between validation and test. Part of it is that we chose C on validation, so the chosen value is a little lucky there; part is ordinary sampling noise on 1,000 reviews. It's a reminder that the test number is the one to report. With all 22,404 labels, TF-IDF reaches 0.921 on validation and 0.913 on test. Its vocabulary grows from 29,754 terms to 399,450, and the best C, 10, is the largest we tried, so even weaker regularisation might do slightly better. More data supports a more complex model. Fitting took a fraction of a second with 1,000 reviews, and a few seconds with all of them. Key terms - Baseline: a simple reference method, evaluated exactly like the method you hope will beat it. - Regularisation: a penalty that discourages large weights, reducing overfitting; in scikit-learn's logistic regression, smaller C means stronger regularisation. - n-grams: sequences of n consecutive words; (1, 2) means single words and word pairs. Check yourself. 1. Why must the TF-IDF vectoriser be fitted on training reviews only? What would leak if it were fitted on all reviews, including test? Worked answer The vectoriser learns which terms exist and how common they are (the IDF weights). Fitted on all reviews, it would learn from the test reviews: terms that appear only in test reviews would get a place in the vocabulary, and the IDF weights would reflect test-set frequencies. The model would then be built partly from test data, so its test score would no longer be an honest estimate for unseen reviews.

title: Rung 2: A Pretrained Model Off the Shelf
text: The second rung uses no IMDb labels at all: the SST-2 sentiment model from Module 7, exactly as downloaded. It's the baseline every adaptation must clearly beat, because it costs nothing to train. We feed it the same head+tail 128-token inputs the fine-tuned models will use (Note 8.2). The helpers below are shared with rung 3: head_tail builds the 128-token inputs, and batches groups reviews of similar length to cut padding (Note 7.4). The off-the-shelf model scores 0.888 on validation and 0.873 on test, without seeing a single IMDb label. Its time per review is printed above; it depends on your processor, so compare it only with other timings from your own run. The bar for any adapted model trained on 1,000 IMDb reviews is therefore already high: someone else's adaptation, on a related task, is free.

title: Rung 3: A Frozen Encoder with a Trained Linear Head
text: The third rung is feature extraction (Note 8.1): DistilBERT's pretrained body stays frozen, mean-pooled into one 768-number vector per review, and a logistic-regression head is trained on the same 1,000 labelled reviews. This is exactly a fine-tuned model minus the fine-tuning: same encoder, same inputs, same labels, but the encoder never changes. Comparing it with Notes 8.4 and 8.5 will show what adapting the encoder itself adds. Each review becomes a vector of 768 features. Computing them for the training reviews takes a few seconds, and that one pass is the only use of the Transformer during training. Now we choose the head's regularisation on validation: The best setting, C=1, gives 0.850 on validation and 0.837 on test. The trained part is tiny: 769 parameters (768 weights and a bias). Everything else comes from pretraining. Key terms - Frozen encoder: a pretrained model used only to compute features, never updated. - Linear head (linear probe): a single linear layer, here logistic regression, trained on frozen features. Check yourself. 1. Rung 3 uses the same encoder, inputs and labels as full fine-tuning will in Note 8.4. If fine-tuning then scores clearly higher, what does that tell you? Worked answer That adapting the encoder's own weights matters for this task. Everything else (encoder, inputs, labels) is the same as rung 3, so a clear gain must come from letting the encoder change its representations to suit IMDb sentiment, rather than reading a fixed representation with a linear head. A sign test on the same test reviews would confirm whether the gain is real.

title: Setting the Evaluation Protocol: Metrics, Fixed Split, Timing
text: 5.1 All rungs side by side Here is every rung on the same 1,000 validation and 1,000 test reviews: Reading the ladder, from the test column: - Every rung clears the floor (0.485) by a wide margin, and all have balanced recall on the two classes, so none is succeeding by favouring one label. - Rung 2, the off-the-shelf SST-2 model, is the strongest method that uses 1,000 labels or fewer, at 0.873 with no IMDb labels. - With 1,000 labels, TF-IDF (0.828) and the frozen encoder (0.837) are close, and both below the off-the-shelf model. - TF-IDF with all 22,404 labels is the strongest of all (0.913). Plenty of labels make even a simple model hard to beat. 5.2 Are the differences real? Differences of a few points on 1,000 reviews can be noise, so we test the important ones with the sign test on paired predictions: the same test reviews, comparing which model gets each one right (Module 5). With 1,000 test reviews, one review is worth 0.1 percentage points. - The off-the-shelf model beats TF-IDF with 1,000 labels: it is right on 126 reviews where TF-IDF is wrong, and wrong on only 81 where TF-IDF is right (p = 0.0022). - The frozen encoder and TF-IDF, both with 1,000 labels, are not reliably different (98 against 89, p = 0.56). - TF-IDF with all labels beats the off-the-shelf model (96 against 56, p = 0.0015). So the honest summary of the baselines: with 1,000 labels, the bar to beat is the off-the-shelf model at 0.873, and with all labels, TF-IDF at 0.913. 5.3 What the protocol fixes Everything Notes 8.4–8.7 compare will follow the same protocol: - Fixed data: the same split, checked by fingerprint, and the same 1,000 training, 1,000 validation and 1,000 test reviews. - Choices on validation only: regularisation strength, learning rates, epochs, checkpoints. - Test once per method, after all choices are made. - The same metrics: accuracy, per-class recall and F1, plus paired sign tests for comparisons. - Costs recorded alongside quality: labels used, parameters trained, and training and inference time (timings printed with units; they vary between machines and runs, so compare them within one run, not across machines). 5.4 Saving the results To let Note 8.7 compare every rung on the same test reviews without retraining anything, we save the results, including each rung's prediction for every test review, to a file. Notes 8.4 and 8.5 will save theirs the same way. The file records the split fingerprints, the training-subset fingerprint and, for each rung, its metrics, settings, costs and test predictions. If Note 8.7 finds a fingerprint that doesn't match, it will refuse to compare, rather than compare different reviews by mistake. Key terms - Evaluation protocol: the fixed rules for how every method is measured: data, metrics, when the test set is used, and how results are compared. - Paired comparison: comparing two methods on the same examples, example by example. - Results file: a saved record of a method's settings, costs, metrics and predictions, for later comparison. Common mistake: comparing your fine-tuned model with a weak baseline, or with one evaluated on different data. Beating "always negative" or a poorly tuned TF-IDF proves little. Tune each baseline on validation as carefully as the model you hope will beat it, and evaluate everything on the same reviews. Check yourself. 1. A colleague reports that their fine-tuned model scored 0.86 on test, against 0.83 for TF-IDF, but the TF-IDF number came from a different random test split. Why can't you conclude anything yet? Worked answer The two numbers come from different test reviews, so the difference could be due entirely to which reviews landed in each test set, not to the methods. A fair comparison needs both methods on the same test reviews (ideally with a paired test), with the same training data and the same rules for choosing settings.

title: The Big Picture: Fine-Tuning End to End
text: Fine-tuning a classifier is a loop around five ideas: 1. Model: a pretrained body plus a new, randomly initialised classification head. 2. Batch: token IDs, an attention mask and labels for a handful of examples. 3. Loss: how wrong the model's predictions are on that batch (cross-entropy). 4. Update: gradients of the loss for every weight, then a small step against them, with a carefully scheduled learning rate. 5. Selection: regularly check validation accuracy, and keep the best version (checkpoint) of the model. Then test once, and save. Figure 8.4.1. Only training batches drive gradients and optimizer updates. Validation selects checkpoints; a declared final test reports the selected setup. The data The same fixed split and the same 1,000 training reviews as Note 8.3, checked by fingerprint, with head+tail truncation to 128 tokens (Note 8.2). We keep each review as a list of token IDs; a data collator pads every batch to its longest member and adds the attention mask.

title: Loading the Model with a Classification Head
text: AutoModelForSequenceClassification loads DistilBERT's pretrained body and adds a classification head (Note 7.1, Section 4). We also give it readable label names, which are saved with the model. The LOAD REPORT that appears is expected. The UNEXPECTED weights are the base model's word-guessing head, which a classifier doesn't use. The MISSING weights are our new head, which starts random. The head is two layers: pre_classifier, 768 → 768, and classifier, 768 → 2, one score per label. All 66,955,010 parameters are trainable. That's what makes this full fine-tuning: every pretrained weight, not just the head, will be updated. Key terms - Classification head: the new layers mapping the body's output to one score per class; here pre_classifier and classifier. - num_labels, id2label, label2id: configuration settings for the number of classes and their names, saved with the model.

title: Inputs, Labels and Attention Masks
text: Each review becomes 128 token IDs, starting with 101 ([CLS]). The attention mask marks real tokens with 1 and padding with 0. The batch is as long as its longest review; any shorter review would be padded with 0s. The labels are plain integers, 1 for positive and 0 for negative. When the batch includes labels, the model computes the loss itself.

title: The Training Objective and Loss
text: The objective is the familiar cross-entropy loss (Module 2): for each review, take the probability the model gives to the correct class, and take minus its logarithm. Averaging over the batch gives the loss. Let's compute it by hand and compare it with the model's own: The new head is random, so its scores (logits) for the two classes are tiny and almost equal: the model has no opinion yet. Our hand-computed loss, 0.6874, matches the model's exactly, and both are close to ln 2 = 0.6931. That's the cross-entropy of a model that gives each of two classes a probability of one half. Checking the starting loss against this value is a quick way to catch bugs before training (Note 6.5 did the same for a language model).

title: Forward Pass, Backpropagation and Updates: The Familiar Loop at Scale
text: One training step is exactly the Module 2 loop: forward pass, loss, backward() to compute gradients, then an optimiser step. Two details matter at this scale. We look at the gradient sizes in each part of the model, and we clip the overall gradient size at 1 (Module 3, Note 6.4), so one unusual batch can't produce a huge update. The gradients are largest at the head (1.424) and shrink steadily towards the input, from 0.451 in the last Transformer layer to 0.134 at the embeddings. The new, random head has the most to learn; the pretrained layers near the input are already useful and get gentler signals. The overall gradient norm, 1.639, is above 1, so clipping scaled it down for this step. After one step, the loss on the same 4 reviews falls from 0.6874 to 0.6379. That's the whole loop in miniature, repeated 63 times below. Key terms - Gradient norm: the overall size of the gradients, as a single number. - Gradient clipping: scaling the gradients down when their norm exceeds a limit (here 1.0), to prevent unstable updates. - AdamW: the Adam optimiser with decoupled weight decay; the standard choice for fine-tuning Transformers. Visual walkthrough: Separate learning from selection. 1. Training forward pass. Training batch → logits → loss. The labels of this training batch define the optimization objective. 2. Backward and update. loss.backward() → optimizer.step(). Trainable parameters change; clear gradients as required before the next accumulation cycle. 3. Validation checkpoint. No gradients · score saved checkpoint. Validation selects settings and checkpoints. It does not directly update weights in this training loop. 4. Final test reporting. Selected setup → held-out test. Repeatedly tuning after inspecting test results requires a fresh final test for an unbiased report. The app adds a paused animation of this same supplied example.

title: Learning Rate (and Why It's Much Smaller), Batch Size, Epochs, Warmup
text: 6.1 Why the learning rate is small When you trained small networks from scratch in Modules 2 and 3, learning rates around 1e-3 were typical. Fine-tuning a pretrained Transformer usually uses something like 1e-5 to 5e-5, twenty or more times smaller. The reason is that the weights are already good: we want to nudge them, not overwrite them. Here's how far a single AdamW step moves one of DistilBERT's feed-forward weight matrices at each learning rate: At 5e-5, one step changes the matrix by 0.120% of its size; at 1e-3, by 2.402%, twenty times more. Over 63 steps, a large rate would move the pretrained weights far from where pretraining left them, destroying much of what made them valuable (and making forgetting, Note 8.1, much worse). We use 5e-5. 6.2 Batch size, epochs and warmup - Batch size 16: large enough for stable gradients, small enough to be fast on a CPU. - One epoch: one pass over the 1,000 reviews, 63 steps. With a pretrained model, one to three epochs is typical; Note 8.1 showed a small dataset overfitting by the third. - Warmup, then linear decay: the learning rate starts near zero, rises to its peak over the first 10% of steps, then falls steadily to zero. Warmup protects the pretrained body in the first steps, while the random head is still producing large, meaningless gradients. With 63 steps, warmup lasts 7 steps, the peak learning rate is 5e-05, and the rate decays to zero by the end. Key terms - Learning rate: the step size of each update; fine-tuning uses small values (here 5e-5). - Warmup: gradually raising the learning rate from near zero at the start of training. - Linear decay: lowering the learning rate steadily to zero by the end of training. - Learning-rate schedule: the plan for how the learning rate changes over training. Check yourself. 1. Why is warmup especially useful when fine-tuning a pretrained body with a new, random head? Worked answer At the start, the head's weights are random, so its outputs are meaningless and the gradients flowing back from it can be large and erratic. With a full learning rate from step one, those erratic gradients would push the carefully pretrained body around before the head has learned anything sensible. Warmup keeps the early steps tiny, so the head can settle first, then lets the learning rate rise once the gradients carry real information.

title: Validation and Checkpoint Selection
text: The model after the last step isn't necessarily the best one. Training can overshoot or start to overfit, and on small data the validation score wobbles. So we evaluate during training and keep the best checkpoint: a copy of the weights at that moment. To keep evaluation cheap during training, we check every 16 steps on the first 200 validation reviews, and keep the checkpoint with the best accuracy. That is a choice made on validation, never on test. After training we restore it and measure it on all 1,000 validation reviews. The helper below returns P(positive) for a list of reviews.

title: Practice: A Custom PyTorch Loop, Then the Hugging Face Trainer
text: 8.1 The custom loop Here is the complete loop: AdamW, the warmup-then-decay schedule, gradient clipping, and a checkpoint check every 16 steps. We start from a freshly loaded model, with the same seed for the new head. At step 16, the model still knows nothing useful: validation accuracy is 0.475, below chance. Then it learns fast: 0.840 at step 32 and 0.865 at step 48, the best checkpoint, before slipping to 0.845 at the last step. The plot shows the two views: The training loss jumps around from step to step, because each batch has only 16 reviews, but its moving average falls steadily: the printed 16-step averages go from 0.671 to 0.425. Validation accuracy rises quickly and then levels off, and the last checkpoint is slightly worse than the one at step 48. That's why we select rather than simply taking the end. We restore the best checkpoint and measure it on the full validation set: The chosen checkpoint scores 0.860 on the 1,000 validation reviews. 8.2 The same recipe with the Trainer Hugging Face's Trainer runs this same loop for you. You describe the recipe in TrainingArguments (batch size, epochs, learning rate, warmup, schedule, clipping), and Trainer handles batching, the optimiser, the schedule, logging, devices and, if asked, saving and evaluation. Two details for this library version: - warmup_steps accepts a fraction, so 0.1 means 10% of all steps. - use_cpu must be set explicitly on a CPU-only run. On a Mac, Trainer would otherwise pick the Apple GPU by itself (Note 7.4 met the same behaviour in pipelines). The Trainer ran on the CPU, as intended. Its logged training loss follows the same path as our loop's (0.674, 0.557, 0.396 at steps 16, 32 and 48), and its final model scores 0.870 on validation, against 0.860 for our chosen checkpoint. The two models agree on 90.4% of validation reviews. They aren't identical, because the batches are shuffled differently and dropout draws different random numbers, but the recipe gives the same quality. A difference of 0.010 on 1,000 reviews is ten reviews in these runs. Repeated runs and a paired uncertainty analysis are needed before claiming the recipes have equivalent quality. So which should you use? Write the loop yourself when you're learning or need unusual control (custom losses, special sampling). Use Trainer for standard jobs: it is less code and fewer chances for bugs, and it brings logging, checkpointing, mixed precision and multi-GPU training for free. Key terms - Checkpoint selection: keeping the weights from the training moment with the best validation score. - Trainer / TrainingArguments: Hugging Face's ready-made training loop and its settings. Common mistake: letting Trainer (or a pipeline) choose the device on its own. On a Mac it may silently train on the Apple GPU, and on a machine with a GPU it will use it even if you intended a CPU comparison. Set the device explicitly when it matters. Check yourself. 1. Our loop kept the checkpoint from step 48 rather than the final one at step 63. Why is it important that this choice was made on the 200 validation reviews and not on test? Worked answer Choosing among checkpoints is a form of tuning: the chosen one is partly the luckiest on the data used to choose. If that data were the test set, the test score would include that luck and overstate how the model will do on new reviews. Choosing on validation keeps the test set untouched, so its single score stays an honest estimate.

title: Saving and Reloading the Fine-Tuned Model
text: 9.1 Save and reload We save the chosen checkpoint and its tokeniser together (Note 7.4), reload them, and check that nothing changed: The folder holds the configuration, the weights (268.5 MB in total) and the tokeniser. The reloaded model gives identical probabilities, and the label names travelled with it: {0: 'NEGATIVE', 1: 'POSITIVE'}. We then delete the copy, since every task fine-tuned this way needs its own full-size copy, a cost Note 8.5 avoids. 9.2 One look at the test set All choices are made, so we use the test set once: The fine-tuned model scores 0.834 on the 1,000 test reviews, with recall 0.8742 on negative reviews and 0.7961 on positive ones. How does that compare with the baselines? Note 8.3 saved each baseline's prediction for every test review, so we can compare on exactly the same reviews with paired sign tests: This is the honest result of the workflow. - Fine-tuning clearly learned the task: it beats the majority-class floor overwhelmingly. - It is statistically not significantly different in this paired comparison from the two cheaper 1,000-label baselines: TF-IDF (105 against 99, p = 0.73) and the frozen encoder with a linear head (78 against 81, p = 0.87). - It is significantly worse than the off-the-shelf SST-2 model (50 against 89, p = 0.0012), and than TF-IDF with all labels. With 1,000 labels, one epoch and 128 tokens, updating all 66,955,010 weights bought nothing over training only a linear head on frozen features (Note 8.3), and less than a model someone else had already adapted on a large sentiment dataset. That's not a failure of the workflow, which ran correctly, but a measured answer to "is fine-tuning worth it here?" Note 8.5 asks the same question of a much cheaper method, and Note 8.7 makes the decision. 9.3 What it cost the model's old skills Finally, Note 8.1's forgetting measure: the word-guessing loss of the original masked-language head on 200 held-out reviews, with the pretrained body and with our fine-tuned body. The loss rises from 3.381 to 4.07. Full fine-tuning on 1,000 reviews has measurably degraded the pretrained skill, even with a small learning rate and a single epoch. Everything is saved for Note 8.7: settings, costs (including a memory estimate of weights, gradients and two Adam states in float32, which Note 8.5 explains), validation and test results, test predictions, the forgetting measure, the loss curve and the checkpoint scores. Interpret the evidence carefully. The retention comparison uses the same tied-output setup explained in 8.1. A loss increase here is evidence of reduced performance on this specific probe, not a comprehensive measure of catastrophic forgetting. Common mistake: reporting the best of several checkpoints by their test scores, or tuning until the test number looks good. Choose everything on validation, test once, and report what you get, even when, as here, it's not the result you hoped for. Check yourself. 1. The fine-tuned model and TF-IDF scored 0.834 and 0.828 on test. Why isn't it enough to say "fine-tuning is better by 0.006"? Worked answer Because 0.006 on 1,000 reviews is six reviews, easily within the variation you'd see from a different test sample or a different training run. The paired sign test on the same reviews showed 105 reviews where only fine-tuning was right and 99 where only TF-IDF was right (p = 0.73), so there's no evidence of a real difference. Quote differences together with a test like this, not on their own.

title: The Big Picture: Adapting a Model While Training Fewer Parameters
text: Full fine-tuning changes every weight W of the pretrained model to W + ΔW, where ΔW (delta W) is whatever training adds. PEFT keeps W frozen and learns only a compact replacement for ΔW, or a few small extra pieces of network. The pretrained model is then shared: one copy of the large weights, plus a small, swappable piece for each task. The rest of this note answers four questions: 1. Why is full fine-tuning so expensive? (Section 2) 2. Why can a small number of trained parameters be enough? (Sections 3–4) 3. How does LoRA work, and what are its settings? (Sections 5–7) 4. Does it work as well, here? (Sections 8–9) Figure 8.5.1. LoRA adds (alpha/r) BA beside a frozen weight matrix. A starts random and B starts at zero, so the initial adapter update is zero; the task head may also train. The data The same fixed split, the same 1,000 training reviews (checked by fingerprint), head+tail truncation to 128 tokens, and the same helpers as Note 8.4. We load the starting model once and copy it for each experiment below.

title: Why Full Fine-Tuning Is Expensive: Weights, Gradients and Optimizer States
text: During training, memory is needed for more than the weights. Every trainable weight also needs a gradient of the same size, and the AdamW optimiser keeps two optimiser states per weight: a running average of the gradients and a running average of their squares. Let's measure all three after one full fine-tuning step on DistilBERT: In float32 the weights take 267.8 MB, the gradients another 267.8 MB, and Adam's states 535.6 MB, twice as much. That is 1071.3 MB in total, four times the model's size, before counting the activations a batch needs. The rule of thumb: full fine-tuning with Adam needs about 16 bytes per parameter in float32 (4 for the weight, 4 for its gradient, 8 for the two states). For a small model that's manageable. For a modern large model it's not: A 7-billion-parameter model (here Qwen2.5-7B, counted from its file header as in Note 7.3) needs 15.2 GB just to run in bfloat16. Fully fine-tuning it in float32 needs about 121.8 GB for weights, gradients and Adam states, far beyond any single consumer GPU. (Mixed-precision training reduces this somewhat, but not by enough to change the conclusion.) And each fine-tuned copy must be stored and served separately. Key terms - Optimiser state: extra numbers an optimiser keeps for each trainable weight; AdamW keeps two (running averages of the gradient and of its square). - Training memory: weights + gradients + optimiser states + activations; about 16 bytes per trainable parameter in float32 with Adam, before activations. Check yourself. 1. If only 1% of a model's parameters are trainable, which parts of the training memory shrink, and which don't? Worked answer Gradients and optimiser states shrink to cover only the trainable 1%, since frozen parameters need neither. The weights themselves don't shrink: the whole model must still be in memory to run the forward and backward passes, and the activations for each batch are about the same size as before. For a large model the weights then dominate, which is why QLoRA (Note 8.6) also compresses them.

title: Frozen vs. Trainable Parameters
text: The simplest way to save memory is to freeze parameters: set requires_grad = False, so PyTorch computes no gradient for them and the optimiser keeps no state for them. Here we freeze DistilBERT's whole body and train only the head, the "head only" end of the spectrum: Only 592,130 of the 66,955,010 parameters are trainable now. After a backward pass, a frozen weight's gradient is None: none was computed, and none is stored. The head's gradient exists, with the shape of the head's weights. Frozen parameters still take memory as weights, and still take part in the forward pass, but they need no gradients and no optimiser state. Freezing the whole body is very cheap, but it's close to feature extraction (Note 8.3), and the body can't adapt at all. PEFT methods keep the body frozen but add a small number of trainable parameters inside it, so the representation itself can adapt. Key terms - requires_grad: the flag that decides whether PyTorch computes a gradient for a tensor; False freezes it. - Trainable parameters: those with requires_grad = True; only these get gradients and optimiser states.

title: The Core Idea Behind PEFT
text: Why should a small number of extra parameters be enough to adapt a model? Because the change that fine-tuning makes seems to be much simpler than the weights themselves. We can check this with a model we already have. The SST-2 sentiment model is DistilBERT base after full fine-tuning (Note 7.1). For one weight matrix, the attention query projection, we take the update ΔW = W(SST-2) − W(base) and ask how many "directions" it really uses. The singular value decomposition splits any matrix into a sum of simple rank-1 pieces, each a direction with a strength, sorted from strongest to weakest. If a few pieces carry most of the update, the update is approximately low-rank. The fine-tuning updates are strongly concentrated. In the last layer, just 8 of the 768 directions carry 55.8% of the update, and 64 directions carry 85.1%. In the first layer the update is more spread out (25.1% in the top 8), but still far more concentrated than a random matrix of the same size, whose top 8 directions hold only 4.0%. The plot shows the whole curve: the fine-tuning updates rise steeply on the left, while the random matrix needs hundreds of directions. That's the core idea behind LoRA. If ΔW is approximately low-rank, we can learn it directly in low-rank form, with far fewer numbers than a full matrix, and leave W untouched. Key terms - Rank: the number of independent directions a matrix uses; a 768 × 768 matrix can have rank up to 768. - Low-rank: representable (exactly or approximately) with few directions. - Singular value decomposition (SVD): splitting a matrix into rank-1 pieces ordered by strength; used here to measure how low-rank an update is. Check yourself. 1. The last layer's update is more concentrated (55.8% in 8 directions) than the first layer's (25.1%). Suggest one reason why fine-tuning might change the last layer in a simpler, more focused way. Worked answer The last layer sits right below the new classification head, so it is where the representation most directly has to change for the new task, for example by emphasising a few sentiment-related directions for the head to read. Changes concentrated on a few task-specific features are naturally low-rank. Earlier layers build general features used for many purposes, and fine-tuning nudges them in more varied, less focused ways.

title: LoRA: The Intuition
text: A rank-r matrix of size 768 × 768 can always be written as the product of a tall, thin matrix B (768 × r) and a short, wide matrix A (r × 768). For r = 8 that's 2 × 8 × 768 = 12,288 numbers instead of 589,824. LoRA uses exactly this: next to a frozen weight matrix W, it adds a trainable update in factorised form, so the layer computes output = W·x + (α / r) · B·(A·x) where x is the input vector, r is the rank, and α (alpha) is a fixed scaling number. Two design details make this work well: - B starts at zero. So at the start of training B·A = 0, and the model behaves exactly like the pretrained model. Training only ever adds a learned correction. - A starts small and random, so the gradients for B are non-zero from the first step and learning can begin. An analogy: W is a large printed map that we're not allowed to redraw. LoRA is a transparent overlay on which we may draw only a few straight strokes (the rank). For many trips, a few strokes are enough to mark the new route.

title: LoRA Matrices and Low-Rank Updates: Rank, Alpha, Target Layers
text: 6.1 A LoRA layer by hand Here is a complete LoRA layer in a few lines, wrapping an ordinary nn.Linear: At the start, the LoRA layer's output is exactly the same as the original layer's, because B is zero. The trainable part is 12,288 numbers instead of the matrix's 589,824, 2.1% of it. 6.2 Rank The rank r sets the size of the update, and the trade-off between capacity and cost: Rank 1 needs only 1,536 numbers (0.3% of the matrix); rank 8, 12,288 (2.1%); rank 64, 98,304 (16.7%). At rank 384, half the matrix's width, LoRA already has as many numbers as the full matrix, and there's nothing left to save. In practice, ranks from 4 to 64 are common, and Section 4's measurements suggest why small ranks often suffice. Alpha scales the update by α / r. Its purpose is practical: when you try a different rank, you can keep α fixed, which changes the explicit scaling factor α/r. The realised update also depends on initialization and optimization, so learning-rate tuning may still be needed. We use r = 8 and α = 16, so the scale is 2. 6.3 Target layers Which matrices get a LoRA update? A Transformer layer (Note 6.4) has the attention projections (query, key, value and output; q_lin, k_lin, v_lin and out_lin in DistilBERT) and the feed-forward network (lin1, lin2). The PEFT library takes a list of names, target_modules, and counts follow directly: LoRA on only the query and value projections adds 147,456 trainable numbers across DistilBERT's 6 layers; on all four attention projections, 294,912; on everything including the feed-forward layers, 663,552. In each case the new classification head (592,130 parameters) is also trained, because it starts random and has to be learned. The original LoRA work found query and value enough for many tasks, and that is our choice. Targeting more layers gives the update more capacity, at a modest cost. Key terms - LoRA rank (r): the inner dimension of the factorised update B·A; it sets how many directions the update can use. - LoRA alpha (α): a scaling constant; the update is multiplied by α / r. - Target modules: the weight matrices that receive LoRA updates. Common mistake: forgetting that the classification head must be trained too. LoRA adapts the frozen body, but a new task's head starts random. The PEFT library trains it automatically when task_type="SEQ_CLS" is set; in a hand-built setup you must make it trainable yourself, to implement the intended trainable-head setup. Visual walkthrough: See why the initial adapter update is zero. 1. Freeze a 2 × 2 base. W₀ = [[1, 0], [0, 1]] · x = [2, 1]. Use rank r = 1 and α = 1, so α/r = 1. This tiny matrix is an illustration, not a measured trained adapter. 2. Initialize the adapter. A = [[0.2, −0.1]] · B = [[0], [0]]. A starts random; B starts zero. Ax = 0.3, but BAx = [0, 0]. The initial combined adapter update is zero. 3. After an illustrative update. B = [[0.5], [−0.2]] · A held as shown. For illustration, B changes to these supplied values. We are not deriving an optimizer step or running training here. 4. Add the low-rank path. W₀x + BAx = [2, 1] + [0.15, −0.06] = [2.15, 0.94]. The base remains frozen while adapters train. A task head may also train; include it when counting trainable parameters. The app adds a paused animation of this same supplied example.

title: Adapters, Prefix Tuning and Other Approaches *(Extension)*
text: LoRA is one member of a family. Two other well-known PEFT methods, for comparison: - Bottleneck adapters insert small two-layer networks inside each Transformer layer: squeeze the 768-number vector down to a small size m, apply a non-linearity, and expand back, with a residual connection around them. The pretrained weights stay frozen. - Prefix tuning (and its simpler relative, prompt tuning) leaves every weight untouched and instead learns a few extra vectors that are prepended to the keys and values in each attention layer: "virtual tokens" the real tokens can attend to. We can compare their sizes for DistilBERT by counting: With a bottleneck size of 64, two adapters per layer add 1,189,632 parameters; prefix tuning with 20 vectors adds 184,320; LoRA with rank 8 on query and value adds 147,456. All three are around 1–2% of the model or less. They differ in other ways: - Adapters add extra layers that run at inference time, which adds a little latency. - Prefix tuning uses up some of the context length. - LoRA's update can be merged into W after training (Section 9), so the final model has no extra cost at all. That last property is a large part of why LoRA became the default choice. Key terms - Bottleneck adapter: a small down-projection, non-linearity and up-projection inserted into each layer, trained while the rest is frozen. - Prefix tuning / prompt tuning: learning extra key/value or input vectors while all weights stay frozen.

title: Practice: LoRA with Hugging Face PEFT, Inspecting Trainable Parameters
text: 8.1 Setting up The PEFT library wraps a model in a few lines: describe LoRA in a LoraConfig, then call get_peft_model. We use rank 8, alpha 16, LoRA dropout 0.1 (dropout applied to the LoRA input during training), and the query and value projections. task_type="SEQ_CLS" tells the library this is sequence classification, so it also makes the new head trainable. The training recipe is Note 8.4's, unchanged except for the learning rate: 1e-3 instead of 5e-5. LoRA trains small new matrices whose combined update starts at zero (A is random; B is zero), not pretrained weights that must be preserved, so it needs larger steps. Rates around 1e-4 to 1e-3 are typical. We use a common default here rather than tuning it, which would mean another training run. print_trainable_parameters reports 739,586 trainable out of 67,694,596, 1.0925%. Of these, 147,456 are the LoRA matrices and 592,130 are the new head. The total count is a little larger than DistilBERT's 66,955,010 because the wrapped model also contains the LoRA matrices and a spare copy of the original head, kept so the adapter can be removed again. 8.2 Training The loop is identical to Note 8.4's, except that the optimiser only receives the trainable parameters, and clipping applies only to them. Checkpoints are checked every 16 steps on 200 validation reviews, and the best one is kept. Validation accuracy on 200 reviews climbs from 0.790 at step 16 to 0.855 at step 32 and 0.870 at step 48, the best checkpoint, then dips to 0.860. LoRA learns faster at the start than full fine-tuning did in Note 8.4: its first checkpoint is already far above chance. That's partly because of its larger learning rate. The chosen checkpoint scores 0.880 on all 1,000 validation reviews. Section 9.4 compares the cost of training with Note 8.4's. Check yourself. 1. LoRA trains about 1% of the parameters, yet training wasn't 100 times faster than full fine-tuning. Why not? Worked answer Because most of the training work isn't in the update itself. Every step still runs the forward pass through the whole frozen model, and the backward pass still has to send gradients back through all the frozen layers to reach the LoRA matrices in every layer. What LoRA saves is computing and storing gradients for the frozen weights, and the optimiser's work and memory for them. That's a real saving, but much less than a factor of 100.

title: Merging LoRA Weights for Inference
text: 9.1 Saving just the adapter Because the pretrained weights never changed, we only need to save what was trained: The adapter folder holds a small configuration file, a README and the trained weights: 3.0 MB in total, against the 267.8 MB of weights a full fine-tuned copy needs (Section 2). Loading the base model and attaching the saved adapter (PeftModel.from_pretrained) gives identical probabilities. A hundred tasks would need one base model plus a hundred small adapters, rather than a hundred full models. 9.2 Merging For deployment we can merge the update into the frozen weights: replace each W with W + (α / r)·B·A. The model then becomes a plain DistilBERT classifier, with no LoRA layers and no extra computation at inference. After merge_and_unload, the model is an ordinary DistilBertForSequenceClassification with no LoRA modules left, and its probabilities differ from the unmerged model by at most 7.75e-07, only floating-point rounding. So you can choose per deployment: keep the adapter separate when one base model serves many tasks, or merge it when a single task needs maximum speed and simplicity. 9.3 One look at the test set All choices are made, so we test once, and compare on the same 1,000 test reviews with the results Notes 8.3 and 8.4 saved: LoRA scores 0.834 on test, with recall 0.8289 on negatives and 0.8388 on positives. Against full fine-tuning (Note 8.4), the result is a dead heat: each is right on 54 reviews the other gets wrong (p = 1). Against the baselines, the picture is the same as for full fine-tuning: - no significant difference from TF-IDF or frozen features at 1,000 labels (p = 0.73 and 0.85); - significantly below the off-the-shelf SST-2 model (43 against 82, p = 0.00062) and TF-IDF with all labels. This is a single training run (as was Note 8.4's), and a different random initialisation of the LoRA matrices would give slightly different numbers. The safe conclusion is not "LoRA equals full fine-tuning to the review", but that on these 1,000 test reviews there's no evidence of a difference, while LoRA trained about 1% of the parameters and saved a 3.0 MB adapter. 9.4 Forgetting Finally, what did each approach cost the pretrained model's other skills? Interpret the evidence carefully. Equal observed accuracy does not mean the classifiers make identical predictions. In the source reference results, full fine-tuning and LoRA disagree on 108 of 1,000 reviews. A paired p-value of 1 does not establish equivalence; stronger equivalence claims need a declared tolerance and an appropriate analysis. With LoRA switched off, every pretrained weight is exactly as it was. Forgetting is literally zero, by construction: the original model is always one switch away. Even merged into the weights, LoRA raised the word-guessing loss only from 3.381 to 3.461. To compare costs, we read Note 8.4's saved results next to ours. The training-memory estimate uses Section 2's accounting: weights, plus gradients and two Adam states for the trainable parameters only. Interpret the evidence carefully. This remains the tied-output retention probe from 8.1. Disabling the adapter restores the frozen base path for this comparison; it does not by itself prove retention of every ability a deployed application might need. LoRA trained 739,586 parameters against 66,955,010, so its estimated training memory is a fraction of full fine-tuning's, mostly the frozen weights themselves. Training was also quicker, though not a hundred times quicker (Check yourself 3). Validation accuracy was similar: 0.880 for LoRA against 0.860 for full fine-tuning. And full fine-tuning's word-guessing loss was 4.07, against LoRA's 3.461: LoRA's small, low-rank update disturbs the pretrained skill much less. Everything is saved for Note 8.7: Common mistake: concluding from one run that LoRA is "better" or "worse" than full fine-tuning by a fraction of a point. Single runs on 1,000 reviews differ by several reviews from initialisation and shuffling alone. Compare on the same test examples with a paired test, and treat small differences as noise unless the test says otherwise.

title: The Big Picture: Adapting an LLM to Follow Instructions
text: A base (or pretrained) language model has learned one thing: to continue text the way text on the internet continues. Ask it a question and it may answer, but it may equally continue with another question, a list or an essay. An instruction-tuned model has been further trained to treat its input as a request and to respond helpfully. The two share the same architecture and almost the same weights; the difference is a stage of fine-tuning. We can see the difference directly. SmolLM2-135M exists in both versions. We give the base model a plain request and the instruct model the same request in its chat format, both with greedy decoding: Both models have 134,515,008 parameters and the same architecture. The base model treats the request as the start of a document. Its continuation sounds plausible but immediately repeats itself ("always try to be as objective as possible", twice). The instruct model treats it as a request and starts a helpful answer ("Here are two…"). Same architecture, same pretraining; the instruction tuning made the difference. Instruction tuning usually happens in stages: 1. Pretraining on huge amounts of text: next-token prediction (Note 6.6). 2. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on curated examples of instructions and good responses. 3. Often, preference tuning: further training from human (or AI) judgements of which of two responses is better. You'll hear of methods such as RLHF and DPO; they're beyond this note. This note is about stage 2, and how it's made affordable. Figure 8.6.1. This assistant-only SFT setup keeps prompt tokens visible as context while masking their targets from loss. Causal prediction shifts targets by one; LoRA adapts selected parameters.

title: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
text: Supervised fine-tuning trains a pretrained language model on pairs of (instruction, desired response). The training objective is the same next-token prediction the model was pretrained with, so nothing new has to be invented. What changes is the data: instead of arbitrary web text, every example shows the model exactly the behaviour we want, an instruction followed by a good response. For SFT to teach this behaviour cleanly, two things must be set up carefully, and the next three sections cover them: - Formatting (Section 3): every example must use the same conversation format, with special markers for who is speaking. This is the format the model will see at inference time. - Masking (Sections 4–5): the loss should reward the model for writing the response, not for predicting the instruction. The user's words aren't something the model should learn to produce. The amount of data needed is often surprisingly small compared with pretraining: thousands to hundreds of thousands of examples. That's because SFT mostly teaches a format and a behaviour the model can already almost produce; the knowledge comes from pretraining. Key terms - Base model: a language model after pretraining only; it continues text. - Instruction-tuned (instruct) model: a base model further trained to follow instructions. - Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): fine-tuning a language model on (instruction, response) examples with the next-token loss. - Preference tuning: further training from judgements of which response is better (for example RLHF or DPO).

title: Instruction-Response Formatting and Chat Templates
text: A chat model reads a conversation as one long token sequence, with special tokens marking where each message starts and ends and who wrote it. The exact format is the model's chat template, stored with its tokeniser, and apply_chat_template produces it. Here is a one-turn conversation with an answer, formatted for SmolLM2: Each message is wrapped in role … . The roles are system, user and assistant, and the tokeniser added SmolLM2's default system message by itself. The markers are single special tokens, with IDs 1 and 2, so the model can recognise turn boundaries exactly. The whole conversation is 53 tokens. Every SFT example must use this exact template, because it's what the model will see at inference time.
