A model fine-tuned on a slightly different format, say with "User:" and "Bot:" in plain text, learns to expect that format, and behaves worse when served with the official one (and vice versa). Key terms - Special tokens: tokens with a reserved meaning, such as and , used to structure a conversation. - Chat template: the model-specific format for turning a list of messages into one token sequence. - System / user / assistant roles: the instruction-setting message, the person's messages and the model's replies.

title: Input and Target Masking
text: In the causal language-modelling loss, every position predicts the next token (Note 6.6). But we don't want the model to learn to write the user's message. We want it to learn the response, given the message. So the loss is computed only on the response tokens. In Hugging Face, any label set to -100 is ignored by the loss. We find where the prompt ends (everything up to and including the start of the assistant's turn) and mask everything before it: Of the 53 tokens, 50 belong to the prompt and are masked with -100; only 3 are trained on: the answer negative, the end-of-turn marker , and a newline (Ċ is how this tokeniser displays a newline). Training on matters: it teaches the model to stop after answering, rather than rambling on. Key terms - Input (prompt) masking: excluding prompt tokens from the loss so the model learns only the response. - Label -100: the value Hugging Face's loss functions ignore. Common mistake: training on the whole conversation, prompt included. The model then spends much of its learning on predicting user messages, and on long prompts with short answers the answer gets only a sliver of the loss. Mask the prompt. Visual walkthrough: Separate visible context from supervised targets. 1. Format a toy exchange. Input tokens: [USER, hi, ASSISTANT, hello, EOS]. These names stand for token IDs in a simplified assistant-only supervised fine-tuning example. 2. Keep context visible. Attention mask: [1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. All five positions are real tokens. A separate causal attention mask prevents future-token access. 3. Mask prompt targets. Labels: [−100, −100, −100, hello, EOS]. −100 means ignore this target in cross-entropy. It does not hide the prompt from the model. 4. Apply causal shifting. logits at ASSISTANT → hello; logits at hello → EOS. Causal-LM loss aligns logits[:-1] with labels[1:]. Only assistant-response targets contribute here. LoRA changes selected parameters during training. The app adds a paused animation of this same supplied example.

title: Causal Language Modelling Loss
text: The causal language-modelling loss is the cross-entropy of predicting each token from all the tokens before it (Note 6.6). Position t's output predicts token t + 1, so the logits and the targets are shifted by one before comparing. Let's compute it by hand on our example and check it against the model's own loss: The model scores a vocabulary of 49,152 tokens at every position, but only 3 positions count, the answer tokens. Our hand computation, 2.9850, matches the model's exactly. Without masking, averaging over every token gives 3.7479, a different number, dominated by how well the model predicts the prompt, which isn't what we want to train. This is the same loss as pretraining. SFT changes what the examples look like and which positions count, not the objective. Check yourself. 1. In a training set, the prompts average 400 tokens and the answers 20. Without masking, roughly what share of the loss would come from the answer tokens? Worked answer About 20 / 420, so under 5% of the loss would come from the answers (assuming similar per-token losses), and over 95% from predicting the prompts. The model would spend almost all of its learning on text it never needs to write. With masking, 100% of the loss comes from the answers.

title: Applying LoRA to an LLM
text: 6.1 What LoRA trains in an LLM LoRA works on a language model exactly as on DistilBERT in Note 8.5: freeze the weights, add trainable low-rank matrices to chosen projections. In LLMs the usual targets are the attention projections (q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj) and often the feed-forward ones (gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj): On SmolLM2-135M, rank 8 on the query and value projections trains 460,800 parameters (0.34%); on all seven projection types, 2,442,240 (1.78%). For a large model the fraction is far smaller. We count from Qwen2.5-7B's configuration file: Qwen2.5-7B has 28 layers, a hidden size of 3584, and smaller key and value projections (512 wide, because many query heads share each key/value head). LoRA rank 8 on the query and value projections trains 2,523,136 parameters, just 0.033% of the 7,615,616,512; on all seven projection types, 20,185,088 (0.265%). The trainable part of a 7B model is smaller than all of DistilBERT. As Note 8.5 explained, the frozen weights still have to fit in memory, which Section 7 deals with. 6.2 A tiny SFT run Let's run real SFT, small enough for a CPU. The task is sentiment as a chat task: the instruct model must answer "positive" or "negative" to a question about a review. We use the fixed IMDb split (Note 7.1; the fingerprints confirm the same reviews): First, how does the instruct model do before fine-tuning? As in Note 8.1, we score each answer by comparing the model's scores for "positive" and "negative" as the first token of its reply, on the first 100 validation reviews (cut to their first 60 words to keep the run short): Its accuracy is 0.43, and it answers "positive" for 0.00 of the reviews: it says "negative" to everything. This small model can produce the right format, but it hasn't connected the question to the review's sentiment. (Note 8.1 showed that a larger, 360M-parameter model in the same family does far better without any fine-tuning.) Now we build SFT examples from 256 training reviews, each a conversation ending in the correct one-word answer, with the prompt masked: Each example is about 125 tokens, of which only 3 are trained on (the answer word, and the newline). We add LoRA, rank 8 on the query and value projections, and train for one pass over the 256 examples, in batches of 8: LoRA trains 460,800 of 134,975,808 parameters (0.3414%). Over the 32 steps, the loss on the answer tokens falls from 1.148 to an average of 0.184 over the last 8 steps. Did the behaviour change? Yes. After SFT on 256 examples, accuracy on the same 100 validation reviews rises from 0.43 to 0.76, and the model now answers "positive" for 0.71 of them instead of never. It has learned to connect the question to the review, though it now leans positive, and 0.76 is well below what the classifiers in Notes 8.3–8.5 reached. A real SFT run would use far more data, a larger model and several checks on validation. The mechanics, though, are exactly these: chat-formatted examples, prompt masking, the causal LM loss and LoRA. Check yourself. 1. After SFT, the model answers "positive" for 0.71 of 100 reviews, about half of which are positive. What does this tell you, and what might you change in a real SFT run? Worked answer It's overcorrecting. Before SFT it always said "negative"; now it says "positive" much more often than the data warrants, so many of its errors are negative reviews called positive. It has learned the format and part of the task, but not a balanced decision. In a real run you'd use more (and balanced) training examples, check the answer distribution and accuracy on a validation set during training, tune the learning rate and number of steps on validation, and perhaps use a larger base model.

title: Quantisation and QLoRA
text: 7.1 The problem: the frozen weights still have to fit LoRA shrinks the trainable part to a fraction of a percent, but the frozen weights still have to sit in memory for every forward and backward pass. For a 7B model in bfloat16 that's about 15.23 GB (Section 8), more than most consumer GPUs have. The idea of QLoRA is to store those frozen weights in 4 bits each, a quarter of bfloat16's 16. The LoRA matrices are still trained in higher precision. During the forward pass, each 4-bit weight is converted back (dequantised) when it's needed. 7.2 4-bit quantisation by hand Note 7.6 quantised weights to 8-bit integers with one scale per row. Four bits can encode 16 levels; this symmetric teaching example uses 15 of them (-7 to 7), so the scale must fit the numbers more closely. QLoRA-style quantisation uses a separate scale for each block of 64 weights. Here is 8-bit and 4-bit blockwise quantisation of one of SmolLM2's feed-forward matrices: The matrix takes 3.54 MB in float32. With 8 bits it shrinks to 0.94 MB, with an average error of only 0.6% of a typical weight's size. With 4 bits it's 0.50 MB, about a seventh of float32, but the average error jumps to 11.7%. Fifteen evenly spaced levels are coarse. QLoRA reduces this error with two further tricks, which we describe rather than implement: - NF4 ("4-bit NormalFloat"): neural-network weights are roughly bell-shaped, concentrated near zero, so instead of 15 evenly spaced levels, NF4 places its 16 levels where weights are most common. More levels near zero means smaller errors for most weights. - Double quantisation: the per-block scales are themselves quantised, saving a little more memory. The 4-bit weights are frozen and never updated. Training only adjusts the LoRA matrices, which learn to work with the quantised model, so the rounding error matters less than in pure inference quantisation. QLoRA also uses paged optimisers, which move optimiser state out of GPU memory when it runs short. In practice QLoRA is run with the bitsandbytes library on NVIDIA GPUs; that's why this note describes it rather than running it. Key terms - Blockwise quantisation: quantising in small blocks (here 64 numbers), each with its own scale. - NF4: a 4-bit format whose levels are spaced to match the bell-shaped distribution of neural-network weights. - QLoRA: LoRA training on top of a frozen model stored in 4-bit (NF4) precision. - Dequantisation: converting quantised values back to higher precision for computation.

title: Hardware Constraints and Practical Decisions
text: Putting it all together: which method fits on which hardware? The table below estimates memory for the weights and training state only. As a rough rule we leave 20% headroom for activations, the KV cache and framework overhead. Real usage depends on sequence length and batch size, so treat these as first estimates, not guarantees. For SmolLM2-135M, the illustrated float32 training-state subtotal is 2.15 GB; activations and runtime allocations are additional. For Qwen2.5-7B, the picture is the one that shapes real projects: - Full fine-tuning needs about 121.85 GB, more than even an 80 GB data-centre GPU. That exceeds the listed 80 GB device under this float32/Adam estimate; other precision, sharding and offload choices change the requirement. - LoRA with bfloat16 weights needs about 15.23 GB, before adapters, activations and runtime workspaces; actual training fit must be measured. - QLoRA brings the frozen weights down to about 4.28 GB, before the remaining runtime allocations; this alone does not establish an 8 GB training fit. That's why QLoRA made fine-tuning large models practical for individuals and small teams. A practical decision guide, building on Note 8.1: 1. Try prompting first (including a few examples in the prompt). If a capable model does the job, there's nothing to train. 2. If you need a behaviour or format the model won't reliably produce, SFT with LoRA on a model that fits your hardware is the default. Use QLoRA if the bfloat16 weights don't fit. 3. Full fine-tuning deserves a clear measured benefit for its cost. Hardware needs depend on model size, precision, sequence length, batch size, sharding and offload; large GPU clusters are not a universal requirement. 4. Whatever you choose, evaluate the adapted model on held-out examples, check for forgetting of the abilities you still need (Notes 8.1 and 8.5), and compare against the prompting baseline. Note 8.7 turns this into a decision process. Figure 8.6.2. Simplified storage arithmetic, not measured peak training memory: float32 full-model Adam state, bfloat16 base weights, and an illustrative four-bit layout. No bar guarantees a GPU training fit or implements NF4. Common mistake: assuming the trainable-parameter count decides whether training fits. With LoRA, the trainable part is tiny; it's the frozen weights (and activations) that fill memory. Estimate from the full model size and its storage format. Check yourself. 1. You have one GPU with 16 GB of memory and want to adapt a 7B model to answer in your company's support style. Which method from the table would you choose, and why? Worked answer QLoRA is a reasonable candidate to benchmark because quantizing the frozen base can reduce storage substantially. The 15.23 GB bfloat16 base leaves insufficient room on a nominal 16 GB device for ordinary training allocations. The illustrative 4.28 GB four-bit subtotal does not guarantee a fit: measure peak memory with the intended sequence length, batch size, adapters, optimizer and implementation. Try smaller batches, shorter inputs, checkpointing or a smaller model if necessary. Compare held-out quality against prompting before deciding that adaptation is worthwhile. The 20% margin is illustrative rather than a sufficient bound. Peak memory depends on sequence length, batch size, saved activations, checkpointing, unquantised modules, adapter/optimizer state and implementation workspaces. The hand-written uniform quantiser is not an executed NF4/QLoRA implementation. Full fine-tuning does not universally require a cluster; that statement depends on model size, hardware and the chosen precision/optimizer/offload recipe.

title: The Big Picture: How Do We Know Adaptation Worked?
text: "Worked" has several meanings, and a good evaluation checks each one: | Question | Where it's answered | |---|---| | Did training behave sensibly? | training and validation curves (Section 2) | | How good is the model, with what uncertainty? | task metrics with confidence intervals (Section 3) | | What does it get wrong, and why? | error analysis (Section 4) | | Did it overfit, or forget? | validation–test gaps, forgetting measure (Section 5) | | Is it better than the alternatives, and at what cost? | the full comparison with paired tests (Section 6) | | Would we get the same result again? | variation and tracking (Section 7) | | Should we use it? | rules decided in advance (Section 8), then a written record (Section 9) | Figure 8.7.1. Evaluation combines training behaviour, held-out metrics, errors, retention, costs, reproducibility and the application decision. A p-value alone does not settle suitability. Loading the results The fixed split is rebuilt with the same function as every other note. Then we load the three results files and check that each one used the same split and the same 1,000 training reviews. If not, comparing them would be meaningless, so the cell stops. Seven methods, all scored on the same 1,000 validation and 1,000 test reviews. The rest of this note works out what these numbers mean.

title: Training vs. Validation Loss
text: During training, two kinds of signal tell you whether things are going well. The training loss shows whether the model is fitting the data it learns from. A validation signal, validation loss or validation accuracy on data the model never trains on, shows whether that learning carries over to new data. Overfitting appears as the two pulling apart: training keeps improving while validation stalls or worsens (Note 8.1). Notes 8.4 and 8.5 saved the training loss at every step and the validation accuracy at each checkpoint: Both runs started at a training loss near ln 2 (0.692 and 0.688 over the first 8 steps, the untrained-head value from Note 8.4) and ended at 0.436 and 0.440 over the last 8 steps. LoRA's loss fell faster early on, mostly because of its larger learning rate, and its first checkpoint was already far above chance, while full fine-tuning's was still at chance. Both peaked on validation at step 48 and dipped slightly at the end: a mild sign that one epoch was about right, and that checkpoint selection mattered. A note on what we didn't record: validation loss. Validation accuracy only counts right and wrong; validation loss also shows whether the model is becoming over-confident on the reviews it gets wrong, often an earlier sign of overfitting. Recording it costs nothing extra during evaluation, and an experiment record should include it. That's a lesson for the next run, not something to invent now. Key terms - Training loss: the loss on the batches being trained on; shows whether the model fits its training data. - Validation loss / accuracy: the same measures on held-out data; shows whether learning generalises.

title: Task-Specific Metrics
text: Our task's metrics are accuracy, recall on each class, and F1 for the positive class (Note 8.2). Any accuracy measured on 1,000 reviews is uncertain, so we add a 95% confidence interval: a range that, by a standard calculation (the Wilson interval), is likely to contain the accuracy we'd see on unlimited reviews like these. The intervals are roughly four to five points wide. Full fine-tuning and LoRA both score 0.834, with intervals of 0.810–0.856. The off-the-shelf SST-2 model scores 0.873 (0.851–0.892), and TF-IDF with all labels 0.913 (0.894–0.929). Overlapping intervals don't settle a comparison on their own; for that we use the paired sign test (Section 6), which is more sensitive because it compares methods review by review. The recall columns show a difference the accuracies hide. Full fine-tuning catches negative reviews well (0.874) but misses more positive ones (0.796), while LoRA is balanced (0.829 and 0.839). If the feature's purpose were to catch unhappy customers, full fine-tuning's profile might even be preferable, despite equal accuracy. Metrics should match what the application needs (Note 7.5). Key terms - Confidence interval: a range likely to contain the true value of a measured quantity; here, accuracy on unlimited data. - Wilson interval: a standard way to compute a confidence interval for a proportion. Check yourself. 1. Two models' 95% intervals overlap. Does that prove there's no real difference between them? What would you do instead? Worked answer No. Overlapping 95% intervals are consistent with a real difference, because each interval reflects the uncertainty of one model on its own, ignoring that both were scored on the same reviews. A paired test, such as the sign test on the reviews where exactly one model is right, uses that pairing and can detect differences that overlapping intervals hide.

title: Qualitative Evaluation and Error Analysis
text: 4.1 Who gets what wrong Metrics count errors; error analysis looks at them. First, how much do methods agree on which reviews are hard? The table counts test reviews that both the row's and the column's method got wrong. The diagonal shows each method's own number of errors. Full fine-tuning and LoRA each get 166 reviews wrong, and 112 of those are shared. They're the same model architecture trained on the same data, so they fail in similar places. LoRA also shares 106 errors with the frozen encoder: all three use the same pretrained DistilBERT representation, which seems to struggle with the same reviews. The SST-2 model and TF-IDF with all labels share far fewer errors with the others: they fail differently. 4.2 Patterns Of the 112 reviews both fine-tuned models got wrong, the SST-2 model got 46 right, so those are worth reading. Only 12 reviews defeat all six methods, perhaps hard or even mislabelled ones. Splitting by length shows something else. On the 121 test reviews that fit within 128 tokens, the DistilBERT-based methods all do well (0.876–0.917). On the 879 longer reviews, which head+tail truncation had to cut, every method that reads only 128 tokens drops, while TF-IDF with all labels, which reads every word, holds at 0.914. Part of the gap between the transformer methods and that TF-IDF model is simply that TF-IDF saw the whole review. Here are the first three reviews that both fine-tuned models got wrong but the SST-2 model got right: All three are positive reviews written with plenty of negative-sounding words. One calls the film "a bad, raunchy, predictable, tacky, salacious soap opera" and then a "guilty pleasure". One praises the film for a reason other than its quality. One opens by comparing it with gory horror films. The fine-tuned models, trained on just 1,000 reviews, seem to have learned that negative words mean a negative review. The SST-2 model, trained on many more labelled sentences, handles the reversal. That points to a concrete improvement: more training examples of exactly this kind of review. Key terms - Error analysis: examining which examples a model gets wrong, and why. - Error overlap: how many errors two models share; low overlap means they fail differently, which also makes them good candidates to combine. Common mistake: choosing error examples by hand because they "look interesting". Choose them by a rule (here, the first three that meet a condition), or you may be picking the examples that support a story you already believe.

title: Detecting Overfitting and Catastrophic Forgetting
text: 5.1 The validation–test gap Settings (regularisation, checkpoints) were chosen on validation, so each method's validation score is slightly optimistic, and the test score is the honest one. A large gap between them warns that a method was tuned to its validation data, a form of overfitting to the selection process. All four methods that chose settings on validation score lower on test, by between 0.013 and 0.046. LoRA has the largest gap (0.880 → 0.834): its validation score looked best among the 1,000-label methods, but on test it is level with the rest. That is why final test reporting must remain separate from selecting settings on validation, and why a single validation result should never be trusted on its own (Section 7 shows how much results vary). 5.2 Forgetting Interpret the evidence carefully. A validation–test gap alone cannot diagnose overfitting: sampling variation and selection on validation can also produce one. Examine training and held-out learning curves, and reserve a fresh final test after any further model selection. The forgetting measure from Note 8.1 tells a clear story: full fine-tuning raised the word-guessing loss from 3.381 to 4.07, while LoRA, even merged, raised it only to 3.461, and with the adapter switched off it is unchanged. For this application we don't need word-guessing, so forgetting doesn't count against either model here. In applications where the adapted model must keep general abilities, it would weigh heavily in LoRA's favour. Check yourself. 1. Why is a validation–test gap expected for every method that chose settings on validation, and when should a gap worry you? Worked answer Choosing settings or checkpoints on validation picks whichever option was luckiest there, so part of the validation score is that luck, and it doesn't carry over to test. A small drop is therefore normal. A gap should worry you when it's much larger than the run-to-run variation you'd expect (here about two points), or when it's large for one method but not others evaluated the same way. That suggests the method was tuned to quirks of the validation set, or that something leaked.

title: Comparing Across the Ladder: Performance, Trainable Parameters, Time, Memory
text: 6.1 The whole ladder Here is every method with what it used and what it cost. Training times were measured in each note on this machine and printed with units; compare them relative to each other, since they vary between machines and runs. The costs span orders of magnitude: - TF-IDF trains tens or hundreds of thousands of word weights in seconds. - The frozen encoder trains 769 weights after one feature pass. - LoRA trains 739,586 parameters, full fine-tuning all 66,955,010. Their estimated training memory is 280 MB and 1071 MB. - The SST-2 model trains nothing on IMDb. Note, though, that it isn't free in an absolute sense: someone else fine-tuned it on a large labelled dataset, and we inherit that work. 6.2 Is anything better than the best cheap baseline? The strongest method using no more than 1,000 IMDb labels is the SST-2 model off the shelf. We compare everything with it on the same test reviews: Every 1,000-label method is significantly worse than the off-the-shelf model: - full fine-tuning: 50 against 89 reviews, p = 0.0012; - LoRA: 43 against 82, p = 0.00062; - the frozen encoder and TF-IDF with 1,000 labels likewise. Only TF-IDF trained on all 22,404 labels beats it (96 against 56, p = 0.0015). The picture in one chart: The chart makes the lesson hard to miss. Training more parameters on the same 1,000 labels didn't buy accuracy: the frozen encoder (769 parameters), LoRA (739,586) and full fine-tuning (66,955,010) all land at about the same height. The two winners got their advantage from more labelled data: the SST-2 model indirectly, through someone else's large dataset, and TF-IDF directly, from all 22,404 IMDb labels. Check yourself. 1. A colleague concludes "fine-tuning doesn't work for sentiment analysis". What's wrong with that conclusion, given what was and wasn't varied here? Worked answer It generalises far beyond what was tested. We fine-tuned one small model, on only 1,000 labels, for one epoch, with 128 tokens of each review and untuned learning rates, on a CPU. The comparison showed that, in this setup, fine-tuning didn't beat a model already fine-tuned on much more sentiment data, or TF-IDF with all labels. With more labels, longer inputs or a better-tuned recipe, the result could change. The correct conclusion is limited to the conditions tested, which is exactly what the decision record's limitations say.

title: Reproducibility and Experiment Tracking
text: 7.1 How much do results vary? Every adapted model here comes from a single training run. How much might a result change with a different random draw? We can't afford to retrain the Transformers many times on a CPU, but we can measure the variation for the cheapest rung: TF-IDF trained on five different random sets of 1,000 training reviews, scored on the same validation reviews. Validation accuracy ranges from 0.840 to 0.859 across the five draws, about two points, purely from which 1,000 reviews were labelled. Fine-tuning runs also vary with initialisation, shuffling and dropout. So differences of one or two points between single runs, like LoRA's 0.880 against full fine-tuning's 0.860 on validation, shouldn't be read as real without repeated runs or a paired test. The paired test said there was no difference on test (Note 8.5). 7.2 Tracking experiments Each note saved its settings, data fingerprints, costs and results to a file. Collecting them into one table, and saving it, is the beginning of experiment tracking: a permanent, comparable record of every run. Tools such as MLflow and Weights & Biases do this at scale, but the principle is the same. The table lists every method with its note, settings, validation and test accuracy, and is saved as results/experiments.csv, alongside the environment (Python 3.12.15, PyTorch 2.14.1, Transformers 5.20.1, PEFT 0.21.2). With the fixed split, the fingerprints and the pinned versions in requirements.txt, anyone can rerun these notes and check the numbers. Key terms - Run-to-run variation: differences in results caused by randomness in data sampling, initialisation and training order. - Experiment tracking: recording each run's settings, data, code versions and results so that runs can be compared and reproduced.

title: The Keep-or-Reject Decision
text: A decision should follow rules written before looking at which model looks best. Otherwise it's easy to find reasons to keep the model you hoped would win. Ours, stated in the cell below before the decision is computed: - R1: an adapted model must beat the strongest baseline that uses no more labels, on the same test reviews, with sign-test p < 0.05. - R2: it must fit the deployment budget (CPU inference, one model per task). All candidates do. - R3: it must not damage abilities we still need. Word-guessing isn't needed here. Both adapted models fail R1: each is significantly worse than the off-the-shelf SST-2 model, not better. The decision is to reject both and, under a 1,000-label budget, use the SST-2 model as it is. If all 22,404 labels can be used, TF-IDF with all labels is better still. Rejecting a model you spent effort on is not a failed project. It's the evaluation doing its job. The experiments answered a real question ("does adapting DistilBERT on 1,000 IMDb labels beat what we can get for free?") with a clear, defensible "no, not in this setup". And the error analysis showed what might change the answer.

title: Documenting Findings, Limitations and Next Steps
text: The record states the question, the exact data (by fingerprint), every method's test accuracy, the decision with its alternative, the limitations that bound the conclusion, and next steps that could change it: - Limitations: a single run per adapted model; only 1,000 reviews, one epoch and 128 tokens; a CPU-sized experiment with learning rates not tuned on validation. - Next steps: - more labels, the clearest lever in our results; - longer inputs, since every 128-token method lost accuracy on long reviews; - repeated runs before claiming small differences; - a fresh test sample for any new winner, since this one has now been used to make a decision. A reader of this record in six months can see what was concluded, how much to trust it, and what to try next. Common mistake: writing up only the winning number. A useful record includes what was compared, on which data, what was rejected and why, what the conclusion depends on, and what would change it.
